T2-0001.e: Literally 'count and calculate'; at a store or restaurant it means paying.
T2-0001.t: At a restaurant, say "계산해 주세요" for "Check, please."

T2-0002.ex: 계산대 앞에 사람이 많이 서 있어요.
T2-0002.x: Lots of people are standing in front of the checkout counter.
T2-0002.e: Literally 'calculating stand': the counter where you pay.

T2-0004.ex: 이 신발을 큰 사이즈로 교환하고 싶어요.
T2-0004.x: I'd like to exchange these shoes for a bigger size.
T2-0004.t: Use N을/를 N(으)로 교환하다: "exchange A for B." In casual speech, 바꾸다 is more common.

T2-0005.e: Literally 'buy in', bringing goods in by buying.
T2-0005.t: More formal than 사다; you'll see it in stores, ads and writing. Pronounced [구이파다].

T2-0006.m: to bring down (a price), to haggle; to peel; to cut, to trim
T2-0006.x: I got the price down a little at the market yesterday.
T2-0006.e: The core idea is shaving something off: 사과를 깎다 'peel an apple', 머리를 깎다 'cut hair'.
T2-0006.t: At a traditional market, "좀 깎아 주세요" means "Could you give me a discount?"

T2-0007.x: Students can get a 10 percent discount.
T2-0007.e: Literally 'cut and pull' the price down.
T2-0007.t: Pronounced [하린]. Use 할인을 받다 for "get a discount" and 할인해 주다 for "give a discount."

T2-0008.x: The department store is having a sale this weekend.
T2-0008.t: 세일 is a store-wide sale event; 할인 is any discount, like a student discount.

T2-0009.ex: 이 박물관은 입장료가 하루 종일 무료예요.
T2-0009.x: Admission to this museum is free all day.
T2-0009.t: 무료 is the neutral word on signs and menus; 공짜 is the casual spoken word.

T2-0010.x: The shop gave me this coffee for free.
T2-0010.e: 'Empty' plus the suffix -짜: something you get for nothing.
T2-0010.t: Casual; use 공짜로 for "for free." In formal contexts and on signs, use 무료.

T2-0011.m: to pay; to put out, to hand in
T2-0011.e: Related to 나다 'come out': the basic idea is making something come out, like money.
T2-0011.t: "제가 낼게요" ("I'll pay") and "제가 살게요" ("It's my treat") are both common when picking up a bill.

T2-0012.x: The convenience store clerk gave me the wrong change.
T2-0012.e: From 거스르다 'to give back change' plus 돈 'money'.
T2-0012.t: In everyday speech, 잔돈 is often used for change too: "잔돈 여기 있어요."

T2-0013.x: Sorry, I don't have any small change right now.
T2-0013.e: 잔- 'small, fine' (as in 잔소리 'nagging') plus 돈 'money'.

T2-0014.x: I have a lot of coins in my pocket.

T2-0015.x: Can I pay by credit card here?
T2-0015.t: People usually just say 카드: "카드로 할게요" means "I'll pay by card."

T2-0016.x: You can't get a refund without a receipt.
T2-0016.t: Customers say 환불을 받다 ("get a refund"); stores say 환불해 드릴게요 ("We'll refund you").

T2-0017.ex: 이 바지 더 큰 사이즈 있어요?
T2-0017.x: Do you have these pants in a bigger size?
T2-0017.e: From English 'size'; used mainly for clothes and shoes.

T2-0018.x: These two bags are about the same size.
T2-0018.e: 크다 'big' plus the noun suffix -기: literally 'bigness'.
T2-0018.t: 크기 is general size of any object; for clothing sizes, Koreans usually say 사이즈.

T2-0019.x: I asked the clerk where the restroom was.

T2-0020.ex: 이 회사에는 직원이 백 명쯤 있어요.
T2-0020.x: This company has about a hundred employees.
T2-0020.t: 직원 is any employee or staff member; 점원 is specifically a clerk in a shop.

T2-0021.x: Last month's electric bill was high.
T2-0021.t: Use 요금 for services like buses, phones and utilities; use 가격 for the price of goods.

T2-0022.x: I get an allowance from my parents every month.
T2-0022.e: 용 'use' plus native 돈 'money': money for personal use.
T2-0022.t: Adult children also give 용돈 to parents: 부모님께 용돈을 드리다. Pronounced [용똔].

T2-0023.x: When I get paid, I save a little.

T2-0024.x: I save half of my salary every month.

T2-0025.x: I exchanged money at the bank before the trip.
T2-0025.t: Use N을/를 N(으)로 환전하다: 달러를 원으로 환전하다 = "exchange dollars for won."

T2-0026.x: The convenience store clerk asked if I needed a bag.
T2-0026.t: Cashiers often ask "봉투 필요하세요?" ("Do you need a bag?"); in Korea bags usually cost extra.

T2-0027.x: This store does gift wrapping for free.
T2-0027.t: At a restaurant or café, 포장이요 means "To go, please"; eating in is 먹고 갈게요.

T2-0028.m: to wrap, to pack; to get (food) to go
T2-0028.x: Please pack up the leftover food for me.

T2-0029.e: Literally 'hand out until it reaches' the customer.
T2-0029.t: 배달 is used for food and local delivery; packages sent by courier are 택배.

T2-0030.ex: 피자 한 판을 집으로 배달해 주세요.
T2-0030.x: Please deliver one pizza to my house.
T2-0030.e: Literally 'hand out until it reaches' the customer.
T2-0030.t: To order delivery food, Koreans often say 시켜 먹다: "치킨 시켜 먹을까요?"

T2-0031.x: You can order over there at the counter.
T2-0031.e: Literally 'note down in writing': writing down what the customer wants.
T2-0031.t: Servers ask "주문하시겠어요?", which means "Are you ready to order?"

T2-0032.x: This phone is secondhand, but it's as clean as a new one.
T2-0032.e: 새 'new' plus 것 'thing', written as one word.

T2-0033.m: to suit, to look good on; to go well with; to get along with
T2-0033.x: That dress really looks good on you.
T2-0033.t: "잘 어울려요!" is the go-to compliment when someone tries on clothes.

T2-0034.m: to fit; to be right, to be correct
T2-0034.ex: 이 바지는 저한테 사이즈가 딱 맞아요.
T2-0034.e: Homonym warning: another 맞다 means 'to get hit', as in 비를 맞다 'get rained on'.
T2-0034.t: "맞아요!" means "That's right!" The dictionary form 맞다 is pronounced [맏따].

T2-0035.x: I bought new furniture for my new place.

T2-0036.x: I bought cosmetics in Myeongdong to give my friend.
T2-0036.e: 화장 'makeup' plus -품 'goods'; -품 = product: 화장품, 식품, 제품.

T2-0037.x: I bought a necklace for my mother's birthday.
T2-0037.e: 목 'neck' plus 걸다 'to hang' plus -이: 'thing hung on the neck'.
T2-0037.t: Wear a necklace with 하다 or 걸다: 목걸이를 했어요.

T2-0038.x: She's wearing a pretty ring on her left hand.
T2-0038.t: Rings are worn with 끼다, not 입다: 반지를 끼다 "put on a ring"; take off is 빼다.

T2-0039.x: I bought milk at the supermarket near my house.
T2-0039.e: From English 'supermarket'; usually shortened to 슈퍼, often a small neighborhood store.

T2-0040.forms: 장(을) 보다: 장을 봐요 · 장 봤어요 · 장 보러 가요
T2-0040.m: to go grocery shopping, to do the shopping
T2-0040.x: I do my grocery shopping at the supermarket every weekend.
T2-0040.e: 장 means 'market' (as in 시장), so it's literally 'see the market'.
T2-0040.t: Use 장 보다 for food and daily necessities; for clothes or fun shopping, say 쇼핑하다.

T2-0041.x: Tap your transit card when you get on the bus.
T2-0041.t: "Tap" your card is 찍다 or 대다; topping it up is 충전하다.

T2-0042.ex: 우리 집에서 지하철역까지 걸어서 오 분 걸려요.
T2-0042.x: It's a five-minute walk from my house to the subway station.
T2-0042.t: Pronounced [지하철력]: an ㄴ sound is added before 역 and then becomes ㄹ after ㄹ.

T2-0043.ex: 내일 아침에 기차역에서 친구를 만나기로 했어요.
T2-0043.x: I'm meeting a friend at the train station tomorrow morning.
T2-0043.e: 기차 is literally 'steam vehicle', from the days of steam trains.

T2-0044.ex: 고속버스 터미널에서 부산 가는 버스를 탔어요.
T2-0044.x: I took a bus to Busan from the express bus terminal.
T2-0044.e: From English 'terminal'; on its own it usually means a bus terminal.

T2-0045.ex: 서울에서 부산까지 고속버스로 네 시간쯤 걸려요.
T2-0045.x: It takes about four hours from Seoul to Busan by express bus.

T2-0046.ex: 저는 학교에 갈 때 시내버스를 타요.
T2-0046.x: I take the city bus to school.
T2-0046.e: 시내 'inside the city, downtown' plus English 'bus'.

T2-0047.ex: 제 동생은 오토바이를 타고 학교에 가요.
T2-0047.x: My younger brother rides a motorcycle to school.
T2-0047.e: Konglish via Japanese, from 'auto' plus 'bi(cycle)'; English speakers say 'motorcycle'.

T2-0048.x: Do you happen to know the teacher's phone number?
T2-0048.e: Literally 'turn number', like a number that marks your turn.
T2-0048.t: For bus lines and exits, use 번: 6번 버스 "bus number 6," 3번 출구 "exit 3."

T2-0049.x: Let's meet in front of exit 3 of the subway station.
T2-0049.e: Literally 'go-out mouth'; -구 = opening: 출구, 입구, 비상구.

T2-0050.x: Please show your ticket at the museum entrance.

T2-0051.ex: 기차 좌석은 미리 예약하는 게 좋아요.
T2-0051.x: It's a good idea to reserve train seats in advance.
T2-0051.t: 좌석 appears on tickets and signs; in everyday speech, people usually say 자리.

T2-0052.ex: 삼십 분 안에 환승을 하면 요금이 무료예요.
T2-0052.x: If you transfer within thirty minutes, it's free.
T2-0052.t: In speech, 갈아타다 is more common; 환승 is what you hear in announcements and see on signs.

T2-0053.m: to be blocked, to be clogged; to be jammed (traffic)
T2-0053.x: Traffic is really bad at rush hour.
T2-0053.t: Pronounced [마키다]: ㄱ and ㅎ merge into ㅋ.

T2-0054.forms: 길이 막혀요 · 길이 막혔어요 · 길이 막힐 거예요
T2-0054.m: there's a traffic jam, the roads are congested
T2-0054.x: I was late for the meeting because of traffic this morning.
T2-0054.t: "길이 막혀서 늦었어요" is the classic Korean excuse for being late.

T2-0055.x: There was a traffic accident in front of the school yesterday.

T2-0056.x: There was a big accident on the highway last night.
T2-0056.e: Homonym warning: a different 사고 means 'thinking'; context makes it clear.
T2-0056.t: Accidents "happen" with 나다, not 하다: 사고가 났어요.

T2-0057.forms: 사고가 나요 · 사고가 났어요 · 사고가 날 뻔했어요
T2-0057.m: an accident happens, to have an accident
T2-0057.ex: 눈이 많이 와서 도로에서 사고가 났어요.
T2-0057.x: It snowed a lot, so there was an accident on the road.
T2-0057.e: Literally 'an accident comes out'; 나다 is used for events like 불이 나다 'a fire breaks out'.

T2-0058.ex: 빨간 신호일 때는 꼭 멈춰야 해요.
T2-0058.x: You must stop when the light is red.
T2-0058.t: 신호등 is the traffic light itself; 신호 is the signal it shows: 신호가 바뀌었어요.

T2-0059.ex: 길을 건널 때는 꼭 횡단보도로 건너세요.
T2-0059.x: Always use the crosswalk when you cross the street.

T2-0060.ex: 저기 다음 사거리에서 오른쪽으로 돌아 주세요.
T2-0060.x: Please turn right at the next intersection up there.
T2-0060.e: 사 'four' plus native 거리 'street': where four streets meet.
T2-0060.t: Common in directions: 사거리에서 왼쪽으로 가세요 "Go left at the intersection."

T2-0061.ex: 이 골목 안에 맛있는 식당이 있어요.
T2-0061.x: There's a great restaurant down this alley.
T2-0061.e: Often seen as 골목길 'alley road' and 먹자골목 'food alley'.

T2-0062.x: The roads are very slippery because of the snow.
T2-0062.t: 도로 is a road for vehicles and sounds more formal; 길 is the everyday word for road or way.

T2-0063.x: The highways are always really jammed during the holidays.

T2-0064.ex: 이 건물 앞에서는 주차를 할 수 없어요.
T2-0064.x: You can't park in front of this building.

T2-0065.x: Excuse me, where can I park my car?

T2-0066.x: There's a big parking garage under the department store.
T2-0066.e: -장 = place for an activity: 주차장, 운동장, 시장.

T2-0067.m: to stop (a vehicle), to pull over; to stand (something) up; to make (a plan)
T2-0067.ex: 기사님, 저기 은행 앞에서 세워 주세요.
T2-0067.x: Driver, please pull over in front of the bank up there.
T2-0067.e: Causative of 서다 'to stand, to stop': make something stand or stop.
T2-0067.t: In a taxi, say "여기서 세워 주세요" ("Please stop here").

T2-0068.x: When the light changes, cross the street at the crosswalk.
T2-0068.e: 건너다 'to cross' plus 가다 'to go': cross over, away from the speaker.

T2-0069.m: to pass, to go past; (of time) to pass
T2-0069.ex: 벌써 약속 시간이 십 분이나 지났어요.
T2-0069.x: It's already ten minutes past our meeting time.
T2-0069.t: Its modifier gives 지난 'last': 지난주 "last week," 지난달 "last month."

T2-0070.m: to pass by, to go past; (of time) to go by
T2-0070.x: The bus just went right past the stop.

T2-0071.forms: 돌아요 · 돌았어요 · 돌 거예요 · 도세요 (ㄹ drops)
T2-0071.m: to turn; to go around, to spin
T2-0071.x: Turn left in front of the bank over there.
T2-0071.t: The ㄹ drops before -세요: say 도세요, not 돌으세요.
rel: to go back, to go around

T2-0072.forms: 쭉 가세요 · 쭉 가다가 왼쪽으로 · 쭉 살았어요
T2-0072.ex: 이 길로 쭉 가면 지하철역이 나와요.
T2-0072.x: If you go straight down this road, you'll come to the subway station.
T2-0072.e: A sound-and-feel word suggesting one long, unbroken stretch.
T2-0072.t: It also means "the whole time": 어릴 때부터 쭉 서울에서 살았어요.

T2-0073.ex: 이 길로 똑바로 가면 학교가 있어요.
T2-0073.x: If you go straight along this road, you'll find the school.

T2-0074.x: Which way do I go for City Hall?

T2-0075.x: The sun rises in the east every morning.
T2-0075.t: Koreans list compass points as 동서남북, "east-west-south-north," not north-south-east-west.

T2-0076.x: In the evening, the sun sets in the west.

T2-0077.x: Jeju Island is at the very south of Korea.

T2-0078.x: Seoul is much farther north than Busan.
T2-0078.t: The same 북 and 남 give 북한 "North Korea" and 남한 "South Korea."

T2-0079.ex: 제가 사는 아파트는 학교 맞은편에 있어요.
T2-0079.x: The apartment I live in is across from the school.
T2-0079.e: 맞은 (facing, from 맞다) + 편 (side): the side facing you.
rel: the other side, across the way

T2-0080.m: to walk (to), to go on foot
T2-0080.x: The weather was nice, so I walked to work today.
T2-0080.e: 걷다 (to walk) + 가다 (to go): literally 'walk and go.'

T2-0081.m: driver (of a taxi or bus), chauffeur
T2-0081.ex: 택시 기사님께 공항까지 가 달라고 했어요.
T2-0081.x: I asked the taxi driver to take me to the airport.
T2-0081.e: Literally 'skilled person'; short for 운전기사, a professional driver.
T2-0081.t: Add -님 when talking to a driver politely: 기사님, 여기서 세워 주세요.

T2-0082.x: I bought a plane ticket to go home over vacation.

T2-0083.ex: 서울로 가는 기차의 출발 시간은 오후 세 시예요.
T2-0083.x: The departure time for the train to Seoul is 3 p.m.

T2-0084.ex: 비행기 도착 시간이 한 시간 늦어졌어요.
T2-0084.x: The plane's arrival time was delayed by an hour.
T2-0084.t: 도착했어요 is pronounced [도차캐써요]: ㄱ plus ㅎ becomes ㅋ.

T2-0085.m: to miss (a bus, a chance), to lose hold of
T2-0085.ex: 아침에 늦게 일어나서 학교 버스를 놓쳤어요.
T2-0085.x: I woke up late this morning and missed the school bus.
T2-0085.e: From 놓다 (to let go) plus an intensifying -치-: to let something slip away.
rel: to put down, to let go

T2-0086.m: to come down, to come downstairs
T2-0086.x: My legs hurt when I came down the mountain.
T2-0086.e: 내리다 (to go down) + 오다 (to come): come down toward the speaker.
rel: to get off, to go down

T2-0087.m: to come up, to come upstairs; to come up to Seoul
T2-0087.x: Take the elevator up to the third floor now.
T2-0087.e: 오르다 (to climb) + 오다 (to come): come up toward the speaker.
T2-0087.t: Koreans say 서울에 올라오다 for traveling to Seoul from anywhere else, no matter the direction on a map.

T2-0088.forms: 들러요 · 들렀어요 · 들를 거예요 · 들르세요 (ㅡ drops)
T2-0088.m: to stop by, to drop in
T2-0088.ex: 집에 가는 길에 편의점에 잠깐 들렀어요.
T2-0088.x: I stopped by the convenience store briefly on my way home.
T2-0088.e: Don't mix it up with 들리다 (to be heard), which sounds similar.
T2-0088.t: It's 들러요, not 들려요: 들르다 just drops ㅡ and is not a 르 irregular.

T2-0089.m: to take (a person or animal) along
T2-0089.x: I'm going to take the kids to the zoo this weekend.
T2-0089.e: 데리다 (to have someone with you) + 가다 (to go): take someone along.
T2-0089.t: Use 데려가다 for people and animals, 가져가다 for things; for elders say 모시고 가다.

T2-0090.x: Can I bring a friend to the party today?
T2-0090.e: 데리다 (to have someone with you) + 오다 (to come): bring someone here.

T2-0091.m: to give (someone) a ride, to pick up
T2-0091.ex: 아빠가 저를 차에 태워서 학교에 데려다주셨어요.
T2-0091.x: My dad gave me a ride to school in his car.
T2-0091.e: Causative of 타다 (to ride): 'make someone ride.' A separate 태우다 means 'to burn.'

T2-0092.forms: 가까이 오다 · 가까이 살다; 가까이에 (near, as a place)
T2-0092.ex: 우리 집 가까이에 큰 공원이 있어요.
T2-0092.x: There's a big park near my house.
T2-0092.t: Before an amount it means 'nearly': 두 시간 가까이 기다렸어요 = I waited nearly two hours.

T2-0093.forms: 멀리 가다 · 멀리 살다; 멀리서 (from far away)
T2-0093.ex: 친구가 멀리 이사 가서 자주 못 만나요.
T2-0093.x: My friend moved far away, so I can't see her often.

T2-0094.x: It's about three kilometers from my house to school.
T2-0094.e: From English 'kilometer.' In speech, 킬로 alone can mean kilometers or kilograms.
T2-0094.t: Use Sino-Korean numbers with it: 삼 킬로미터, not 세 킬로미터.

T2-0095.x: My chest suddenly hurt, so I went to the hospital.
T2-0095.e: Also the seat of feelings: 가슴이 아프다 can mean 'heartbroken.'

T2-0096.ex: 하루 종일 컴퓨터를 해서 등이 아파요.
T2-0096.x: I've been on the computer all day, so my back hurts.
T2-0096.e: Homonym warning: 등 also means 'lamp' and 'etc.' (and so on).
T2-0096.t: For lower-back pain Koreans usually say 허리가 아파요, not 등이 아파요.

T2-0097.ex: 어제 등산을 많이 해서 무릎이 아파요.
T2-0097.x: I hiked a lot yesterday, so my knees hurt.
T2-0097.e: Also means 'lap': 무릎에 앉다 = to sit on someone's lap.
T2-0097.t: Alone it sounds like [무릅], but the ㅍ comes back before a vowel: 무릎이 [무르피].

T2-0098.ex: 새로 산 신발이 작아서 발가락이 아파요.
T2-0098.x: My new shoes are small, so my toes hurt.
T2-0098.e: 발 (foot) + 가락 (a long thin strand); compare 손가락, finger.

T2-0099.ex: 단 음식을 많이 먹어서 이가 아파요.
T2-0099.x: I ate a lot of sweets, so my tooth hurts.
T2-0099.e: Homonym warning: 이 also means 'this' and 'two'; 치아 is the formal word for tooth.
T2-0099.t: In compounds it often becomes 니: 앞니 (front tooth), 어금니 (molar).

T2-0100.ex: 뜨거운 국을 급하게 먹어서 혀가 아파요.
T2-0100.x: I ate hot soup too fast, so my tongue hurts.

T2-0101.ex: 겨울에는 입술이 자주 말라서 립밤을 발라요.
T2-0101.x: In winter my lips often get dry, so I put on lip balm.
T2-0101.t: Pronounced [입쑬]: the ㅅ becomes tense after ㅂ.

T2-0102.ex: 감기에 걸려서 오늘 목소리가 좀 이상해요.
T2-0102.x: I caught a cold, so my voice sounds a bit strange today.
T2-0102.t: Pronounced [목쏘리]: the ㅅ becomes tense after ㄱ.

T2-0103.ex: 제 언니는 피부가 하얗고 정말 좋아요.
T2-0103.x: My older sister has fair, really nice skin.

T2-0104.x: I fell on the street and my knee was bleeding.
T2-0104.t: Say 피가 나다 for bleeding: 코피가 나요 = My nose is bleeding.

T2-0105.ex: 어제 찬 음식을 너무 많이 먹어서 배탈이 났어요.
T2-0105.x: I ate too much cold food yesterday and got an upset stomach.
T2-0105.t: It almost always appears as 배탈이 나다, 'to get an upset stomach.'

T2-0106.forms: 배탈이 났어요 (I have an upset stomach) · 배탈이 날 것 같아요 (I think my stomach will act up)
T2-0106.ex: 길에서 산 음식을 먹고 배탈이 났어요.
T2-0106.x: I ate food I bought on the street and got an upset stomach.
T2-0106.t: Use the past tense for how you feel now: 배탈이 났어요 means you have an upset stomach.

T2-0107.ex: 두통이 심해서 오늘 회사에 못 갔어요.
T2-0107.x: My headache was bad, so I couldn't go to work today.
T2-0107.e: Literally 'head pain'; -통 = pain: 두통, 복통, 치통.

T2-0108.forms: 열이 나요 · 열이 났어요; 열이 많이 나다 (to have a high fever)
T2-0108.m: to have a fever, to run a temperature
T2-0108.ex: 아이가 밤새 열이 나서 병원에 갔어요.
T2-0108.x: My child had a fever all night, so we went to the hospital.

T2-0109.ex: 감기 때문에 밤에 기침이 계속 나요.
T2-0109.x: Because of my cold, I keep coughing at night.
T2-0109.e: Used with 나다 or 하다: 기침이 나다 (a cough comes), 기침을 하다 (to cough).

T2-0110.ex: 그 학생은 수업 시간에 계속 기침했어요.
T2-0110.x: That student kept coughing during class.

T2-0111.ex: 감기에 걸려서 아침부터 콧물이 계속 나요.
T2-0111.x: I caught a cold, and my nose has been running since morning.
T2-0111.e: 코 (nose) + 물 (water), joined by a linking ㅅ: 'nose water.'
T2-0111.t: Pronounced [콘물]: the linking ㅅ turns into ㄴ before ㅁ.

T2-0112.forms: 감기에 걸렸어요 (I have a cold) · 감기에 걸리지 마세요 (Don't catch a cold)
T2-0112.x: The weather suddenly got cold, and I caught a cold.
T2-0112.e: 걸리다 means 'to be caught' or 'hooked': you get caught by a cold.
T2-0112.t: Use the past tense for a cold you have now: 감기에 걸렸어요 = I have a cold.

T2-0113.ex: 겨울이 되기 전에 독감 예방 주사를 맞았어요.
T2-0113.x: I got a flu shot before winter came.
T2-0113.e: Literally 'poisonous cold': a really bad cold, the flu.

T2-0114.ex: 이가 아파서 내일 치과에 가야 해요.
T2-0114.x: My tooth hurts, so I have to go to the dentist tomorrow.
T2-0114.e: Literally 'tooth department'; -과 = medical department: 치과, 안과, 내과.

T2-0115.ex: 병원에 감기 환자가 많아서 오래 기다렸어요.
T2-0115.x: There were a lot of patients with colds at the hospital, so I waited a long time.
T2-0115.e: Literally 'illness person'; -자 = person: 환자, 과학자, 운전자.

T2-0116.x: The child was scared of the shot and cried a lot.
T2-0116.e: Literally 'pour and shoot': liquid shot into the body.
T2-0116.t: Careful: 주사가 있다 can mean 'gets nasty when drunk', which is a different word.

T2-0117.forms: 주사를 맞았어요 (I got a shot) · 주사를 놓다 (to give a shot)
T2-0117.m: to get a shot, to get an injection
T2-0117.ex: 어제 병원에서 감기 때문에 주사를 맞았어요.
T2-0117.x: I got a shot at the hospital yesterday for my cold.
T2-0117.e: 맞다 here means 'to receive (be hit by)'; the nurse 놓다, 'puts in', the shot.

T2-0118.ex: 약사가 이 약을 하루에 세 번 먹으라고 했어요.
T2-0118.x: The pharmacist told me to take this medicine three times a day.

T2-0119.ex: 감기약을 먹으면 졸려서 운전하면 안 돼요.
T2-0119.x: Cold medicine makes you sleepy, so you shouldn't drive.
T2-0119.t: Koreans 'eat' medicine: 약을 먹다 is the normal way to say 'take medicine.'

T2-0120.ex: 자전거를 타다가 넘어져서 다리에 상처가 났어요.
T2-0120.x: I fell off my bike and got a cut on my leg.
T2-0120.t: 상처를 받다 means 'to have your feelings hurt,' and 상처를 주다 means 'to hurt someone.'

T2-0121.forms: 나아요 · 나았어요 · 나을 거예요 · 나으세요 (ㅅ irregular)
T2-0121.m: to get better, to recover, to heal
T2-0121.ex: 약을 먹고 푹 쉬었더니 감기가 다 나았어요.
T2-0121.x: I took medicine and got plenty of rest, and now my cold is all better.
T2-0121.e: Homonym: the adjective 낫다 means 'to be better (than)' and conjugates the same way.
T2-0121.t: The classic get-well wish is 빨리 나으세요! = Get well soon!

T2-0122.x: I started dieting before summer came.
T2-0122.e: From English 'diet'; in Korean it almost always means dieting to lose weight.

T2-0123.ex: 요즘 운동을 안 해서 살이 많이 쪘어요.
T2-0123.x: I haven't been exercising lately, so I've gained a lot of weight.
T2-0123.e: Homonym: 살 also counts age (다섯 살, five years old).

T2-0124.forms: 살이 쪘어요 (I've gained weight) · 살이 빠졌어요 (I've lost weight)
T2-0124.m: to gain weight, to put on weight
T2-0124.ex: 방학 동안 많이 먹어서 살이 쪘어요.
T2-0124.x: I ate a lot over vacation and gained weight.
T2-0124.t: Some Koreans casually say 살 쪘네! to friends, but as a learner it's safer not to comment on weight.

T2-0125.m: to take out, to remove, to leave out; to lose (weight); to subtract
T2-0125.x: I lost 5 kilos for my health.
T2-0125.e: Opposite of 넣다 (to put in); 빠지다 is its 'come out by itself' partner.
T2-0125.t: Handy when ordering food: 오이 빼 주세요 = Please leave out the cucumber.
rel: to fall out, to be lost

T2-0126.ex: 저는 매일 아침에 일어나서 몸무게를 재요.
T2-0126.x: I weigh myself every morning when I get up.
T2-0126.e: 몸 (body) + 무게 (weight); 무게 is related to 무겁다 (heavy).

T2-0127.ex: 아침을 못 먹어서 힘이 하나도 없어요.
T2-0127.x: I couldn't eat breakfast, so I have no energy at all.
T2-0127.e: The base of 힘들다 (hard, tiring) and 힘내다 (to cheer up).
T2-0127.t: 힘내세요! is the classic way to say 'Hang in there!' or 'You can do it!'
rel: to cheer up, to keep going

T2-0128.ex: 회사 일이 많아서 요즘 정말 힘들어요.
T2-0128.x: I have a lot of work these days, so things are really tough.
T2-0128.e: 힘 (strength) + 들다 (to take, to be needed): 'takes a lot of strength.'
T2-0128.t: 힘들다 is about effort or exhaustion; 어렵다 is about something being hard to understand or solve.

T2-0129.m: to be sleepy, to feel drowsy
T2-0129.ex: 어젯밤에 늦게 자서 지금 너무 졸려요.
T2-0129.x: I went to bed late last night, so I'm really sleepy now.
T2-0129.e: From 졸다 (to doze): feeling like you'll nod off.

T2-0130.forms: 졸아요 · 졸았어요 · 졸 거예요 · 조는 (+noun) (ㄹ drops)
T2-0130.x: I dozed off in class and got scolded by the teacher.
T2-0130.e: The root of 졸리다 (sleepy) and 졸음 (drowsiness).
T2-0130.t: Homonym: 졸다 also means 'to boil down,' as when soup reduces on the stove.

T2-0131.m: to wake up; to sober up
T2-0131.x: It was noisy outside, so I woke up at dawn.
T2-0131.e: Homonym warning: another 깨다 means 'to break' (glass, eggs).
T2-0131.t: 깨다 is waking; 일어나다 is getting up, so you can 깨다 and still stay in bed.

T2-0132.ex: 내일 아침 일곱 시에 저 좀 깨워 주세요.
T2-0132.x: Please wake me up at seven tomorrow morning.
T2-0132.e: Causative of 깨다 (to wake): 'make someone wake.'

T2-0133.forms: 푹 자다 (sleep soundly) · 푹 쉬다 (rest well) · 푹 익히다 (cook thoroughly)
T2-0133.ex: 이번 주말에는 집에서 푹 쉬고 싶어요.
T2-0133.x: I want to get some good rest at home this weekend.
T2-0133.e: A sound-symbolic word that suggests sinking deep into something.
T2-0133.t: 푹 쉬세요 is a warm way to tell a sick or tired person 'Get plenty of rest.'

T2-0134.ex: 할머니는 입원 기간 동안 많이 좋아지셨어요.
T2-0134.x: My grandmother got much better during her hospital stay.
T2-0134.e: Literally 'entering the institution'; -원 = institution: 병원, 학원.

T2-0135.m: to be hospitalized, to be admitted to a hospital
T2-0135.ex: 아버지가 교통사고로 일주일 동안 병원에 입원하셨어요.
T2-0135.x: My father was in the hospital for a week after a car accident.

T2-0136.ex: 할아버지의 수술이 잘 끝나서 가족들이 기뻐했어요.
T2-0136.x: Grandpa's surgery went well, so the family was happy.
T2-0136.t: Patients 수술을 받다, 'receive surgery,' while doctors 수술하다, 'operate.'

T2-0137.x: I had a blood test at the hospital yesterday.
T2-0137.t: Homonym: 검사 also means 'prosecutor,' a different word with different hanja.

T2-0138.m: to be careful, to watch out
T2-0138.ex: 눈이 와서 길이 미끄러우니까 운전 조심하세요.
T2-0138.x: It snowed and the roads are slippery, so drive carefully.
T2-0138.e: Literally 'hold the heart': keep your mind in check.
T2-0138.t: 조심히 가세요 ('Get home safely') is a common, caring way to say goodbye.

T2-0139.ex: 밤에 혼자 산에 가는 것은 위험해요.
T2-0139.x: Going to the mountains alone at night is dangerous.

T2-0140.ex: 이 동네는 밤에도 안전해서 걱정 없어요.
T2-0140.x: This neighborhood is safe even at night, so there's nothing to worry about.

T2-0141.m: to get worse, to go bad
T2-0141.x: As the weather got colder, my cold got worse.
T2-0141.t: -아/어지다 turns adjectives into 'become' verbs: 나빠지다, 좋아지다, 추워지다.

T2-0142.m: to get better, to improve; to come to like
T2-0142.ex: 약을 먹고 나서 몸이 많이 좋아졌어요.
T2-0142.x: I feel much better after taking the medicine.

T2-0143.x: I fell while skiing and broke my leg.
T2-0143.e: Used for long, hard things like bones or pencils; glass and dishes use 깨지다.
T2-0143.t: Korean says 'my leg broke' (다리가 부러졌어요) where English says 'I broke my leg.'

T2-0144.ex: 한 시간 동안 운동을 해서 땀을 많이 흘렸어요.
T2-0144.x: I exercised for an hour and sweated a lot.

T2-0145.forms: 땀이 나요 · 땀이 났어요; 땀이 많이 나다 (to sweat a lot)
T2-0145.ex: 날씨가 너무 더워서 가만히 있어도 땀이 나요.
T2-0145.x: It's so hot that I sweat even sitting still.
T2-0145.e: Literally 'sweat comes out'; 나다 works the same way in 열이 나다 and 화가 나다.

T2-0146.ex: 아버지는 건강 때문에 담배를 끊기로 하셨어요.
T2-0146.x: My father decided to quit smoking for his health.
T2-0146.e: Probably from Portuguese 'tabaco', which reached Korea through Japan.

T2-0147.m: to smoke (a cigarette); to make (a fire) burn; to make (flowers) bloom
T2-0147.x: You're not allowed to smoke here.
T2-0147.e: Causative of 피다 (to bloom, to burn): 'make something bloom or burn.'
T2-0147.t: Standard Korean is 담배를 피우다; you'll hear 담배를 피다 in speech, but avoid it in writing.

T2-0148.m: to quit (smoking, drinking); to cut (off); to hang up (the phone)
T2-0148.x: My uncle completely quit smoking last year.
T2-0148.e: Covers cutting physical things and habits alike; 전화를 끊다 = to hang up.
T2-0148.t: Pronounced [끈타]; ending a call, 끊을게요 means 'I'll hang up now.'

T2-0149.ex: 그는 자기 감정을 잘 표현하지 않아요.
T2-0149.x: He doesn't really express his feelings.
T2-0149.t: 기분 is your mood right now; 감정 is the general word for emotions.

T2-0150.ex: 친구가 약속을 또 잊어버려서 화가 났어요.
T2-0150.x: My friend forgot our plans again, so I got angry.
T2-0150.e: Literally 'fire': anger as heat rising inside you.
T2-0150.t: It usually appears as 화가 나다 (to feel angry) or 화를 내다 (to show anger).

T2-0151.forms: 화가 났어요 (I'm angry) · 화가 많이 났어요 (I'm really angry)
T2-0151.m: to get angry, to be angry
T2-0151.ex: 동생이 말도 없이 제 옷을 입어서 화가 났어요.
T2-0151.x: My younger sibling wore my clothes without asking, so I got angry.
rel: to be in a bad mood

T2-0152.m: to get angry (at someone), to lose one's temper
T2-0152.x: My mom got angry because I came home late.
T2-0152.t: 화가 나다 is feeling angry; 화내다 is showing it, usually at someone: 저한테 화내지 마세요.

T2-0153.m: to be glad, to be happy (about), to rejoice
T2-0153.ex: 부모님이 제 합격 소식을 듣고 많이 기뻐하셨어요.
T2-0153.x: My parents were very happy to hear I'd passed.
T2-0153.t: Use -어하다 for other people's feelings: 저는 기뻐요, but 친구가 기뻐해요.

T2-0154.m: to be sad, to grieve, to mourn
T2-0154.x: The child was very sad when the puppy died.

T2-0155.ex: 가족과 함께 보내는 시간이 저에게는 가장 큰 행복이에요.
T2-0155.x: Time with my family is my greatest happiness.

T2-0156.ex: 시험 걱정 때문에 어젯밤에 잠을 못 잤어요.
T2-0156.x: I couldn't sleep last night because I was worried about the exam.
T2-0156.e: Becomes verbs easily: 걱정하다 (to worry), 걱정되다 (to feel worried).
T2-0156.t: Pronounced [걱쩡]; 걱정 마세요 is the everyday way to say 'Don't worry.'

T2-0157.forms: 걱정해요 · 걱정했어요 · 걱정할 거예요 · 걱정하지 마세요
T2-0157.x: My mom worries a lot about my health.
T2-0157.e: Drop 하다 to get the noun 걱정 'worry': 걱정이 많아요 = I have a lot of worries.
T2-0157.t: 걱정하지 마세요 'Don't worry' is one of the most useful phrases; casually, just say 걱정 마.

T2-0158.forms: 놀라요 · 놀랐어요 · 놀랄 거예요 · 놀라지 마세요
T2-0158.m: to be surprised, to be startled
T2-0158.x: Everyone was surprised when they saw the test results.
T2-0158.e: Often paired with 깜짝 'with a start': 깜짝 놀라다 = to jump in surprise.

T2-0159.ex: 그 영화가 어떻게 끝나는지 정말 궁금해요.
T2-0159.x: I'm really curious how that movie ends.
T2-0159.e: 궁금한 점, 'a point you're curious about,' is how Koreans often say 'a question'.
T2-0159.t: Teachers say 궁금한 거 있으면 물어보세요, 'If you're curious about anything, ask,' all the time.

T2-0160.ex: 제 친구는 영어를 잘해서 정말 부러워요.
T2-0160.x: My friend speaks English well, so I'm really jealous.
T2-0160.e: Add -어하다 to describe someone else's envy: 친구가 저를 부러워해요.
T2-0160.t: 부러워요! is a friendly 'I'm so jealous!'; bitter or romantic jealousy is 질투하다.

T2-0161.x: I feel shy about singing in front of people.
T2-0161.t: 부끄럽다 covers both shyness and shame; 창피하다 is a stronger, 'humiliated' kind of embarrassment.

T2-0162.ex: 말이 잘 안 통해서 너무 답답해요.
T2-0162.x: I can't get my point across, so it's really frustrating.
T2-0162.e: Works for a stuffy room and a stuffed-up, frustrated heart — think 'I can't breathe'.
T2-0162.t: Pronounced [답따파다]: the second ㄷ tenses, and ㅂ + ㅎ becomes ㅍ.

T2-0163.x: When you live alone abroad, you sometimes get lonely.
T2-0163.e: Probably built from 외- 'single, alone' (as in 외아들 'only son') + -롭다.

T2-0164.x: I really miss my parents back home.
T2-0164.e: Related to the old verb 그리다 'to long for'; the verb form is 그리워하다 'to miss'.
T2-0164.t: 보고 싶어요 is the everyday 'I miss you'; 그리워요 sounds deeper and more poetic.

T2-0165.x: I have high hopes for the new semester.
T2-0165.e: Literally 'expect and wait' — waiting with hope.
T2-0165.t: Don't confuse it with native 기대다 'to lean on': 벽에 기대요 = I lean against the wall.

T2-0166.m: to look forward to, to expect
T2-0166.x: I'm really looking forward to the weekend trip.
T2-0166.t: 기대돼요! 'I can't wait!' is the most natural way to show excitement about plans.

T2-0167.forms: 실망해요 · 실망했어요 · 실망할 거예요 · 실망하지 마세요
T2-0167.x: I was really disappointed when I saw my test results.
T2-0167.t: 'Disappointed in someone' uses 한테 or 에게: 너한테 실망했어 = I'm disappointed in you.

T2-0168.x: I had a fight with my friend yesterday, so I'm really upset.
T2-0168.e: Native 속 'inside, gut' + 'hurt': your insides feel wounded.

T2-0169.m: sorry (that something ends or is missed), a pity, regretful
T2-0169.x: It's such a shame the trip is already over.
T2-0169.t: 아쉽다 has no perfect English match: think 'what a pity' or 'I wish it had lasted longer'.

T2-0170.m: to be excited, to have a blast
T2-0170.x: The kids see the snow and run around excitedly.
T2-0170.e: 신 'high spirits' + 나다 'to come out': excitement bubbling out.

T2-0171.x: Korea's subway system is really fascinating.
T2-0171.t: Use 신기하다 for cool, surprising things, like 'Whoa, neat!', not for 'weird' in a bad sense.

T2-0172.x: These days I'm enjoying studying Korean.
T2-0172.e: Add 있다 or 없다: 재미있다 'fun', 재미없다 'boring'.
T2-0172.t: 재미있게 보내세요! 'Have fun!' is a friendly goodbye before a trip or weekend.

T2-0173.x: That class was so long that it was boring.
T2-0173.t: 지루하다 means something is tedious; 심심하다 means you're bored with nothing to do.

T2-0174.forms: 긴장해요 · 긴장했어요 · 긴장할 거예요 · 긴장하지 마세요
T2-0174.m: to be nervous, to be tense
T2-0174.ex: 면접 전에 너무 긴장해서 손이 떨렸어요.
T2-0174.x: Before the interview I was so nervous that my hands shook.
T2-0174.e: Literally 'tight and stretched', like a pulled string.

T2-0175.m: to tremble, to shake; to feel nervous
T2-0175.ex: 많은 사람 앞에서 발표할 때 목소리가 떨려요.
T2-0175.x: My voice shakes when I give a presentation in front of a lot of people.
T2-0175.e: Passive of 떨다 'to shake': 떨려요 = 'I'm shaky', i.e. nervous.

T2-0176.x: It's really comfortable when I sit on this sofa.

T2-0177.forms: N이/가 마음에 들어요 · 마음에 드세요? (ㄹ drops)
T2-0177.m: to like, to be pleased with
T2-0177.ex: 이 가방 색깔이 정말 마음에 들어요.
T2-0177.x: I really like the color of this bag.
T2-0177.e: Literally 'to enter the heart' — what you like gets into your heart.
T2-0177.t: The liked thing is the subject: 이 옷이 마음에 들어요, not 이 옷을.

T2-0178.x: It's raining, so going out feels like too much trouble.
T2-0178.e: Probably shrunk from 귀하지 않다 'not precious' — not worth the effort.
T2-0178.t: Pronounced [귀찬타], but 귀찮아요 sounds like [귀차나요] — the ㅎ goes silent before a vowel.

T2-0179.x: My younger sibling keeps getting cranky, so it's hard.
T2-0179.e: 짜증을 내다 = to show irritation; 짜증이 나다 = to feel irritated.

T2-0180.m: to be annoyed, to be irritated
T2-0180.x: The bus isn't coming, so I'm really annoyed.
T2-0180.e: 짜증 'irritation' + 나다 'to arise': irritation rises up in you.

T2-0181.x: I feel anxious because of tomorrow's test.
T2-0181.t: The prefix 불- 'not' becomes 부- before ㄷ or ㅈ: 불안, but 부족 'lack'.

T2-0182.m: to be satisfied, to be content
T2-0182.x: I'm very satisfied with my life right now.
T2-0182.t: Pronounced [만조카다]; 'satisfied with something' is N에 만족하다.

T2-0183.m: worry, concern; something weighing on one's mind
T2-0183.x: These days moving has been weighing on my mind a lot.
T2-0183.e: Literally 'bitter anguish' — a problem you keep turning over.
T2-0183.t: 고민 is weighing a problem or decision; 걱정 is fearing that something bad will happen.

T2-0184.forms: 고민해요 · 고민했어요 · 고민할 거예요 · 고민하지 마세요
T2-0184.m: to agonize over, to think hard about, to worry
T2-0184.x: I thought hard for a long time about which clothes to buy.
T2-0184.e: Literally 'to suffer bitter anguish', though Koreans use it lightly, even about lunch.

T2-0185.m: hateful, detestable; annoying (often of a loved one)
T2-0185.x: I really can't stand the friend who lied.
T2-0185.e: In 미운 정 고운 정, Koreans say bonds grow through both annoyance and fondness.

T2-0186.x: I burst out laughing when I heard that story.
T2-0186.e: From 웃다 'to laugh' + -음, which turns verbs into nouns.

T2-0187.x: The movie was so sad that I teared up.

T2-0188.x: My younger sibling has a bright, easygoing personality.
T2-0188.e: Literally 'nature's pattern' — the shape of who you are.
T2-0188.t: 성격이 좋아요 means 'has a nice personality'; 성격이 급해요 means 'is impatient'.

T2-0189.ex: 제 친구는 성격이 활발해서 인기가 많아요.
T2-0189.x: My friend has an outgoing personality, so she's very popular.
T2-0189.e: Literally 'lively and vigorous' — full of energy.

T2-0190.ex: 우리 할머니는 아침 일찍 일어나시는 부지런한 분이에요.
T2-0190.x: My grandmother is a hardworking person who gets up early in the morning.
T2-0190.t: 부지런하다 means busy and active; for steady, honest effort, Koreans prefer 성실하다.

T2-0191.x: I get a little lazy when the weekend comes.

T2-0192.ex: 그 학생은 성실해서 숙제를 항상 해 와요.
T2-0192.x: That student is conscientious, so they always do their homework.
T2-0192.e: Literally 'sincere and true' — someone you can count on.

T2-0193.ex: 솔직하게 말하면 그 음식은 맛이 없었어요.
T2-0193.x: To be honest, that food didn't taste good.
T2-0193.e: Literally 'frank and straight' — saying it straight out.
T2-0193.t: 솔직히 말하면 'to be honest' is a common way to soften a criticism.

T2-0194.x: My nephew is young but very smart.
T2-0194.e: Homonym hook: 똑똑 is also the knock-knock sound on a door.

T2-0195.ex: 그분은 많은 사람을 도운 훌륭한 의사예요.
T2-0195.x: He is an admirable doctor who has helped many people.

T2-0196.m: to be funny, to make (someone) laugh; to be ridiculous
T2-0196.ex: 그 친구는 말을 정말 웃기게 해요.
T2-0196.x: That friend says things in a really funny way.
T2-0196.e: Causative of 웃다 'to laugh': literally 'to make someone laugh'.
T2-0196.t: 웃기네! can sarcastically mean 'That's ridiculous!', so watch your tone.

T2-0197.x: I've been eating a lot lately, so I've gotten a bit chubby.
T2-0197.t: Calling someone 뚱뚱하다 is rude; 통통하다 'plump, chubby' is a gentler word.

T2-0198.x: My older sister is tall and slim.

T2-0199.forms: 말라요 · 말랐어요 · 마를 거예요 · 마른 (+noun) (르 irregular)
T2-0199.m: to be thin, to be skinny; to dry, to dry up
T2-0199.x: My younger sibling is so thin that I'm worried.
T2-0199.e: One verb, two senses: water 'drying up' and a body 'thinning out'.
T2-0199.t: Use the past to describe someone: 말랐어요 'is thin'; and 목이 말라요 means 'I'm thirsty'.

T2-0200.m: to be good-looking, to be handsome
T2-0200.ex: 드라마에 나오는 그 배우는 정말 잘생겼어요.
T2-0200.x: That actor in the drama is really handsome.
T2-0200.e: 잘 'well' + 생기다 'to be formed': literally 'well formed'.
T2-0200.t: Use the past form for present looks: 잘생겼어요 means 'He's handsome', not 'He was handsome'.

T2-0201.m: to be ugly, to be unattractive
T2-0201.x: Our puppy is ugly, but so cute.
T2-0201.e: 못 'poorly' + 생기다 'to be formed' — the opposite of 잘생기다.

T2-0202.ex: 저는 외모보다 성격이 더 중요하다고 생각해요.
T2-0202.x: I think personality matters more than looks.

T2-0203.m: appearance, figure, look; the way someone looks
T2-0203.x: The child looks so lovely when smiling.
T2-0203.t: It usually follows a modifier: 웃는 모습 'how someone looks smiling', 예전 모습 'how it used to look'.

T2-0204.ex: 오늘은 시간이 없어서 화장을 안 했어요.
T2-0204.x: I didn't put on makeup today because I had no time.
T2-0204.t: 화장실 'restroom' literally means 'makeup room', a handy memory link.

T2-0205.m: to put on makeup, to do one's makeup
T2-0205.ex: 언니는 매일 아침 삼십 분 동안 화장해요.
T2-0205.x: My older sister does her makeup for thirty minutes every morning.

T2-0206.x: The weather forecast says it'll rain tomorrow.
T2-0206.t: This 일기 means 'weather', not 일기 'diary'; context always makes it clear.

T2-0207.x: The temperature dropped a lot this morning.
T2-0207.t: 기온 is only for air temperature; for water, rooms or bodies, use 온도.

T2-0208.ex: 방 온도가 너무 높아서 창문을 열었어요.
T2-0208.x: The room was too warm, so I opened the window.

T2-0209.forms: Sino number + 도: 삼십 도, 영하 오 도
T2-0209.ex: 오늘 서울 기온은 삼십 도까지 올라가요.
T2-0209.x: Today the temperature in Seoul will go up to 30 degrees.
T2-0209.e: Korea uses Celsius: 30도 is hot, and 0도 is freezing.
T2-0209.t: Read it with Sino-Korean numbers: 이십 도 for 20 degrees, never with native numbers.

T2-0210.ex: 내일 아침은 영하 십 도까지 떨어져요.
T2-0210.x: Tomorrow morning it will drop to ten below zero.
T2-0210.t: The opposite is 영상 'above zero'; forecasts say 영상 3도 for 3°C.

T2-0211.forms: 눈이 와요 · 눈이 왔어요 · 눈이 올 거예요
T2-0211.ex: 어젯밤에 눈이 많이 와서 길이 미끄러워요.
T2-0211.x: It snowed a lot last night, so the roads are slippery.
T2-0211.e: Literally 'snow comes'; 눈 also means 'eye', but context makes it clear.

T2-0212.forms: 비가 와요 · 비가 왔어요 · 비가 올 거예요
T2-0212.x: It's raining, so be sure to take an umbrella.
T2-0212.e: Literally 'rain comes': Korean weather 'comes' instead of using 'it'.

T2-0213.ex: 갑자기 소나기가 와서 옷이 다 젖었어요.
T2-0213.x: A sudden shower came, and my clothes got soaked.
T2-0213.e: A brief summer downpour; also the title of a famous Korean short story about first love.

T2-0214.ex: 한국은 여름에 장마 때문에 비가 많이 와요.
T2-0214.x: In Korea it rains a lot in summer because of the rainy season.
T2-0214.e: Korea's summer rainy season, usually from late June to late July.

T2-0215.ex: 태풍 때문에 오늘 비행기가 모두 취소됐어요.
T2-0215.x: All of today's flights were canceled because of the typhoon.
T2-0215.e: Sounds like English 'typhoon' — the two words are probably related.

T2-0216.ex: 아침에 안개가 많이 껴서 앞이 잘 안 보여요.
T2-0216.x: There's so much fog this morning that I can't see ahead well.

T2-0217.x: Sunlight comes in through the window, so the room is bright.
T2-0217.e: 해 'sun' + 빛 'light'; the ㅅ in between is a linking sound.
T2-0217.t: 햇빛 is light you see (bright, dazzling); 햇볕 is heat you feel (warm, burning).

T2-0218.x: The sun was so hot that I wore a hat.
T2-0218.e: 해 'sun' + 볕 'warm sunshine': the sun you feel on your skin.

T2-0219.ex: 비가 그친 후에 하늘에 무지개가 떴어요.
T2-0219.x: After the rain stopped, a rainbow appeared in the sky.
T2-0219.e: Probably from old words for 'water' and 'gate' — a water gate in the sky.

T2-0220.ex: 더우니까 음료수에 얼음을 많이 넣어 주세요.
T2-0220.x: It's hot, so please put lots of ice in my drink.
T2-0220.e: From 얼다 'to freeze' + -음: literally 'the frozen thing'.
T2-0220.t: Pronounced [어름]; at cafés, 얼음 많이 'lots of ice' or 얼음 빼고 'no ice' come in handy.

T2-0221.forms: 얼어요 · 얼었어요 · 얼 거예요 · 언 (+noun) (ㄹ drops)
T2-0221.x: It was so cold that the river froze.
T2-0221.e: Root of 얼음 'ice': ice is simply 'frozen stuff'.

T2-0222.ex: 봄이 되면 산에 있는 눈이 녹아요.
T2-0222.x: When spring comes, the snow on the mountains melts.
T2-0222.e: Add -이- to make it transitive: 녹이다 'to melt something'.

T2-0223.x: Now that it's fall, it's chilly in the mornings and evenings.
T2-0223.e: Also describes a cold, unfriendly attitude: 쌀쌀한 사람 'a cold person'.
T2-0223.t: 쌀쌀하다 is unpleasantly chilly; 선선하다 is pleasantly cool.

T2-0224.x: In the evening the breeze is cool, so it's nice for a walk.

T2-0225.ex: 겨울에는 공기가 건조해서 피부가 자주 가려워요.
T2-0225.x: In winter the air is dry, so my skin often gets itchy.

T2-0226.x: The heat this summer is really intense.
T2-0226.e: Noun from 덥다 'hot': the ㅂ softens into 우, giving 더위.
T2-0226.t: 더위를 타다 means 'to be sensitive to heat'; 더위를 먹다 means to get sick from the heat.

T2-0227.ex: 저는 추위를 많이 타서 겨울이 싫어요.
T2-0227.x: I really feel the cold, so I don't like winter.
T2-0227.e: Noun from 춥다 'cold': the ㅂ softens into 우, giving 추위.

T2-0228.x: In the afternoon, the rain will stop and the skies will clear.
T2-0228.e: Homonym warning: 개다 also means 'to fold' clothes, and 개 alone is 'dog'.
T2-0228.t: You'll mostly hear 개다 in forecasts; in conversation people often say 날씨가 맑아졌어요.

T2-0229.m: to stop (of rain, snow or crying)
T2-0229.x: When the rain stops, let's go for a walk together.
T2-0229.e: Used for things that stop on their own.
T2-0229.t: 그치다 is for rain, snow or crying; for cars or machines that stop, use 멈추다.

T2-0230.forms: 불어요 · 불었어요 · 불 거예요 · 부세요 (ㄹ drops)
T2-0230.x: The wind is blowing hard today, so it's cold.
T2-0230.e: Covers both wind blowing and you blowing: 촛불을 불다 'to blow out candles'.

T2-0231.ex: 가을에 설악산에 가면 단풍이 정말 예뻐요.
T2-0231.x: If you go to Seoraksan in the fall, the autumn leaves are really beautiful.
T2-0231.e: Literally 'red maple'; now it means any leaves turning color.

T2-0232.x: There are lots of fallen leaves on the street.

T2-0233.ex: 사월에는 벚꽃을 보러 공원에 많이 가요.
T2-0233.x: In April, lots of people go to the park to see the cherry blossoms.

T2-0234.ex: 봄이 되면 공원에 꽃이 많이 피어요.
T2-0234.x: When spring comes, lots of flowers bloom in the park.
T2-0234.e: Also used for faces: 얼굴이 피다 'to look healthier, to glow'.
T2-0234.t: In speech 피어요 often shortens to 펴요: 꽃이 폈어요 = The flowers have bloomed.

T2-0235.m: to set (sun, moon); to wither, to fall (flowers, leaves)
T2-0235.ex: 여름에는 저녁 여덟 시쯤 해가 져요.
T2-0235.x: In summer, the sun sets around eight in the evening.
T2-0235.e: Homonym warning: 지다 also means 'to lose' (a game) and 'to carry on your back'.
T2-0235.t: Opposite pairs: 해가 뜨다 (sun rises) vs. 해가 지다 (sun sets); 꽃이 피다 vs. 꽃이 지다.

T2-0236.ex: 한국에는 봄, 여름, 가을, 겨울 사계절이 있어요.
T2-0236.x: Korea has four seasons: spring, summer, fall, and winter.
T2-0236.t: Koreans often say 사계절이 뚜렷해요, 'the four seasons are distinct,' when describing Korea.

T2-0237.ex: 주말 여가 시간에 보통 뭐 하세요?
T2-0237.x: What do you usually do in your free time on weekends?
T2-0237.e: Literally 'leftover leisure' — time left over after work.
T2-0237.t: Usually appears as 여가 시간 (free time) or 여가 활동 (leisure activities).

T2-0238.ex: 저는 요즘 한국 음악에 관심이 많아요.
T2-0238.x: I'm really interested in Korean music these days.
T2-0238.e: Literally 'the heart connected' — your mind is tied to something.
T2-0238.t: Use the particle 에: 음악에 관심이 있어요 'I'm interested in music' — not 을/를.

T2-0239.ex: 친구들하고 노래방에 가서 두 시간 동안 노래했어요.
T2-0239.x: I went to a karaoke room with friends and sang for two hours.
T2-0239.t: Korean karaoke happens in private rooms; going to 노래방 is a classic after-dinner activity with friends or coworkers.

T2-0240.ex: 지난 주말에 대학로에서 친구와 연극을 봤어요.
T2-0240.x: Last weekend I saw a play with a friend in Daehangno.
T2-0240.t: Seoul's Daehangno (대학로) neighborhood is famous for its many small theaters showing 연극.

T2-0241.ex: 이번 토요일에 좋아하는 가수의 공연이 있어요.
T2-0241.x: My favorite singer has a concert this Saturday.
T2-0241.t: Say 공연을 보다 for 'watch a show' and 공연하다 for 'to perform'.

T2-0242.ex: 요즘 미술관에서 사진 전시회를 하고 있어요.
T2-0242.x: There's a photo exhibition at the art museum these days.
T2-0242.e: Literally 'an event for displaying and showing'.

T2-0243.ex: 비가 오는 날에는 미술관에 가는 것을 좋아해요.
T2-0243.x: On rainy days, I like going to the art museum.
T2-0243.e: 미술 'fine art' + -관 = public building: 도서관, 박물관, 대사관.

T2-0244.ex: 어릴 때부터 악기를 하나 배우고 싶었어요.
T2-0244.x: Ever since I was little, I've wanted to learn an instrument.
T2-0244.t: Pronounced [악끼] — ㄱ after ㄱ becomes tense.

T2-0245.m: to play (a musical instrument), to perform (music)
T2-0245.ex: 제 동생은 피아노를 아주 잘 연주해요.
T2-0245.x: My younger sibling plays the piano really well.
T2-0245.t: In daily speech, 치다 is used for piano and guitar, 불다 for wind instruments; 연주하다 works for all.

T2-0246.ex: 저는 일곱 살 때부터 바이올린을 배웠어요.
T2-0246.x: I've been learning the violin since I was seven.
T2-0246.e: From English 'violin'; Korean has no 'v', so it becomes ㅂ.
T2-0246.t: For the violin, Koreans say 바이올린을 켜다 or simply 바이올린을 하다.

T2-0247.x: Every weekend I play badminton with my dad in the park.
T2-0247.t: Racket and ball-hitting sports use 치다: 배드민턴을 치다, 테니스를 치다, 탁구를 치다.

T2-0248.x: I played ping-pong with coworkers during lunch.
T2-0248.t: Pronounced [탁꾸] — ㄱ after ㄱ becomes tense.

T2-0249.ex: 겨울 방학에 가족들과 스키를 타러 갔어요.
T2-0249.x: During winter break, I went skiing with my family.
T2-0249.t: Skiing uses 타다 'to ride': 스키를 타다, just like 자전거를 타다.

T2-0250.ex: 이번 주말에 강원도에 있는 스키장에 가요.
T2-0250.x: This weekend I'm going to a ski resort in Gangwon Province.
T2-0250.e: 스키 'ski' + -장 = place for it: 수영장, 경기장, 주차장.

T2-0251.ex: 우리 아파트 근처에 큰 수영장이 생겼어요.
T2-0251.x: A big swimming pool opened near our apartment.

T2-0252.ex: 우리 아이는 매일 태권도를 배우러 가요.
T2-0252.x: My child goes to taekwondo lessons every day.
T2-0252.e: Literally 'the way of kicking and punching'.

T2-0253.x: I watched a soccer game until late last night.
T2-0253.t: Homonym: 경기 also means 'the economy' (경기가 나빠요), and 경기도 is the province around Seoul.

T2-0254.x: Since it was the weekend, the stadium was really crowded.

T2-0255.ex: 그 선수는 우리 팀에서 제일 빨라요.
T2-0255.x: That player is the fastest on our team.
T2-0255.e: Literally 'chosen hand' — someone picked for their skill.

T2-0256.t: 팀장 'team leader' is a very common job title at Korean companies.

T2-0257.m: to cheer (for), to root for, to support
T2-0257.ex: 우리는 경기장에서 한국 팀을 열심히 응원했어요.
T2-0257.x: We cheered hard for the Korean team at the stadium.
T2-0257.e: Literally 'responding with help' — backing someone up.
T2-0257.t: Also used for encouraging people in life: 항상 응원할게요 'I'll always be rooting for you.'

T2-0258.ex: 이번 시험에서 점수가 생각보다 잘 나왔어요.
T2-0258.x: My score on this test came out better than I expected.

T2-0259.x: My father goes fishing at the river every weekend.
T2-0259.e: Related to 낚다 'to hook, to catch (a fish)'.
T2-0259.t: Slang: 낚시 also means clickbait, and 낚였어요 means 'I got fooled (hooked).'

T2-0260.ex: 여름에 가족과 함께 산으로 캠핑을 갔어요.
T2-0260.x: In the summer, I went camping in the mountains with my family.

T2-0261.m: to hike, to go hiking, to climb a mountain
T2-0261.x: When the weather is nice, I go hiking with friends on weekends.
T2-0261.t: Hiking is hugely popular in Korea; you'll see colorful 등산복 (hiking outfits) on every weekend trail.

T2-0262.forms: 올라요 · 올랐어요 · 오를 거예요 · 오르세요 (르 irregular)
T2-0262.m: to climb, to go up; to rise (prices, temperature)
T2-0262.ex: 우리는 두 시간 동안 산에 올랐어요.
T2-0262.x: We climbed the mountain for two hours.
T2-0262.e: Root of 올라가다 'to go up' and 올리다 'to raise'.
T2-0262.t: Prices and temperatures rise with 오르다 too: 물가가 올랐어요 'Prices went up.'

T2-0263.x: The weather was nice, so we went for a drive to the beach.
T2-0263.e: From English 'drive', but only for a leisure drive; everyday driving is 운전.
T2-0263.t: Common patterns: 드라이브(를) 가다 'go for a drive' and 드라이브하다.

T2-0264.x: In the spring, the students went on a picnic to the park.
T2-0264.e: Originally 'strolling in the breeze'; today mostly a school outing or picnic.
T2-0264.t: Korean kids traditionally bring 김밥 in a lunch box on 소풍 day.

T2-0265.x: On Children's Day, I went to an amusement park with the kids.

T2-0266.x: I saw elephants and lions at the zoo on the weekend.
T2-0266.t: Pronounced [동무뤈] — the ㄹ links into the next syllable.

T2-0267.ex: 저는 시장에서 이것저것 구경하는 것을 좋아해요.
T2-0267.x: I like looking around at all sorts of things at the market.
T2-0267.e: Think 'browsing': 구경하다 is looking around for fun, not for a purpose.
T2-0267.t: 구경만 할게요 'I'm just looking' is handy when a shop clerk approaches you.

T2-0268.ex: 저는 주말에 만화를 보는 것을 좋아해요.
T2-0268.x: I like reading comics on the weekend.
T2-0268.e: Literally 'casual pictures'; English 'manhwa' means Korean comics, like 'manga' for Japanese.

T2-0269.ex: 요즘 재미있는 한국 소설을 읽고 있어요.
T2-0269.x: These days I'm reading an interesting Korean novel.
T2-0269.e: Literally 'small talk' — once considered minor stories, not serious writing.

T2-0270.ex: 카페에서 패션 잡지를 읽으면서 친구를 기다렸어요.
T2-0270.x: I waited for my friend at a café, reading a fashion magazine.
T2-0270.e: Literally 'mixed record' — a bit of everything.
T2-0270.t: Pronounced [잡찌] — ㅈ after ㅂ becomes tense.

T2-0271.ex: 우리 할아버지는 매일 아침 신문을 읽으세요.
T2-0271.x: My grandfather reads the newspaper every morning.

T2-0272.ex: 국어 시간에 유명한 시를 한 편 외웠어요.
T2-0272.x: In Korean class, I memorized a famous poem.
T2-0272.e: Homonym warning: 시 also means 'o'clock' and 'city'.
T2-0272.t: Count poems with 편: 시 한 편 'one poem'.

T2-0273.forms: 모아요 · 모았어요 · 모을 거예요 · 모으세요 (ㅡ drops)
T2-0273.m: to collect, to gather; to save (money)
T2-0273.ex: 저는 여행을 갈 때마다 엽서를 모아요.
T2-0273.x: I collect postcards every time I travel.
T2-0273.e: Same root as 모이다 'to gather together' and 모임 'gathering'.
T2-0273.t: 돈을 모으다 means 'to save up money' — a very common phrase.

T2-0274.ex: 매달 첫째 토요일에 대학교 친구들 모임이 있어요.
T2-0274.x: I have a get-together with college friends on the first Saturday of every month.
T2-0274.e: Noun from 모이다 'to gather' + -ㅁ: literally 'a gathering'.

T2-0275.x: On weekends, I relax and enjoy movies at home.
T2-0275.e: Related to 즐겁다 'to be fun, joyful'.
T2-0275.t: 즐겨 + verb means 'often, by preference': 즐겨 듣는 음악 'music I like to listen to.'

T2-0276.ex: 제주도는 한국 사람들에게 인기 있는 여행지예요.
T2-0276.x: Jeju Island is a popular travel destination for Koreans.

T2-0277.ex: 우리는 서울에서 이틀 동안 시내 관광을 했어요.
T2-0277.x: We went sightseeing around Seoul for two days.
T2-0277.e: Literally 'viewing the light' — taking in the sights.

T2-0278.ex: 명동에는 주말마다 외국인 관광객이 정말 많아요.
T2-0278.x: Myeongdong is packed with foreign tourists every weekend.

T2-0279.ex: 경주는 오래된 절이 많은 관광지로 유명해요.
T2-0279.x: Gyeongju is famous as a tourist spot with many old temples.

T2-0280.ex: 저는 이번 여름에 처음으로 해외여행을 가요.
T2-0280.x: This summer I'm traveling abroad for the first time.

T2-0281.ex: 여행사에서 비행기 표와 호텔을 같이 예약했어요.
T2-0281.x: I booked my plane ticket and hotel together through a travel agency.

T2-0282.ex: 공항에 있는 안내 데스크에서 무료 지도를 받았어요.
T2-0282.x: I got a free map at the information desk in the airport.
T2-0282.e: The syllables don't help here; just remember 안내 데스크 'information desk'.
T2-0282.t: 안내 방송 is a public announcement, like the ones you hear on every Seoul subway train.

T2-0283.m: to guide, to show (someone) around; to inform
T2-0283.x: A staff member kindly showed us to our room.
T2-0283.t: Staff say 안내해 드릴게요 'Let me show you,' using humble 드리다 when helping customers.

T2-0284.ex: 길을 몰라서 휴대폰 지도를 보고 호텔을 찾았어요.
T2-0284.x: I didn't know the way, so I found the hotel using the map on my phone.
T2-0284.t: Homonym: 지도 also means 'guidance, coaching' (지도하다), a different Sino-Korean word.

T2-0285.ex: 가이드가 박물관의 역사를 재미있게 설명해 줬어요.
T2-0285.x: The guide explained the museum's history in a fun way.

T2-0286.ex: 이번 여행 일정이 너무 바빠서 좀 피곤해요.
T2-0286.x: This trip's itinerary is so packed that I'm a bit tired.
T2-0286.e: Literally 'day route' — the plan for each day.
T2-0286.t: Pronounced [일쩡] — ㅈ after ㄹ becomes tense in Sino-Korean words.

T2-0287.ex: 우리는 다음 달 여행을 같이 계획하고 있어요.
T2-0287.x: We're planning next month's trip together.
T2-0287.t: With the noun, say 계획을 세우다 'to make a plan' — literally 'to stand up a plan.'

T2-0288.ex: 인기 있는 식당이라서 일주일 전에 예약을 했어요.
T2-0288.x: It's a popular restaurant, so I made a reservation a week ahead.
T2-0288.t: For tickets (movies, trains), Koreans usually say 예매; for tables and rooms, 예약.

T2-0289.ex: 갑자기 비가 많이 와서 야구 경기가 취소됐어요.
T2-0289.x: It suddenly rained hard, so the baseball game was canceled.
T2-0289.t: Use 취소되다 when something gets canceled without saying who canceled it.

T2-0290.x: I was sick, so I canceled my hotel reservation.

T2-0291.x: Our place was close to the beach, which was really nice.
T2-0291.t: Pronounced [숙쏘] — ㅅ after ㄱ becomes tense.

T2-0292.x: My luggage was so heavy that it was tough at the airport.
T2-0292.e: Also figurative: 짐이 되다 'to be a burden' on someone.

T2-0293.forms: 짐을 싸요 · 짐을 쌌어요; opposite: 짐을 풀다
T2-0293.ex: 내일 아침 일찍 떠나서 오늘 밤에 짐을 싸야 해요.
T2-0293.x: I'm leaving early tomorrow morning, so I have to pack tonight.
T2-0293.t: Also figurative for quitting or moving out: 짐을 싸서 나갔어요 'packed up and left.'

T2-0294.ex: 엄마가 아침마다 학교 도시락을 싸 주셨어요.
T2-0294.x: My mom packed my school lunch every morning.
T2-0294.e: Homonym warning: 싸다 also means 'cheap' — context tells you which.
T2-0294.t: Common collocations: 짐을 싸다 'pack bags', 도시락을 싸다 'pack a lunch', 선물을 싸다 'wrap a gift.'

T2-0295.forms: 풀어요 · 풀었어요 · 풀 거예요 · 푸세요 (ㄹ drops)
T2-0295.m: to untie, to unpack; to solve; to relieve (stress)
T2-0295.ex: 호텔에 도착하자마자 짐을 풀고 좀 쉬었어요.
T2-0295.x: As soon as I got to the hotel, I unpacked and rested a bit.
T2-0295.e: Core idea: loosening — knots, bags, problems, even stress.
T2-0295.t: 스트레스를 풀다 'to relieve stress' and 문제를 풀다 'to solve a problem' are very common.

T2-0296.x: I bought a souvenir for my friend at the airport.

T2-0297.x: I took photos with my family to mark my graduation.
T2-0297.t: ~ 기념으로 means 'to mark or celebrate ~': 생일 기념으로 'for my birthday.'

T2-0298.ex: 산 위에서 보는 경치가 정말 아름다웠어요.
T2-0298.x: The view from the top of the mountain was really beautiful.
T2-0298.t: 경치가 좋다 'the view is nice' is the most common way to praise scenery.

T2-0299.x: The scenery outside the train window was as pretty as a picture.
T2-0299.t: 경치 is a view you admire; 풍경 is broader — any scene or landscape, also in art.

T2-0300.x: During summer break, I swam at the beach.
T2-0300.e: 바다 'sea' + 가 'edge', linked by ㅅ; compare 강가 'riverside', 길가 'roadside'.
T2-0300.t: Pronounced [바다까] — the ㅅ just makes the ㄱ tense.

T2-0301.ex: 배를 타고 한 시간쯤 가면 작은 섬이 있어요.
T2-0301.x: If you take a boat for about an hour, there's a small island.
T2-0301.e: Island names use Sino-Korean -도 instead: 제주도, 독도, 울릉도.

T2-0302.ex: 공원 안에 있는 호수에서 오리 배를 탔어요.
T2-0302.x: We rode a duck boat on the lake in the park.

T2-0303.ex: 산속에 있는 조용한 절에서 하룻밤을 보냈어요.
T2-0303.x: I spent a night at a quiet temple in the mountains.
T2-0303.e: Homonym warning: 절 also means 'a deep bow' (절하다).
T2-0303.t: Temple names end in Sino-Korean -사 'temple': 불국사, 해인사, 조계사.

T2-0304.ex: 유학을 가려면 먼저 학생 비자를 받아야 해요.
T2-0304.x: To study abroad, you first have to get a student visa.

T2-0305.ex: 우리는 내일 아침 일찍 부산으로 떠나요.
T2-0305.x: We're leaving for Busan early tomorrow morning.
T2-0305.t: The place you leave takes 을/를 (집을 떠나다); the destination takes (으)로 (부산으로 떠나다).

T2-0306.m: to go and come back, to visit (and return)
T2-0306.x: Last week I went to Jeju Island with my family.
T2-0306.e: Built from 다니다 'to go around' + 오다 'to come': go and return.
T2-0306.t: Set phrases when leaving home: 다녀오겠습니다 'I'll be back' and 다녀오세요 'See you later.'

T2-0307.m: to walk around, to wander, to get around
T2-0307.ex: 하루 종일 시내를 돌아다녀서 다리가 아파요.
T2-0307.x: I walked around downtown all day, so my legs hurt.
T2-0307.e: 돌다 'to turn' + 다니다 'to go around': moving from place to place.

T2-0308.x: Jeju is an island with a beautiful sea and Hallasan Mountain.

T2-0309.ex: 서울에서 부산까지 KTX로 두 시간 반쯤 걸려요.
T2-0309.x: It takes about two and a half hours from Seoul to Busan by KTX.
T2-0309.e: Literally 'cauldron mountain', probably named after a pot-shaped hill.
T2-0309.t: Busan's 해운대 (Haeundae) is Korea's most famous beach.

T2-0310.ex: 이번 겨울에 베트남으로 여행을 가려고 해요.
T2-0310.x: I'm planning to travel to Vietnam this winter.

T2-0311.ex: 태국 음식은 맵고 달고 정말 맛있어요.
T2-0311.x: Thai food is spicy, sweet, and really delicious.
T2-0311.e: Literally 'great country'; -국 = country: 한국, 중국, 미국.

T2-0312.x: Australia's seasons are the opposite of Korea's, so December is summer.
T2-0312.e: Shortened from an old character spelling of 'Australia' plus 'continent'; the syllables don't help.
T2-0312.t: The English name 오스트레일리아 exists too, but everyday Korean almost always uses 호주.

T2-0313.ex: 저는 작년 여름에 캐나다로 여행을 갔어요.
T2-0313.x: I took a trip to Canada last summer.

T2-0314.ex: 파리에 가면 에펠탑을 꼭 보고 싶어요.
T2-0314.x: If I go to Paris, I really want to see the Eiffel Tower.
T2-0314.e: From French 'Paris'. Homonym warning: native 파리 also means 'fly' (the insect).

T2-0315.x: On weekends, I do the housework together with my husband.
T2-0315.t: Pronounced [지반닐] — an extra ㄴ sound is inserted before 일.

T2-0316.ex: 밥을 먹은 후에 제가 설거지를 할게요.
T2-0316.x: After we eat, I'll do the dishes.
T2-0316.e: Means the act of washing up, not the dishes themselves; dishes are 그릇.

T2-0317.m: to do the dishes, to wash up
T2-0317.x: My younger sibling does the dishes every evening.
T2-0317.t: You can also say 설거지를 하다 with the object particle; both are equally common.

T2-0318.m: to do the laundry, to wash clothes
T2-0318.x: The weather was nice, so I did the laundry this morning.
T2-0318.e: 빨래 (laundry) comes from 빨다 'to wash clothes'.
T2-0318.t: 빨래 means both the washing and the clothes themselves: 빨래를 널다 = to hang out the laundry.

T2-0319.x: I cleaned my room with the vacuum this morning.
T2-0319.t: For 'to vacuum', say 청소기를 돌리다, literally 'to run the vacuum'.

T2-0320.ex: 다 먹은 컵은 저기 쓰레기통에 버리세요.
T2-0320.x: Please throw your empty cup in the trash can over there.

T2-0321.m: to throw away, to throw out; to abandon
T2-0321.ex: 이사하기 전에 오래된 옷을 모두 버렸어요.
T2-0321.x: Before moving, I threw away all my old clothes.
T2-0321.t: After another verb, -아/어 버리다 means 'completely' or 'unfortunately': 다 먹어 버렸어요 = I ate it all up.

T2-0322.ex: 이사 후에 짐 정리가 아직 안 끝났어요.
T2-0322.x: I still haven't finished unpacking and organizing since the move.
T2-0322.t: Pronounced [정니] — ㄹ turns into ㄴ after ㅇ.

T2-0323.m: to organize, to tidy up; to sum up
T2-0323.x: I neatly organized my desk over the weekend.

T2-0324.m: to clean up, to clear away, to put away
T2-0324.x: I cleaned up the living room before the guests came.
T2-0324.t: 치우다 means removing clutter or dishes; 청소하다 means actually cleaning dust and dirt.

T2-0325.x: I folded the dry laundry and put it in the closet.
T2-0325.e: Homonym warning: 개다 also means 'to clear up' (weather), and 개 alone is 'dog'.
T2-0325.t: Use 개다 for clothes and bedding (이불을 개다); for paper, use 접다.

T2-0326.ex: 우리 집은 빨래를 보통 베란다에서 말려요.
T2-0326.x: At our house, we usually dry the laundry on the balcony.
T2-0326.e: Causative of 마르다 'to become dry'. Homonym: 말리다 also means 'to stop someone'.
T2-0326.t: For hair, say 머리를 말리다 = to dry your hair.

T2-0327.m: to get wet, to be wet
T2-0327.x: I didn't have an umbrella, so my clothes got completely wet.
T2-0327.e: Opposite pair: 젖다 (get wet) and 마르다 (get dry).
T2-0327.t: Usually used in the past tense for a current state: 옷이 젖었어요 = my clothes are wet.

T2-0328.ex: 어제 비가 와서 새 신발이 더러워졌어요.
T2-0328.x: It rained yesterday, so my new shoes got dirty.
T2-0328.e: 더럽다 (dirty) + -어지다 (to become); the ㅂ changes to 워.
T2-0328.t: -아/어지다 turns adjectives into 'become' verbs: 깨끗해지다, 추워지다.

T2-0329.forms: 깨끗이 씻다 · 깨끗이 청소하다 · 깨끗이 먹다 (eat it all up)
T2-0329.ex: 밥 먹기 전에 손을 깨끗이 씻으세요.
T2-0329.x: Wash your hands well before you eat.
T2-0329.t: Spelled 깨끗이, not 깨끗히 — a spelling mistake even native speakers make.

T2-0330.x: My parents usually sleep in the master bedroom.
T2-0330.e: Native 안 (inner) + 방 (room); traditionally the inner room of the lady of the house.

T2-0331.ex: 우리 집에는 침실이 두 개 있어요.
T2-0331.e: Literally 'sleeping room'. -실 = room: 욕실, 교실, 사무실.

T2-0332.x: My younger sibling is taking a shower in the bathroom right now.
T2-0332.t: 화장실 is the everyday word for bathroom or restroom; 욕실 stresses a room for bathing.

T2-0333.ex: 집에 들어올 때 신발은 현관에서 벗어 주세요.
T2-0333.x: Please take off your shoes in the entryway when you come in.
T2-0333.e: Originally a Buddhist temple term for a gate; the syllables don't help, so learn it whole.
T2-0333.t: Koreans take off their shoes in the 현관 before stepping up into the house.

T2-0334.x: My mom grows flowers on the balcony.
T2-0334.e: From English 'veranda'; in Korean apartments it is usually an enclosed, glassed-in balcony.

T2-0335.ex: 할머니 댁 마당에서 강아지가 놀고 있어요.
T2-0335.x: A puppy is playing in the yard at Grandma's house.
T2-0335.t: 마당 is an open yard of dirt or pavement; a yard planted with flowers and trees is a 정원.

T2-0336.ex: 우리 집 정원에 장미꽃이 많이 피었어요.
T2-0336.x: Lots of roses have bloomed in our garden.
T2-0336.e: Literally 'courtyard garden'. Homonym: another 정원 means 'seating capacity'.

T2-0337.x: I hung a family photo on the living room wall.

T2-0338.ex: 한국에서는 바닥에 앉아서 밥을 먹기도 해요.
T2-0338.x: In Korea, people sometimes sit on the floor to eat.
T2-0338.e: Also the bottom of anything: 신발 바닥 'sole of a shoe', 손바닥 'palm'.

T2-0339.x: The elevator was broken, so I went up the stairs.
T2-0339.t: In everyday speech it's usually pronounced [게단]; ㅖ after a consonant often sounds like ㅔ.

T2-0340.x: I take the elevator up to the 10th floor every day.

T2-0341.x: When I open the curtains in the morning, sunlight comes in.
T2-0341.t: 커튼을 치다 = to draw the curtains closed; 커튼을 걷다 = to pull them open.

T2-0342.x: I put my winter clothes away in the closet.
T2-0342.e: Native 옷 (clothes) + 장 (cabinet). -장 = cabinet: 책장, 신발장.
T2-0342.t: Pronounced [옫짱] — the ㅈ becomes tense after the final consonant.

T2-0343.x: The socks are in the bottom drawer.

T2-0344.ex: 제 방 책장에는 만화책이 가득 있어요.
T2-0344.x: The bookshelf in my room is full of comic books.
T2-0344.e: Literally 'book cabinet'. Homonym: another 책장 means 'page of a book'.

T2-0345.x: Mom set out the side dishes on the dining table.

T2-0346.x: I heated the rice in the microwave for two minutes.
T2-0346.e: 전자 'electronic' + English 'range' (a stove) — a Konglish blend, not 'microwave'.

T2-0347.ex: 밥솥에 밥이 아직 조금 남아 있어요.
T2-0347.x: There's still a little rice left in the rice cooker.
T2-0347.t: Pronounced [밥쏟] — the ㅅ becomes tense after ㅂ.

T2-0348.ex: 오늘 너무 더워서 아침부터 선풍기를 켰어요.
T2-0348.x: It was so hot today that I turned on the fan in the morning.

T2-0349.x: I turned off the light in my room to save electricity.

T2-0350.ex: 컴퓨터 고장 때문에 숙제를 못 했어요.
T2-0350.x: I couldn't do my homework because my computer broke down.
T2-0350.e: Literally 'a hindrance' — something gets in the way of working.

T2-0351.forms: 고장 나요 · 고장 났어요 · 고장 날 거예요 · 고장 난 (+noun)
T2-0351.m: to break down, to be out of order
T2-0351.ex: 세탁기가 고장 나서 빨래를 못 해요.
T2-0351.x: The washing machine broke, so I can't do the laundry.
T2-0351.t: Used for machines; for snapped or shattered things, use 부러지다 or 깨지다 instead.

T2-0352.m: to fix, to repair; to correct; to cure
T2-0352.x: My dad fixed the broken chair.
T2-0352.t: Works for objects, mistakes and illnesses: 의자를 고치다, 틀린 글자를 고치다, 병을 고치다.

T2-0353.x: It took a week to repair the car.
T2-0353.t: 수리하다 is more formal than 고치다 and is used only for objects, not mistakes or illnesses.

T2-0354.x: Our neighbors are all very kind.
T2-0354.e: Builds compounds: 이웃집 'house next door', 이웃 나라 'neighboring country'.
T2-0354.t: With a vowel after it, the ㅅ moves over: 이웃이 [이우시], 이웃을 [이우슬].

T2-0355.m: the house next door, next-door neighbor
T2-0355.x: A new family moved in next door.
T2-0355.t: Pronounced [엽찝] — the ㅈ becomes tense after ㅂ.

T2-0356.x: I sent this month's rent to the landlord.

T2-0357.x: The monthly rent for this studio is 500,000 won.
T2-0357.t: Korea also has 전세: you pay one large deposit, get it back later, and pay no monthly rent.

T2-0358.x: I lived in a boarding house during my freshman year of college.
T2-0358.e: 하숙 (lodging with meals included) + native 집 (house).
T2-0358.t: A 하숙집 usually includes home-cooked meals, which a 원룸 does not.

T2-0359.x: Most freshmen live in the school dorms.
T2-0359.t: Pronounced [기숙싸] — the ㅅ becomes tense after ㄱ.

T2-0360.ex: 다음 달에 새 아파트로 이사를 가요.
T2-0360.x: I'm moving to a new apartment next month.
T2-0360.t: Say 이사(를) 가다 when moving out somewhere and 이사(를) 오다 when moving in here.

T2-0361.m: to move, to carry; to transfer
T2-0361.x: Please move this box over there.
T2-0361.e: Causative of 옮다 'to shift' or 'to spread' (as a cold does).
T2-0361.t: Also for changing places: 회사를 옮기다 = to change jobs.

T2-0362.m: to put, to place; to leave (somewhere)
T2-0362.ex: 집에 오면 열쇠를 항상 책상 위에 둬요.
T2-0362.x: When I get home, I always put my keys on the desk.
T2-0362.t: -아/어 두다 means doing something ahead of time: 표를 사 두다 = to buy tickets in advance.

T2-0363.forms: 걸어요 · 걸었어요 · 걸 거예요 · 거세요 (ㄹ drops)
T2-0363.m: to hang; to make (a phone call)
T2-0363.ex: 이사한 후에 거실 벽에 예쁜 그림을 걸었어요.
T2-0363.x: After moving, I hung a pretty picture on the living room wall.
T2-0363.t: Also for calls: 전화를 걸다 = to make a phone call.

T2-0364.m: to stick, to attach, to paste
T2-0364.ex: 잊어버리지 않으려고 냉장고 문에 메모를 붙였어요.
T2-0364.x: I stuck a note on the fridge door so I wouldn't forget.
T2-0364.e: Causative of 붙다 'to stick, to be attached'.
T2-0364.t: Pronounced [부치다] — ㅌ before 이 becomes ㅊ (palatalization).

T2-0365.m: to take off, to remove, to detach
T2-0365.ex: 방을 정리하면서 벽에서 오래된 포스터를 뗐어요.
T2-0365.x: While tidying my room, I took the old poster off the wall.

T2-0366.m: to take out, to pull out
T2-0366.ex: 아침에 냉장고에서 차가운 우유를 꺼내서 마셨어요.
T2-0366.x: In the morning, I took cold milk out of the fridge and drank it.
T2-0366.e: Ends in 내다 'to put out', which signals outward motion in compound verbs.

T2-0367.m: to pile up, to stack; to build up (experience)
T2-0367.ex: 다 읽은 책을 책상 위에 쌓아 두었어요.
T2-0367.x: I stacked the books I'd finished on my desk.
T2-0367.t: Pronounced [싸타]; before a vowel the ㅎ goes silent: 쌓아요 [싸아요].

T2-0368.ex: 오늘 밤은 추우니까 이불을 덮고 주무세요.
T2-0368.x: It's cold tonight, so sleep with a blanket over you.
T2-0368.e: Source of 덮개 'cover' and 덮밥 'rice topped with food'.
T2-0368.t: 책을 덮다 = to close a book; 책을 펴다 = to open it.

T2-0369.m: to open, to spread out, to unfold; to straighten
T2-0369.x: Everyone, now open your books to page 30.
T2-0369.t: A classic classroom phrase: 책을 펴세요 'Open your books'; also 우산을 펴다 'open an umbrella'.

T2-0370.ex: 먼저 이 종이를 반으로 한 번 접으세요.
T2-0370.x: First, fold this paper in half once.

T2-0371.ex: 베개가 너무 높아서 잠을 잘 못 잤어요.
T2-0371.x: My pillow was too high, so I didn't sleep well.
T2-0371.e: From 베다 'to rest one's head on' + -개 (tool).

T2-0372.ex: 면접 날에 검은색 정장을 입고 갔어요.
T2-0372.x: I wore a black suit on the day of my interview.
T2-0372.t: 정장 is any formal outfit for men or women; 양복 is specifically a men's Western-style suit.

T2-0373.ex: 아버지는 매일 양복을 입고 회사에 가세요.
T2-0373.x: My father wears a suit to work every day.
T2-0373.e: Literally 'Western clothes', in contrast to 한복 'Korean clothes'.

T2-0374.x: I often wear comfortable jeans on weekends.

T2-0375.ex: 저는 여름에 더워서 반바지를 자주 입어요.
T2-0375.x: I often wear shorts in the summer because it's hot.

T2-0376.x: It was cold, so I put on a thick sweater.

T2-0377.x: I packed underwear and socks in my suitcase.
T2-0377.t: Pronounced [소곧]; with a particle the ㅅ comes back: 속옷이 [소고시].

T2-0378.x: As soon as I get home, I change into my pajamas.

T2-0379.x: Our whole family wore hanbok on Lunar New Year.
T2-0379.t: Koreans often wear hanbok on holidays like 설날 and 추석, and at weddings.

T2-0380.x: Most high school students in Korea wear school uniforms.

T2-0381.ex: 오늘은 밖이 많이 추우니까 장갑을 끼세요.
T2-0381.x: It's really cold outside today, so put on your gloves.
T2-0381.t: Gloves take the verb 끼다, not 입다: 장갑을 끼다 = to put on gloves.

T2-0382.ex: 엄마가 저에게 따뜻한 목도리를 만들어 주셨어요.
T2-0382.x: My mom made me a warm scarf.
T2-0382.t: 목도리 is a thick winter scarf; a thin fashion scarf is a 스카프. Both take 하다 or 두르다.

T2-0383.ex: 어머니 생신 선물로 예쁜 스카프를 샀어요.
T2-0383.x: I bought a pretty scarf for my mother's birthday.
T2-0383.e: From English 'scarf'; usually means a thin, decorative one.

T2-0384.ex: 오늘은 중요한 회의가 있어서 넥타이를 맸어요.
T2-0384.x: I have an important meeting today, so I wore a tie.
T2-0384.t: Ties take the verb 매다: 넥타이를 매다 = to put on a tie.

T2-0385.ex: 새로 산 바지가 좀 커서 벨트를 했어요.
T2-0385.x: My new pants were a little big, so I wore a belt.
T2-0385.e: From English 'belt'; the native word is 허리띠.

T2-0386.ex: 저는 휴대폰을 항상 바지 주머니에 넣어요.
T2-0386.x: I always keep my phone in my pants pocket.
T2-0386.e: Originally a small cloth pouch tied to traditional clothes, which had no pockets.

T2-0387.m: to put on, to wear (glasses, gloves, rings); to fit into
T2-0387.x: My eyesight is bad, so I wear glasses.
T2-0387.e: Short form of 끼우다 'to insert'. Homonym: 끼다 also means 'to form' (fog, clouds).
T2-0387.t: Use 끼다 for things you slip on: rings, gloves, contact lenses; glasses take 끼다 or 쓰다.

T2-0388.m: to wear (a watch, belt); to kick
T2-0388.x: My father always wears a wristwatch.
T2-0388.e: Homonyms: other 차다 verbs mean 'to be full'; the adjective 차다 means 'cold'.
T2-0388.t: Use 차다 for things worn at the wrist or waist: 시계를 차다, 벨트를 차다.

T2-0389.x: Change into comfortable clothes before you work out.
T2-0389.t: Pattern: 옷으로 갈아입다 = change into clothes; same 갈아- as 갈아타다 'to transfer'.

T2-0390.x: The pattern on this shirt is really pretty.
T2-0390.e: Combines with nouns: 꽃무늬 'floral print', 줄무늬 'stripes'.
T2-0390.t: Pronounced [무니]; ㅢ after a consonant sounds like ㅣ.

T2-0391.x: I often wear brown dress shoes.
T2-0391.e: Literally 'brown color'; -색 turns many words into color names.

T2-0392.ex: 오늘은 회색 바지에 흰 셔츠를 입었어요.
T2-0392.x: Today I wore gray pants with a white shirt.
T2-0392.t: 회색 하늘 means a gloomy, overcast sky.

T2-0393.x: My little sister likes pink dresses the most.
T2-0393.e: Literally 'powder-red color', like pale red face powder.
T2-0393.t: In casual speech many people just say 핑크 instead.

T2-0394.ex: 보라색 우산을 잃어버려서 하나 다시 샀어요.
T2-0394.x: I lost my purple umbrella, so I bought another one.
T2-0394.e: 보라 is probably borrowed from Mongolian; 색 means 'color'.

T2-0395.x: When spring comes, the mountains turn green.
T2-0395.t: Pronounced [초록쌕]; traffic lights are often called 초록불 or 파란불.

T2-0396.ex: 면접 때는 보통 검은색 정장을 입어요.
T2-0396.x: People usually wear a black suit for job interviews.
T2-0396.e: From native 검다 'to be black' plus 색 'color'.
T2-0396.t: 까만색 and 검정색 mean the same; 검정 can also stand alone as a noun.

T2-0397.e: From native 희다 'to be white' plus 색 'color'.
T2-0397.t: 흰색 and 하얀색 are interchangeable; pronounced [힌색].

T2-0398.ex: 빨간색 신호일 때는 길을 건너면 안 돼요.
T2-0398.x: You must not cross the street when the light is red.
T2-0398.e: From native 빨갛다 'to be red', modifier 빨간, plus 색.

T2-0399.x: The sky is clear, so the sea is blue too.
T2-0399.e: From native 파랗다 'to be blue', modifier 파란, plus 색.
T2-0399.t: 파란 can also cover green in set phrases like 파란불 'green light'.

T2-0400.x: In fall, ginkgo leaves turn yellow.
T2-0400.e: From native 노랗다 'to be yellow', modifier 노란, plus 색.

T2-0401.ex: 파티에 너무 화려한 옷을 입고 갔어요.
T2-0401.x: I wore clothes that were too flashy to the party.
T2-0401.t: Opposite in fashion is 수수하다 'plain, simple'.

T2-0402.x: The sunlight was strong, so I put on sunglasses.
T2-0402.e: From English 'sunglasses'; count it as one item: 선글라스 하나.
T2-0402.t: Glasses and sunglasses take the verb 쓰다, not 입다: 선글라스를 쓰다.

T2-0403.x: On the weekend I put on a backpack and went to the mountains.
T2-0403.t: Use 메다 for backpacks: 배낭을 메다.

T2-0404.x: My younger sibling is in third grade in elementary school.
T2-0404.t: Pronounced [항년] — nasalization; use Sino numbers: 일 학년, 이 학년.

T2-0405.ex: 이번 학기에는 수업을 다섯 개 들어요.
T2-0405.x: I'm taking five classes this semester.

T2-0406.x: My child started elementary school this year.
T2-0406.t: Often shortened to 초등 or 초딩 (slang) in casual talk.

T2-0407.x: I was on the soccer team in middle school.

T2-0408.x: I graduated from high school and went to college.
T2-0408.t: Korean high school is three years, so 고등학교 1학년 equals American tenth grade.

T2-0409.x: I go to an English academy after work.
T2-0409.e: Literally 'study institute'; a huge part of Korean after-school life.
T2-0409.t: Use 다니다 for attending regularly: 학원에 다니다.

T2-0410.x: My father is a university professor.
T2-0410.t: Always add -님 when speaking to or about your professor: 교수님.

T2-0411.ex: 학교 선배가 맛있는 밥을 사 줬어요.
T2-0411.x: An upperclassman from school bought me a nice meal.
T2-0411.e: Literally 'earlier generation' — someone who started before you.
T2-0411.t: Based on who started first, not age; juniors often call them 선배님.

T2-0412.x: I gave my old books to a junior student.
T2-0412.e: Literally 'later generation' — someone who started after you.

T2-0413.x: I'm going to study abroad in the US next year.
T2-0413.e: Literally 'stay and study' — living away to study.
T2-0413.t: Common patterns: 유학을 가다 and 유학을 하다.

T2-0414.x: There are many international students in our class.

T2-0415.t: Ask someone's major politely with 전공이 뭐예요?

T2-0416.m: to major in, to specialize in
T2-0416.x: I majored in computer engineering in college.

T2-0417.e: Literally 'category item' — one item in the list of studies.

T2-0418.ex: 수학 문제가 너무 어려워서 못 풀었어요.
T2-0418.x: The math problem was too hard, so I couldn't solve it.
T2-0418.e: Literally 'number study'. -학 = field of study: 수학, 과학, 경제학.
T2-0418.t: Don't confuse with 수학여행 'school field trip'; that 수학 means 'cultivating learning', a different Sino-Korean word.

T2-0420.ex: 한국 역사에 관심이 많아서 책을 자주 읽어요.
T2-0420.x: I'm very interested in Korean history, so I read books about it often.
T2-0420.t: Pronounced [역싸] — the ㅅ becomes tense after ㄱ.

T2-0421.x: I went to an art exhibition with a friend on the weekend.
T2-0421.t: 미술 means visual art; 예술 is art in the broad sense, including music and dance.

T2-0422.ex: 오늘 강의는 오후 두 시에 시작해요.
T2-0422.t: Pronounced [강의] or [강이]; students 강의를 듣다, professors 강의를 하다.

T2-0423.x: I didn't know where the lecture room was, so I asked.

T2-0424.x: I caught a cold, so I missed school yesterday.
T2-0424.t: Pronounced [결써카다]; the opposite is 출석하다 'to attend'.

T2-0425.m: to be late (for school or work)
T2-0425.x: I overslept and was late for work.
T2-0425.t: 지각하다 is for school or work; for meeting friends just say 늦다.

T2-0426.ex: 다음 주에 중간고사가 있어서 도서관에 가요.
T2-0426.x: I have midterms next week, so I'm going to the library.
T2-0426.t: Often shortened to 중간 in casual talk: 중간 끝났어요?

T2-0427.x: Vacation starts right after finals are over.

T2-0428.x: My grades went up a lot this semester.
T2-0428.t: Grades 오르다 (go up) or 떨어지다 (drop); 성적이 좋다/나쁘다 for good or bad.

T2-0429.ex: 합격 소식을 듣고 가족들이 정말 기뻐했어요.
T2-0429.x: My family was really happy to hear the news that I passed.

T2-0430.m: to pass (an exam), to be accepted
T2-0430.x: My older brother got into the university he wanted.
T2-0430.t: Takes 에: 시험에 합격하다, 대학교에 합격하다.

T2-0431.m: to fall, to drop; to fail (an exam)
T2-0431.x: I studied hard, but I failed the exam.
T2-0431.e: Basic meaning is 'to fall'; failing an exam is falling off the list.
T2-0431.t: Also used for prices or grades going down: 성적이 떨어졌어요.

T2-0432.m: to stick, to be attached; to pass (an exam)
T2-0432.x: This time I really want to pass the exam.
T2-0432.e: Basic meaning is 'to stick'; passing means your name sticks on the list.
T2-0432.t: Pronounced [붇따]; 붙다 is the casual way to say 합격하다.

T2-0433.x: My grades were good, so I got a scholarship.

T2-0434.x: I'm busy because I have to turn in an assignment by tomorrow.
T2-0434.t: University students say 과제; 숙제 sounds more like grade-school homework.

T2-0435.x: I gave a presentation in Korean in class.

T2-0436.x: The government announced a new policy today.
T2-0436.t: Also used for releasing results or albums: 합격자를 발표하다, 신곡을 발표하다.

T2-0437.x: I understood after hearing the teacher's explanation.

T2-0438.ex: 이 단어의 뜻을 다시 설명해 주세요.
T2-0438.x: Please explain the meaning of this word again.
T2-0438.t: 설명해 주세요 is the go-to way to ask a teacher to explain something.

T2-0439.x: After class, I always review at home.
T2-0439.t: Pronounced [복쓰파다]; pairs with 예습하다 'preview before class'.

T2-0440.m: to prepare for a lesson, to preview
T2-0440.x: I previewed the material we're going to learn tomorrow.

T2-0441.m: to memorize, to learn by heart
T2-0441.x: I memorize twenty words every day.
T2-0441.t: 외우다 is actively memorizing; 기억하다 is simply remembering.

T2-0442.m: to be wrong, to get wrong
T2-0442.x: I got two questions wrong on the test.
T2-0442.t: Many speakers say 틀리다 for 'different', but standard Korean uses 다르다 for that.

T2-0443.m: to get (an answer) right, to guess correctly; to hit (a target)
T2-0443.ex: 이 문제의 정답을 맞힌 사람이 없어요.
T2-0443.x: Nobody got the right answer to this question.
T2-0443.e: Causative of 맞다 'to be correct' — literally 'make it correct'.
T2-0443.t: Don't mix up with 맞추다 'to match or fit'; for answers, standard Korean uses 맞히다.

T2-0444.x: Korean grammar was a little difficult at first.

T2-0445.ex: 한국 친구가 제 발음이 좋다고 했어요.
T2-0445.x: My Korean friend said my pronunciation is good.

T2-0446.m: reading (as a skill or test section)
T2-0446.x: Reading is easier for me than listening.
T2-0446.e: Verb 읽다 'to read' plus noun-making -기; same for 쓰기, 듣기, 말하기.
T2-0446.t: Pronounced [일끼]; TOPIK sections are 듣기, 읽기 and 쓰기.

T2-0447.m: writing (as a skill or test section)
T2-0447.x: I ran out of time on the writing test.

T2-0448.m: listening (as a skill or test section)
T2-0448.ex: 듣기 실력을 높이려고 한국 드라마를 봐요.
T2-0448.x: I watch Korean dramas to improve my listening skills.
T2-0448.e: Verb 듣다 'to listen' plus noun-making -기; ㄷ stays ㄷ before -기.

T2-0449.m: speaking (as a skill or test section)
T2-0449.ex: 말하기 연습을 위해 한국 친구를 만나요.
T2-0449.x: I meet Korean friends to practice speaking.

T2-0450.ex: 요즘 영어 회화 수업을 듣고 있어요.
T2-0450.x: These days I'm taking an English conversation class.
T2-0450.t: 회화 is language-class conversation; an everyday chat is 대화 or 이야기.

T2-0451.x: The translation of this book is very natural.
T2-0451.t: 번역 is written translation; spoken interpreting is 통역.

T2-0452.x: I translated Korean song lyrics into English.
T2-0452.t: Pattern: A를 B(으)로 번역하다 'translate A into B'.

T2-0453.ex: 글자가 너무 작아서 잘 안 보여요.
T2-0453.x: The letters are too small, so I can't see them well.

T2-0454.x: Could you lend me an eraser?
T2-0454.e: From 지우다 'to erase' plus -개 'tool': like 덮개 'cover'.

T2-0455.x: I cut the paper in half with scissors.

T2-0456.x: I stuck the photo in my notebook with glue.
T2-0456.e: Homonym: 풀 also means 'grass'; context makes it clear.

T2-0457.x: The teacher wrote a problem on the board.

T2-0458.ex: 아이가 무거운 책가방을 메고 학교에 가요.
T2-0458.x: The child goes to school carrying a heavy school bag.

T2-0459.x: My friend lent me an umbrella.
T2-0459.e: 빌리다 'to borrow' plus 주다 'to give' — borrowing given to someone.
T2-0459.t: 빌려주다 is to lend — a very common mix-up.

T2-0460.x: I'll give back the book I borrowed by tomorrow.
T2-0460.e: 돌리다 'to turn' plus 주다 'to give' — turning it back to the owner.

T2-0461.x: If there's anything you don't know, ask anytime.
T2-0461.t: With superiors, use 질문을 드리다 instead of 질문하다.

T2-0462.e: Literally 'real power' — what you can actually do.
T2-0462.t: Common collocation: 실력이 늘다 'skills improve'; 실력이 좋다 'to be skilled'.

T2-0463.forms: 늘어요 · 늘었어요 · 늘 거예요 · 는 (+noun) (ㄹ drops)
T2-0463.m: to increase, to grow; to improve (skills)
T2-0463.x: I practiced every day, so my cooking skills improved.
T2-0463.e: Causative 늘리다 'to increase something' comes from it.

T2-0464.forms: 줄어요 · 줄었어요 · 줄 거예요 · 준 (+noun) (ㄹ drops)
