T2-0464.x: The number of students has dropped a lot lately.
T2-0464.e: Also seen in 줄어들다 'to shrink' and 줄이다 'to reduce'.
T2-0464.t: Because the ㄹ drops, 줄 거예요 and 준 look like forms of 주다 'to give'.

T2-0465.ex: 공연 전에 매일 두 시간씩 연습을 해요.
T2-0465.x: Before the performance, I practice two hours every day.

T2-0466.ex: 제 수준에 맞는 책을 찾고 있어요.
T2-0466.x: I'm looking for a book that fits my level.
T2-0466.e: Literally 'water level' — like a carpenter's level.
T2-0466.t: Common collocations: 수준이 높다/낮다 'the level is high/low'.

T2-0467.x: In Korea, students usually start school in March.

T2-0468.ex: 부모님이 제 졸업식에 꽃을 들고 오셨어요.
T2-0468.x: My parents came to my graduation with flowers.

T2-0469.m: start of the school term, school opening
T2-0469.ex: 다음 주 월요일에 개학이라서 숙제를 빨리 끝내야 해요.
T2-0469.x: School starts next Monday, so I have to finish my homework quickly.
T2-0469.t: Opposite of 방학 (vacation); 개학하다 means the term starts again after a break.

T2-0470.ex: 요즘 젊은 사람들이 일자리를 찾기가 어려워요.
T2-0470.x: These days it's hard for young people to find jobs.
T2-0470.e: Built from 일 'work' + 자리 'seat, spot': a spot to work.
T2-0470.t: Pronounced [일짜리] — the ㅈ becomes tense after ㄹ.

T2-0471.x: I work a part-time job at a café every weekend.
T2-0471.e: From German 'Arbeit' (work), not English; in Korean it means a part-time job.
T2-0471.t: In casual speech it's almost always shortened to 알바, and a part-timer is 알바생.

T2-0472.m: going to work, getting to work
T2-0472.ex: 출근 시간에는 지하철에 사람이 정말 많아요.
T2-0472.x: The subway is really crowded during rush hour.

T2-0473.m: to go to work, to report for work
T2-0473.ex: 저는 보통 아침 여덟 시에 회사에 출근해요.
T2-0473.x: I usually get to the office at eight in the morning.
T2-0473.t: Use 회사에 출근하다 for the place; 회사로 출근하다 also works to show direction.

T2-0474.ex: 퇴근 후에 친구하고 저녁을 먹기로 했어요.
T2-0474.x: I decided to have dinner with a friend after work.
T2-0474.t: 퇴근 후에 'after work' is a very common phrase for evening plans.

T2-0475.m: to leave work, to get off work
T2-0475.ex: 오늘은 일이 많아서 늦게 퇴근할 거예요.
T2-0475.x: I have a lot of work today, so I'll get off late.

T2-0476.m: to work, to be on duty, to serve
T2-0476.ex: 제 형은 은행에서 오 년 동안 근무했어요.
T2-0476.x: My older brother worked at a bank for five years.
T2-0476.e: Literally 'diligent tasks': working at a job.
T2-0476.t: More formal than 일하다; common on job ads and forms: 근무 시간, 근무 장소.

T2-0477.x: Our boss is very kind to the employees.
T2-0477.e: -장 = head of something: 사장, 반장, 교장, 시장.
T2-0477.t: Always add 님 when talking to or about the boss: 사장님. Shop owners are also called 사장님.

T2-0478.ex: 회사 동료들과 같이 점심을 먹으러 갔어요.
T2-0478.x: I went to have lunch with my coworkers.
T2-0478.t: Pronounced [동뇨] — ㄹ becomes ㄴ after ㅇ.

T2-0479.ex: 오후 두 시에 회의실에서 회의가 있어요.
T2-0479.x: There's a meeting in the conference room at 2 p.m.

T2-0480.ex: 이 서류에 이름을 쓰고 사인해 주세요.
T2-0480.x: Please write your name on this document and sign it.
T2-0480.e: Literally 'written things of a kind': paperwork.

T2-0481.ex: 내일까지 보고서를 써서 부장님께 드려야 해요.
T2-0481.x: I have to write the report and give it to the manager by tomorrow.
T2-0481.t: Use 보고서를 쓰다 (write) and 보고서를 내다/제출하다 (hand in).

T2-0482.x: Could I ask you to make copies of the meeting materials?

T2-0483.m: to copy, to photocopy; to copy (on a computer)
T2-0483.ex: 이 서류를 다섯 장 복사해 주세요.
T2-0483.x: Please make five copies of this document.
T2-0483.t: On a computer, copy and paste is 복사하고 붙여넣다, often just 복붙 in slang.

T2-0484.ex: 점심시간에 회사 근처 식당에서 비빔밥을 먹었어요.
T2-0484.x: I ate bibimbap at a restaurant near the office during lunch break.
T2-0484.e: 점심 literally 'a dot on the heart' — a light snack to tide you over.

T2-0485.x: On my day off, I want to get a good rest at home.
T2-0485.t: 휴일 is any day off; a national holiday on the calendar is 공휴일.

T2-0486.ex: 내일 회사 면접이 있어서 조금 긴장돼요.
T2-0486.x: I have a job interview tomorrow, so I'm a little nervous.
T2-0486.t: The applicant says 면접을 보다 'take an interview'; the verb 하다 is used less.

T2-0487.x: I got a job after graduating from college.

T2-0488.m: to get a job, to be employed
T2-0488.ex: 제 친구는 작년에 큰 회사에 취직했어요.
T2-0488.x: My friend got a job at a big company last year.
T2-0488.t: Pronounced [취지카다] — ㄱ and ㅎ combine into ㅋ. Use N에 취직하다 for the company.

T2-0489.m: to quit, to stop, to give up
T2-0489.ex: 일이 너무 힘들어서 회사를 그만두고 싶어요.
T2-0489.x: The work is so hard that I want to quit my job.
T2-0489.e: Built from 그만 'stop there, that much' + 두다 'to leave as is'.
T2-0489.t: Takes an object: 회사를/일을/공부를 그만두다. 그만두세요 can sound like 'Stop it!'

T2-0490.x: My dream is to become a civil servant.
T2-0490.e: -원 = staff member: 공무원, 은행원, 회사원, 직원.
T2-0490.t: Government jobs are very popular in Korea for stability; people study for the 공무원 시험 for years.

T2-0491.ex: 은행원이 통장 만드는 방법을 친절하게 알려 줬어요.
T2-0491.x: The bank clerk kindly showed me how to open an account.
T2-0491.e: 은행 is literally 'silver shop'; -원 = staff member.

T2-0492.ex: 기자들이 유명한 배우에게 질문을 많이 했어요.
T2-0492.x: The reporters asked the famous actor a lot of questions.
T2-0492.e: -자 = person who does it: 기자, 과학자, 운전자.

T2-0493.ex: 제 동생은 지금 군인이라서 집에 자주 못 와요.
T2-0493.x: My younger brother is a soldier now, so he can't come home often.
T2-0493.t: Most Korean men serve in the military; 군대에 가다 means to start mandatory service.

T2-0494.x: I got lost, so I asked a police officer for directions.
T2-0494.t: In everyday speech people usually just say 경찰 or, politely, 경찰관님.

T2-0495.ex: 그 운동선수는 매일 여섯 시간씩 연습해요.
T2-0495.x: That athlete practices six hours every day.
T2-0495.e: 선수 is literally 'chosen hand': someone picked for their skill.

T2-0496.ex: 길에서 유명한 연예인을 봐서 깜짝 놀랐어요.
T2-0496.x: I was surprised to see a famous celebrity on the street.
T2-0496.e: Literally 'performing-arts person': singers, actors, TV hosts.

T2-0497.ex: 핸드폰을 집에 두고 와서 연락을 못 했어요.
T2-0497.x: I left my phone at home, so I couldn't contact you.
T2-0497.e: Konglish from English 'hand' + 'phone'; English speakers say 'cell phone'.
T2-0497.t: 휴대폰 and 휴대전화 mean the same; 휴대전화 is the formal word used in news.

T2-0498.ex: 요즘은 스마트폰으로 뭐든지 할 수 있어요.
T2-0498.x: These days you can do anything with a smartphone.
T2-0498.e: From English 'smartphone'; note 스마트 has three syllables in Korean.

T2-0499.forms: 전화를 걸어요 · 걸었어요 · 걸 거예요 · 거세요 (ㄹ drops)
T2-0499.m: to make a phone call, to call
T2-0499.ex: 어제 저녁에 고향에 계신 어머니께 전화를 걸었어요.
T2-0499.x: Yesterday evening I called my mother back home.
T2-0499.e: 걸다 means 'to hang, to hook': you hook up a line to someone.
T2-0499.t: In speech 전화하다 is more common; 전화를 걸다 stresses dialing the call.

T2-0500.forms: 전화를 받아요 · 받았어요 · 받을 거예요 · 받으세요
T2-0500.m: to answer the phone, to take a call
T2-0500.ex: 수업 중이라서 전화를 받을 수 없었어요.
T2-0500.x: I was in class, so I couldn't answer the phone.
T2-0500.e: 받다 means 'to receive': you receive the call.
T2-0500.t: When you answer, say 여보세요; to hang up is 전화를 끊다.

T2-0501.ex: 지금 통화 중이니까 잠깐만 기다려 주세요.
T2-0501.x: I'm on a call right now, so please wait a moment.
T2-0501.t: Watch out: 통화 'phone call' sounds the same as 통화 'currency'.

T2-0502.m: to talk on the phone, to speak by phone
T2-0502.ex: 어제 친구와 한 시간 동안 통화했어요.
T2-0502.x: I talked on the phone with my friend for an hour yesterday.
T2-0502.t: Use N하고/N와 통화하다 'talk on the phone with N'.

T2-0503.ex: 집에 도착하면 저에게 문자 보내 주세요.
T2-0503.x: Please send me a text when you get home.
T2-0503.e: Literally 'written characters'; short for 문자 메시지 'text message'.
T2-0503.t: Pronounced [문짜]; the usual verb is 문자를 보내다 'send a text'.

T2-0504.x: I got a birthday message from my friend.
T2-0504.e: From English 'message'; often spelled 메세지 informally, but 메시지 is standard.

T2-0505.m: to contact, to get in touch
T2-0505.x: Get in touch anytime you have time.
T2-0505.t: Pronounced [열라카다] — ㄴ becomes ㄹ before ㄹ, and ㄱ + ㅎ become ㅋ.

T2-0506.x: Please write your name and contact number here.
T2-0506.t: Pronounced [열락처]; asking 연락처 좀 알려 주세요 is a polite way to ask for a number.

T2-0507.m: reply, written answer (to a letter, text, email)
T2-0507.ex: 어제 보낸 문자에 아직 답장이 없어요.
T2-0507.x: There's still no reply to the text I sent yesterday.
T2-0507.t: Use 답장 for written replies; a spoken answer to a question is 대답.

T2-0508.x: My phone got fully charged overnight.

T2-0509.m: to charge (a battery); to top up, to reload (a card)
T2-0509.x: I put 10,000 won on my transit card at the convenience store.
T2-0509.e: Literally 'fill with electricity' + 하다; also used for adding money.
T2-0509.t: Koreans also say they need to 충전 themselves, meaning recharge with rest.

T2-0510.x: I didn't bring my charger, so I borrowed one from a friend.

T2-0511.ex: 배터리가 얼마 안 남아서 충전해야 해요.
T2-0511.x: My battery is almost dead, so I need to charge it.
T2-0511.t: Say 배터리가 없어요 or 배터리가 다 됐어요 when your phone is dead.

T2-0512.ex: 이 앱으로 택시를 쉽게 부를 수 있어요.
T2-0512.x: You can easily call a taxi with this app.
T2-0512.t: Many people say 어플 in conversation; 앱 is the standard form.

T2-0513.x: I found a good restaurant by searching online.

T2-0514.x: Try looking up words you don't know on the internet.
T2-0514.t: Pronounced [검새카다]; use it for online searches, and 찾다 for looking for things in general.

T2-0515.x: Check the school website for details.
T2-0515.e: From English 'homepage'; Koreans use it for a whole website, not just the main page.

T2-0516.ex: 이 사이트에서 옷을 싸게 살 수 있어요.
T2-0516.x: You can buy clothes cheaply on this site.

T2-0517.ex: 비밀번호를 잊어버려서 새 비밀번호를 다시 만들었어요.
T2-0517.x: I forgot my password, so I made a new one.
T2-0517.t: Often shortened to 비번 in casual speech.

T2-0518.x: I forgot my username, so I looked it up again.
T2-0518.e: From English 'ID'; in Korean it means a login username.
T2-0518.t: An ID card is 신분증, not 아이디.

T2-0519.m: to join, to sign up, to register
T2-0519.ex: 이 사이트에 가입하면 할인 쿠폰을 줘요.
T2-0519.x: If you sign up for this site, they give you a discount coupon.
T2-0519.t: Pronounced [가이파다]; use N에 가입하다: 사이트에, 동아리에, 보험에 가입하다.

T2-0520.ex: 회원이 되면 책을 무료로 빌릴 수 있어요.
T2-0520.x: If you become a member, you can borrow books for free.

T2-0521.m: to raise, to lift, to put up; to post, to upload; to raise (prices)
T2-0521.ex: 어제 찍은 여행 사진을 인스타그램에 올렸어요.
T2-0521.x: I posted the travel photos I took yesterday on Instagram.
T2-0521.e: Causative of 오르다 'to go up': literally 'make it go up'.
T2-0521.t: Online, 올리다 means to post or upload: 사진을/글을 올리다.

T2-0522.ex: 제 글에 댓글이 백 개나 달렸어요.
T2-0522.x: My post got as many as a hundred comments.
T2-0522.e: From 대 'in response to' + 글 'writing'; the ㅅ joins the two parts.
T2-0522.t: Write a comment is 댓글을 달다/쓰다; comments appear is 댓글이 달리다.

T2-0523.ex: 핸드폰 화면이 깨져서 잘 안 보여요.
T2-0523.x: My phone screen cracked, so it's hard to see.

T2-0524.ex: 저는 주말에 카페에서 노트북으로 숙제를 했어요.
T2-0524.x: I did my homework on my laptop at a café on the weekend.
T2-0524.e: Konglish from English 'notebook (computer)'; it means a laptop.
T2-0524.t: A paper notebook is 공책 or 노트, not 노트북.

T2-0525.x: I'll send you the report file by email.
T2-0525.e: From English 'file'; Korean has no 'f', so it becomes ㅍ.

T2-0526.ex: 컴퓨터를 끄기 전에 파일을 꼭 저장하세요.
T2-0526.x: Be sure to save the file before turning off the computer.
T2-0526.t: Also used for saving a number: 전화번호를 저장하다.

T2-0527.m: to erase, to delete; to remove (makeup, stains)
T2-0527.x: I deleted the photos I didn't need from my phone.
T2-0527.e: Related to 지우개 'eraser': -개 turns the verb into a tool.

T2-0528.forms: 눌러요 · 눌렀어요 · 누를 거예요 · 누르세요 (르 irregular)
T2-0528.x: If you press this button, the door opens.
T2-0528.e: Same root as 눌리다 'to be pressed'; the 르 turns into ㄹㄹ before -어.
T2-0528.t: Online, 좋아요를 누르다 means to hit 'Like'.

T2-0529.m: to turn on, to come on (by itself), to be switched on
T2-0529.x: When I went into the room, the light came on automatically.
T2-0529.t: Use 켜다 when someone turns it on (불을 켜다), 켜지다 when it comes on (불이 켜지다).

T2-0530.m: to go off, to turn off, to go out (light, fire); to die (battery)
T2-0530.x: My phone suddenly died because the battery ran out.
T2-0530.e: 끄다 'to turn off' + -어지다 'become'; the ㅡ drops.
T2-0530.t: Careful: 꺼져! said to a person is a rude 'Get lost!'

T2-0531.ex: 저는 인터넷 동영상을 보고 요리하는 방법을 배웠어요.
T2-0531.x: I learned how to cook by watching videos online.
T2-0531.t: Film a video is 동영상을 찍다; watch one is 동영상을 보다.

T2-0532.m: broadcast, broadcasting; TV or radio program; announcement
T2-0532.ex: 이 프로그램은 매주 토요일 저녁에 방송돼요.
T2-0532.x: This program airs every Saturday evening.
T2-0532.t: Also used for announcements: 안내 방송 in the subway or a store.

T2-0533.ex: 저는 운전할 때 항상 라디오를 들어요.
T2-0533.x: I always listen to the radio when I drive.
T2-0533.e: From English 'radio'; pronounced with three clear syllables, ra-di-o.

T2-0534.ex: 동영상을 볼 때마다 광고가 나와서 좀 짜증나요.
T2-0534.x: An ad comes on every time I watch a video, which is a bit annoying.

T2-0535.ex: 제가 제일 좋아하는 프로그램은 요리 프로그램이에요.
T2-0535.x: My favorite program is a cooking show.
T2-0535.e: From English 'program'; Korean adds vowels, so it has four syllables.
T2-0535.t: Often shortened to 프로 in speech: 요리 프로, 예능 프로.

T2-0536.x: I bought ingredients at the market to make gimbap.

T2-0537.ex: 고기에 양념을 하고 한 시간 동안 두세요.
T2-0537.x: Season the meat and leave it for an hour.
T2-0537.e: Probably from older 약념, 'medicinal seasoning' — spices were thought to be good for health.
T2-0537.t: Pronounced [양념]; at chicken shops, 양념 means the sweet-spicy red sauce vs. 후라이드 (fried).

T2-0538.ex: 국이 싱거우면 간장을 조금 더 넣으세요.
T2-0538.x: If the soup is bland, add a little more soy sauce.
T2-0538.e: 간 'saltiness' + 장 'fermented sauce'; -장 marks fermented pastes and sauces.

T2-0539.ex: 비빔밥에 고추장을 넣고 잘 비벼서 드세요.
T2-0539.x: Add gochujang to the bibimbap, mix it well, and eat.

T2-0540.ex: 어머니가 끓여 주신 된장찌개가 정말 맛있어요.
T2-0540.x: The doenjang stew my mother made is really delicious.
T2-0540.e: 된 'thick' + 장 'fermented sauce': the thick paste, unlike runny soy sauce.
T2-0540.t: Most often eaten as 된장찌개, one of the most common Korean home dishes.

T2-0541.m: oil, cooking oil; fat, grease; gasoline
T2-0541.ex: 프라이팬에 기름을 조금 두르고 계란을 부치세요.
T2-0541.x: Put a little oil in the frying pan and fry the egg.
T2-0541.e: Also used for car fuel: 기름을 넣다 means to fill up with gas.
T2-0541.t: 참기름 (sesame oil) and 들기름 (perilla oil) are key flavors in Korean cooking.

T2-0542.x: Korean food uses a lot of garlic.
T2-0542.e: In the Dangun founding myth, a bear ate garlic and mugwort to become a woman.

T2-0543.x: Ramyeon tastes better if you add green onion.
T2-0543.e: Homonym warning: 파 also means 'party, faction'; 양파 'onion' is literally 'Western 파'.
T2-0543.t: 파전 is a savory green onion pancake, popular on rainy days with makgeolli.

T2-0544.x: This chili pepper is a lot spicier than I thought.
T2-0544.e: Base of 고추장 and 고춧가루 'chili powder'; chili reached Korea only around the 1600s.
T2-0544.t: Children's slang also uses 고추 for a boy's private part, so context matters.

T2-0545.ex: 저는 어렸을 때 당근을 정말 싫어했어요.
T2-0545.x: I really hated carrots when I was little.
T2-0545.e: In casual speech 당근이지! is slang for 'of course!', a pun on 당연하지.

T2-0546.x: In summer, I often eat cold cucumber soup.
T2-0546.t: 오이소박이, stuffed cucumber kimchi, is a popular summer side dish.

T2-0547.x: My mom makes kimchi with napa cabbage.
T2-0547.e: Probably from an old borrowed reading of Chinese 'white vegetable'; now felt as native.
T2-0547.t: A whole head of cabbage is counted with 포기: 배추 한 포기.

T2-0548.ex: 무를 넣으면 국 맛이 더 시원해져요.
T2-0548.x: Adding radish makes the soup taste more refreshing.
T2-0548.e: Homonym warning: the Sino prefix 무- means 'without', as in 무료 'free of charge'.
T2-0548.t: For soups, 시원하다 means 'refreshing,' not 'cool' — a classic compliment for radish soup.

T2-0549.x: In Korea, tofu and soybean paste are made from soybeans.
T2-0549.e: Proverb: 콩 심은 데 콩 난다, 'where you plant beans, beans grow' — you reap what you sow.

T2-0550.x: I like stew with tofu in it.
T2-0550.e: Literally 'bean curd'. People traditionally eat tofu after release from prison, for a fresh start.

T2-0551.ex: 겨울에 따뜻한 고구마를 먹으면 정말 맛있어요.
T2-0551.x: Warm sweet potatoes taste really good in winter.
T2-0551.e: Probably from a Japanese dialect word for sweet potato, brought to Korea in the 1700s.
T2-0551.t: Slang: a 고구마 story is frustratingly slow, like eating dry sweet potato without water.

T2-0552.x: I drink tomato juice every morning.

T2-0553.ex: 여름에는 달고 맛있는 복숭아가 많이 나와요.
T2-0553.x: In summer, lots of sweet, delicious peaches come into season.
T2-0553.e: Peach blossoms are 복숭아꽃, or in poetic style 복사꽃.

T2-0554.x: I put lemon in warm water and drink it.

T2-0555.x: In fall, lots of persimmons grow on the persimmon trees.
T2-0555.e: Homonym warning: 감 also means 'feeling, hunch', as in 감이 좋다 'to have a good feeling'.

T2-0556.ex: 오늘 저녁에는 닭을 넣고 국을 끓였어요.
T2-0556.x: For dinner tonight, I made soup with chicken.
T2-0556.e: Hidden in 달걀 'egg', from 닭의 알, 'chicken's egg'.
T2-0556.t: Pronounced [닥] alone, but [달기] in 닭이 — the ㄹ comes back before a vowel.

T2-0557.x: I put ham and egg in the gimbap.

T2-0558.x: Please put more cheese on the pizza.
T2-0558.e: From English 'cheese', with an extra 으 vowel added at the end.
T2-0558.t: Koreans say '김치' or '치즈' when posing for photos, like 'say cheese'.

T2-0559.ex: 빵이나 국수를 만들 때 밀가루가 필요해요.
T2-0559.x: You need flour when you make bread or noodles.

T2-0560.x: I had warm noodles for lunch.
T2-0560.e: The everyday word for noodles; 면 is the Sino word used in names like 냉면.
T2-0560.t: '국수 언제 먹여 줄 거예요?' means 'When are you getting married?' — noodles are wedding food.

T2-0561.ex: 아플 때는 따뜻한 죽을 먹는 게 좋아요.
T2-0561.x: When you're sick, it's good to eat warm porridge.
T2-0561.e: Proverb: 죽 쒀서 개 준다, 'cook porridge and give it to the dog' — wasted effort.
T2-0561.t: Koreans eat 죽 when they're sick, the way Americans eat chicken soup.

T2-0562.ex: 오늘 저녁에는 맛있는 찌개를 끓일 거예요.
T2-0562.x: I'm going to make a delicious stew for dinner tonight.
T2-0562.e: Thicker and saltier than 국 'soup'; often shared from one pot at the table.
T2-0562.t: Use 끓이다, not 만들다, for making stew: 찌개를 끓여요.

T2-0563.ex: 저는 돼지고기를 넣은 김치찌개를 제일 좋아해요.
T2-0563.x: I like kimchi stew with pork the most.
T2-0563.e: 김치 + 찌개 'stew'; it tastes best made with sour, well-fermented kimchi.

T2-0564.x: The soybean paste stew my mom makes is the best.

T2-0565.ex: 주말에 가족과 함께 갈비를 먹으러 갔어요.
T2-0565.x: On the weekend, I went out with my family to eat galbi.
T2-0565.e: Literally 'rib'; beef ribs are 소갈비, pork ribs are 돼지갈비.

T2-0566.x: Yesterday I grilled pork belly with my friends.
T2-0566.e: 삼 'three' + 겹 'layer' + 살 'flesh': three layers of fat and meat.

T2-0567.x: Rice is delicious wrapped in seaweed.
T2-0567.e: Homonym warning: 김 also means 'steam', and it's a very common family name.
T2-0567.t: Seaweed for soup is 미역; 김 is the thin, dried, roasted sheets.

T2-0568.x: I made dumplings with my family on Lunar New Year.
T2-0568.e: From a Chinese word for 'steamed bun'; in Korea it means filled dumplings.

T2-0569.ex: 어제 남은 밥으로 맛있는 볶음밥을 만들었어요.
T2-0569.x: I made tasty fried rice with yesterday's leftover rice.

T2-0570.m: jjajangmyeon, noodles in black bean sauce
T2-0570.ex: 이사하는 날에는 보통 짜장면을 시켜 먹어요.
T2-0570.x: On moving day, people usually order jjajangmyeon.
T2-0570.e: From Chinese 'fried-sauce noodles'; a Korean-Chinese dish. 짜장면 and 자장면 are both standard.

T2-0571.x: I ordered a whole pizza with my friends.
T2-0571.e: From English 'pizza'; one whole pizza is 한 판.

T2-0572.x: I didn't have time, so I ate a burger for lunch.
T2-0572.e: From English 'hamburger'; often shortened to 버거.

T2-0573.x: I made a quick sandwich for breakfast.
T2-0573.e: From English 'sandwich', with extra vowels added: 샌-드-위-치.

T2-0574.ex: 저는 매일 회사에 도시락을 싸 가요.
T2-0574.x: I pack a lunch to take to work every day.
T2-0574.e: Convenience-store 도시락 are a popular, cheap lunch in Korea.
T2-0574.t: Use 싸다 'to pack, wrap' with it: 도시락을 싸다 means to pack a lunch.

T2-0575.x: The kids have a snack when school is over.

T2-0576.x: After the meal, we had fruit for dessert.
T2-0576.t: 디저트 is just as common, especially for café sweets; restaurants often say 후식 for the after-meal treat.

T2-0577.x: It was hot, so I bought a cold drink at the convenience store.
T2-0577.t: Pronounced [음뇨수] — ㄹ becomes ㄴ after ㅁ.

T2-0578.ex: 저는 식사 후에 녹차를 자주 마셔요.
T2-0578.x: I often drink green tea after meals.
T2-0578.t: Black tea is 홍차, literally 'red tea'.

T2-0579.x: I drank wine with my friends at the birthday party.
T2-0579.e: From English 'wine'; for alcohol in general, Koreans say 술.

T2-0580.x: I was busy, so I couldn't eat breakfast today.
T2-0580.e: 아침 'morning' + 밥 'rice, meal'; in casual speech, 아침 alone also means breakfast.

T2-0581.x: On weekends, I often eat out with my family.
T2-0581.t: Add 하다 to make the verb: 외식하다 'to eat out'.

T2-0582.x: My foreign friends really like Korean food.

T2-0583.ex: 오늘은 한식 말고 양식을 먹고 싶어요.
T2-0583.x: Today I want Western food instead of Korean food.
T2-0583.e: Literally 'ocean food' — food from across the ocean, meaning the West.
T2-0583.t: Homonym warning: 양식 also means 'form, format' in documents.

T2-0584.m: to boil (something); to make (soup, stew, ramen)
T2-0584.x: After boiling the water, add the ramen.
T2-0584.e: 끓다 'to boil' + causative -이-: 'to make something boil'.
T2-0584.t: Pronounced [끄리다] — the ㅎ is silent before a vowel.

T2-0585.x: When the water boils, turn the heat down.
T2-0585.e: Add -이- to get 끓이다 'to boil something'.

T2-0586.forms: 구워요 · 구웠어요 · 구울 거예요 · 구우세요 (ㅂ irregular)
T2-0586.m: to grill, to roast, to bake
T2-0586.x: In the evening, we grilled meat in the yard and ate it.
T2-0586.e: One verb covers grilling meat, baking bread and roasting sweet potatoes: 군고구마.
T2-0586.t: Homonym warning: 굽다 'to be bent' is regular — 굽어요, not 구워요.

T2-0587.ex: 야채를 기름에 볶아서 밥과 함께 드세요.
T2-0587.x: Stir-fry the vegetables in oil and eat them with rice.
T2-0587.e: Root of 볶음 'stir-fried dish' and 볶음밥 'fried rice'.

T2-0588.x: Potatoes taste better when you deep-fry them in oil.
T2-0588.e: Root of 튀김 'fried food'; 감자튀김 are French fries.

T2-0589.x: Put the eggs in a pot and boil them for 10 minutes.
T2-0589.e: Think 삶은 계란 'boiled egg'. Don't confuse it with 삶 'life', from 살다.
T2-0589.t: Use 삶다 for solid food like eggs or noodles; use 끓이다 for water, soup or stew.

T2-0590.m: to steam; to gain weight (살이 찌다)
T2-0590.x: I steamed potatoes and gave them to the kids as a snack.
T2-0590.t: To gain weight is 살이 찌다; to lose weight is 살이 빠지다.

T2-0591.m: to heat up, to warm up (food or drinks)
T2-0591.ex: 자기 전에 전자레인지에 우유를 데워서 마셨어요.
T2-0591.x: Before bed, I warmed some milk in the microwave and drank it.
T2-0591.e: Used for reheating: 다시 데우다 'to reheat'. The opposite is letting food 식다 'cool'.

T2-0592.forms: 썰어요 · 썰었어요 · 썰 거예요 · 써세요 (ㄹ drops)
T2-0592.m: to slice, to cut (with a knife)
T2-0592.ex: 먼저 양파와 감자를 얇게 썰어 주세요.
T2-0592.x: First, please slice the onions and potatoes thinly.
T2-0592.t: Use 썰다 for food and knives; use 자르다 for paper, hair or scissors.

T2-0593.x: Please mix the flour and sugar well.

T2-0594.forms: 부어요 · 부었어요 · 부을 거예요 · 부으세요 (ㅅ irregular)
T2-0594.x: Pour two cups of water into the pot.
T2-0594.e: Homonym warning: 붓다 also means 'to swell', as in 얼굴이 부었어요 'my face is puffy'.
T2-0594.t: For pouring a drink into a glass, Koreans usually say 따르다: 술을 따르다.

T2-0595.m: to sprinkle, to spray, to scatter
T2-0595.x: Sprinkle a little salt and pepper on the meat.
T2-0595.e: Used for anything sprinkled or sprayed: salt, water, even perfume (향수를 뿌리다).

T2-0596.m: to be cooked, to be done; to ripen
T2-0596.x: When the meat is fully cooked, turn off the heat.
T2-0596.e: Means both 'be cooked' and 'ripen'; also 'familiar', as in 낯익다 'to look familiar'.

T2-0597.m: to cool down, to get cold
T2-0597.ex: 커피가 다 식기 전에 빨리 드세요.
T2-0597.x: Drink your coffee quickly before it gets cold.
T2-0597.e: Also used for feelings: 사랑이 식다 'love cools off'.

T2-0598.x: Put water in a big pot and bring it to a boil.

T2-0599.ex: 부엌에서 칼을 사용할 때는 항상 조심하세요.
T2-0599.x: Always be careful when you use a knife in the kitchen.
T2-0599.e: 칼국수 'knife-cut noodles' is named after it.

T2-0600.x: Taste the soup before you add salt.
T2-0600.e: 맛 'taste' + 보다 'to see, to try': literally 'see the taste'.
T2-0600.t: Pronounced [맏뽀다]; -아/어 보다 after any verb means 'try': 먹어 보세요.

T2-0601.x: If the soup is a little bland, add salt.
T2-0601.e: Also describes people: 싱거운 사람 tells silly, flat jokes.
T2-0601.t: 싱겁다 means not salty enough, not 'tasteless'; its opposite is 짜다 'salty'.

T2-0602.ex: 이 레몬은 너무 셔서 먹을 수 없어요.
T2-0602.x: This lemon is so sour I can't eat it.
T2-0602.e: 시 + 어요 shortens to 셔요; 신 김치 is sour, well-aged kimchi.

T2-0603.m: nutty, savory (like sesame or roasted grains)
T2-0603.x: I added sesame oil, and now it smells really nutty.
T2-0603.e: Homonym warning: a different 고소하다 means 'to sue'.
T2-0603.t: Used for the smell of roasted sesame, nuts or fresh bread — English has no exact match.

T2-0604.x: I worked out a lot, so I'm really thirsty.
T2-0604.e: 목 'throat' + 마르다 'to be dry': literally 'throat is dry'.

T2-0605.x: Don't leave any food; please eat it all.
T2-0605.e: 남다 'to remain' + causative -기-: 'to make something remain'.
T2-0605.t: Also used for messages: 메시지를 남기다 'to leave a message'.

T2-0606.ex: 어제 먹고 남은 피자가 냉장고에 있어요.
T2-0606.x: There's leftover pizza from yesterday in the fridge.
T2-0606.e: Add -기- to get 남기다 'to leave something over'.

T2-0607.x: Three servings of pork belly and one naengmyeon, please.
T2-0607.t: At Korean BBQ places, you often must order at least 2인분 of meat.

T2-0608.x: I'll just have one slice of cake.
T2-0608.e: Homonym warning: a different 조각 means 'sculpture'.
T2-0608.t: It works as a counter: 피자 두 조각 'two slices of pizza'.

T2-0609.m: great place to eat, popular restaurant
T2-0609.x: There's a famous restaurant near here.

T2-0610.x: Excuse me, could you show me the menu?
T2-0610.t: 메뉴 alone often means the dishes themselves: 오늘 메뉴가 뭐예요? 'What's on today?'

T2-0611.x: I was invited to my friend's birthday party.
T2-0611.t: Being invited is 초대를 받다; inviting someone is 초대하다.

T2-0612.x: I made a pretty invitation for the birthday party.
T2-0612.t: A wedding invitation has its own word: 청첩장.

T2-0613.ex: 이번 주말에 새 집에서 집들이를 해요.
T2-0613.x: We're having a housewarming party at our new place this weekend.
T2-0613.e: 집 'house' + 들이다 'to bring in'; guests often bring toilet paper or laundry detergent.

T2-0614.x: My older sister's wedding is next month.
T2-0614.t: Guests usually give cash in an envelope (축의금) instead of buying a registry gift.

T2-0615.x: The groom and bride greeted the guests together.
T2-0615.t: Pronounced [실랑] — ㄴ becomes ㄹ before ㄹ.

T2-0616.ex: 하얀 드레스를 입은 신부가 정말 아름다워요.
T2-0616.x: The bride in the white dress is really beautiful.
T2-0616.t: Homonym warning: 신부 also means 'Catholic priest', written with different characters.

T2-0617.ex: 졸업식 날 많은 사람들에게 축하를 받았어요.
T2-0617.x: On graduation day, lots of people congratulated me.
T2-0617.t: Pronounced [추카]; say 축하해요, or more politely 축하드려요, for 'congratulations'.

T2-0618.x: I apologized to my friend first.
T2-0618.e: Literally 'apologize for a fault'. 사과 'apple' is a different word.

T2-0619.x: I was late for class, so I apologized to the teacher first.
T2-0619.e: Literally 'apologize for a fault' + 하다 'to do'.
T2-0619.t: Mark the person with 에게 or 한테 (께 for elders): 친구에게 사과하다.

T2-0620.ex: 친구가 진심으로 사과해서 저는 친구를 용서했어요.
T2-0620.x: My friend sincerely apologized, so I forgave them.
T2-0620.t: A common plea: 한 번만 용서해 주세요 'Please forgive me just this once.'

T2-0621.ex: 처음에는 누구나 실수를 할 수 있어요.
T2-0621.x: Anyone can make mistakes at first.
T2-0621.e: Literally 'lose hold with the hand' — a slip of the hand.

T2-0622.ex: 어제 발표할 때 너무 긴장해서 실수했어요.
T2-0622.x: I was so nervous during my presentation yesterday that I made a mistake.
T2-0622.e: Literally 'slip of the hand' + 하다 'to do'.
T2-0622.t: 실수 is an honest slip; 잘못 suggests real fault or wrongdoing.

T2-0623.x: This whole thing is my fault.
T2-0623.e: Built from 잘 'well' + 못 'cannot': something not done well.
T2-0623.t: 제 잘못이에요 'It's my fault' is a key phrase for a sincere apology.

T2-0624.m: to do wrong, to make a mistake
T2-0624.x: I treated my younger sibling badly, so I apologized first.
T2-0624.t: Pronounced [잘모타다]; 잘못했어요 'I was wrong' is the standard sincere apology.

T2-0625.ex: 도와주신 모든 분들께 깊은 감사를 드립니다.
T2-0625.x: I offer my deep thanks to everyone who helped.
T2-0625.t: 감사를 드리다 is the polite set phrase for 'to give thanks'; 감사합니다 is a bit more formal than 고맙습니다.

T2-0626.ex: 항상 저를 도와주셔서 선생님께 정말 감사하다고 말씀드렸어요.
T2-0626.x: I told my teacher I was really grateful to her for always helping me.
T2-0626.t: 감사합니다 and 고맙습니다 mean the same; 감사합니다 sounds slightly more formal and is safest with strangers.

T2-0627.m: to greet, to say hello; to bow
T2-0627.x: I greeted my neighbor with a smile in the morning.
T2-0627.e: Literally 'human affairs' — greeting as basic social manners.

T2-0628.ex: 친구 소개로 지금 남자 친구를 만났어요.
T2-0628.x: I met my current boyfriend through a friend's introduction.
T2-0628.e: Literally 'connect in between' — like a go-between.

T2-0629.ex: 오늘은 제가 우리 가족을 한 명씩 소개하겠습니다.
T2-0629.x: Today I'll introduce my family members one by one.

T2-0630.x: I introduced myself in Korean in the first class.
T2-0630.t: Use with 하다: 자기소개를 하다; Koreans often start with 처음 뵙겠습니다 or 안녕하세요.

T2-0631.x: I have a small favor to ask my friend.
T2-0631.e: Literally 'hand over and entrust' something to someone.

T2-0632.x: I asked my younger sibling to pick up some milk.
T2-0632.t: Pronounced [부타카다] — ㄱ and ㅎ merge into ㅋ.

T2-0633.ex: 다음 주에 일이 있어서 사장님께 휴가를 부탁드렸어요.
T2-0633.x: I have something going on next week, so I asked my boss for time off.
T2-0633.e: 부탁 'favor' plus humble 드리다 'to give (to a superior)'.
T2-0633.t: Humble form: use it when asking someone older or higher in rank; the person asked takes 께.
rel: I look forward to working with you

T2-0634.m: to refuse, to decline, to turn down
T2-0634.ex: 너무 바빠서 친구의 부탁을 미안하지만 거절했어요.
T2-0634.x: I was too busy, so I turned down my friend's request, though I felt sorry.

T2-0635.m: to keep (a promise, rule); to protect, to guard
T2-0635.ex: 친구와 만날 때는 약속 시간을 꼭 지키세요.
T2-0635.x: When you meet friends, be sure to be on time.
T2-0635.e: One verb for both 'keep a promise or rule' and 'guard something'.
T2-0635.t: Common collocations: 약속을 지키다 (keep a promise), 시간을 지키다 (be punctual), 규칙을 지키다 (follow rules).

T2-0636.ex: 우리의 첫 만남은 학교 앞 작은 도서관에서였어요.
T2-0636.x: Our first meeting was at a small library in front of the school.
T2-0636.e: From 만나다 'to meet' plus the noun ending -ㅁ.

T2-0637.ex: 주말에 여자 친구와 한강에서 데이트를 했어요.
T2-0637.x: I went on a date with my girlfriend at the Han River on the weekend.
T2-0637.e: From English 'date'; only the romantic meaning, not a calendar date (날짜).
rel: to date, to go out with

T2-0638.m: to go out with, to date; to make friends
T2-0638.ex: 우리는 사귄 지 일 년이 됐어요.
T2-0638.x: We've been going out for a year.
T2-0638.e: Covers both making friends (친구를 사귀다) and dating someone.
T2-0638.t: In speech 사귀어요 is often shortened to [사겨요]; 저랑 사귈래요? means 'Will you go out with me?'

T2-0639.m: to break up; to part, to say goodbye
T2-0639.ex: 어제 남자 친구와 헤어져서 너무 슬퍼요.
T2-0639.x: I broke up with my boyfriend yesterday, so I'm very sad.
T2-0639.e: One verb for both everyday 'part ways' after meeting and romantic 'break up'.

T2-0640.ex: 제 남자 친구는 요리를 아주 잘해요.
T2-0640.x: My boyfriend is very good at cooking.
T2-0640.t: For a male friend who is not a boyfriend, Koreans say 남사친 or just 친구, since 남자 친구 implies romance.

T2-0641.x: I gave my girlfriend flowers for her birthday.

T2-0642.ex: 실례지만 혹시 지금 만나는 애인 있어요?
T2-0642.x: Excuse me, but are you seeing anyone right now?
T2-0642.t: Gender-neutral and common, unlike English 'lover'; it doesn't suggest an affair.

T2-0643.m: to go to see, to visit (someone); to go looking for
T2-0643.x: During vacation I went to visit my grandmother in my hometown.
T2-0643.e: 찾다 'to look for' plus 가다 'go': go to find someone.

T2-0644.m: to come to see, to come visit
T2-0644.x: A friend came to visit my house on the weekend.
T2-0644.e: 찾다 'to look for' plus 오다 'come': come to find someone.

T2-0645.x: News of the president's visit came out on the news.
T2-0645.e: Literally 'visit and inquire' — calling on someone to ask after them.
T2-0645.t: Homonym: 방문 also means 'room door' (방 + 문); context tells them apart.

T2-0646.x: I'm scheduled to visit a client's company tomorrow.

T2-0647.ex: 어머니 생신에 예쁜 목도리를 하나 선물했어요.
T2-0647.x: I gave my mother a pretty scarf for her birthday.

T2-0648.x: I feel good because my teacher praised me.
T2-0648.t: 'To be praised' is 칭찬을 듣다 or 칭찬을 받다, literally 'hear' or 'receive' praise.

T2-0649.ex: 부장님이 회의에서 제 보고서를 많이 칭찬했어요.
T2-0649.x: My manager praised my report a lot in the meeting.

T2-0650.x: I had a conversation in Korean with a Korean friend.

T2-0651.m: to share; to divide, to split; to exchange (words, greetings)
T2-0651.x: I split the pizza in half with my friend and ate it.
T2-0651.e: Core idea is 'split into parts' — sharing food, dividing numbers, exchanging talk.
T2-0651.t: Common collocations: 이야기를 나누다 (chat), 인사를 나누다 (exchange greetings), 음식을 나누다 (share food).

T2-0652.x: Don't get mad. That was just a joke.
T2-0652.t: 'To tell a joke' is 농담하다; 농담이에요? means 'Are you kidding?'

T2-0653.ex: 집에 돌아가시면 부모님께 안부 꼭 전해 주세요.
T2-0653.x: When you get home, please be sure to give my regards to your parents.
T2-0653.e: Literally 'safe or not' — asking whether someone is doing well.
T2-0653.t: Set phrases: 안부를 묻다 (ask how someone is) and 안부를 전하다 (send regards).

T2-0654.m: to pass on, to convey, to deliver (a message)
T2-0654.ex: 수업에 못 온 친구에게 선생님 말씀을 전했어요.
T2-0654.x: I passed on the teacher's message to a friend who missed class.

T2-0655.ex: 우리 이제 많이 친하니까 반말로 이야기할까요?
T2-0655.x: We're pretty close now, so shall we talk casually?
T2-0655.e: Literally 'half speech' — sentences cut short without the polite ending.
T2-0655.t: Don't switch to 반말 with older people or new acquaintances until they suggest it — it can sound rude.

T2-0656.x: You use polite speech with people you've just met.
T2-0656.t: Pronounced [존댄말] — the ㅅ between 존대 and 말 nasalizes to ㄴ.

T2-0657.ex: 그 학생은 어른들에게 항상 예의가 발라요.
T2-0657.x: That student is always polite to adults.
T2-0657.t: Say 예의가 바르다 for 'well-mannered' and 예의가 없다 for 'rude'; the 의 in 예의 is usually pronounced [이].

T2-0658.x: Sincere congratulations to you both on your wedding.
T2-0658.e: 축하 'celebrate and congratulate' plus humble 드리다 'give'.
T2-0658.t: Pronounced [추카드림니다] — ㄱ+ㅎ becomes ㅋ, and ㅂ before ㄴ becomes ㅁ.

T2-0659.m: excuse me, but …; sorry to bother you, but …
T2-0659.ex: 실례지만 이 근처에 화장실이 어디에 있어요?
T2-0659.x: Excuse me, but where is a restroom around here?
T2-0659.e: Literally 'it's a lapse of manners, but …'.
T2-0659.t: Perfect for polite openers to strangers, e.g. 실례지만 성함이 어떻게 되세요? 'May I ask your name?'

T2-0660.m: keep up the good work; take care (said when leaving)
T2-0660.ex: 오늘 커피 정말 맛있게 잘 마셨어요. 수고하세요!
T2-0660.x: The coffee was really good today. Have a good one!
T2-0660.t: Said to clerks or coworkers when leaving; avoid it with your boss or elders — use 수고하셨습니다 or 먼저 가 보겠습니다.

T2-0661.m: I'll be back; see you later (said when leaving home or the office)
T2-0661.x: Mom, I'm heading off to school now!
T2-0661.e: 다니다 'go about' plus 오다 'come': literally 'I'll go and come back'.
T2-0661.t: The family replies 잘 다녀와 or 다녀오세요; it's a fixed daily ritual in Korean homes.

T2-0662.ex: 엄마, 학교 다녀왔습니다! 오늘 정말 배고파요.
T2-0662.x: Mom, I'm home from school! I'm really hungry today.
T2-0662.e: Past form of 다녀오다 'go and come back': literally 'I went and came back'.

T2-0663.m: long time no see; it's been a while
T2-0663.ex: 민수 씨, 정말 오랜만이에요! 잘 지냈어요?
T2-0663.x: Minsu, long time no see! How have you been?
T2-0663.e: 오랜만 is short for 오래간만 'after a long while' (오래 'long time').
T2-0663.t: Often spelled wrongly as 오랫만; the correct spelling is 오랜만.

T2-0664.forms: 새해 복 많이 받아 (casual) · 받으세요 (polite) · 받으십시오 (formal)
T2-0664.m: Happy New Year (literally 'receive lots of blessings in the new year')
T2-0664.e: Literally 'receive many blessings in the new year'.
T2-0664.t: Said with a deep bow (세배) to elders on 설날; 많이 is pronounced [마니].

T2-0665.x: Thanks so much for helping. — You're welcome, anytime.
T2-0665.e: 천만 'ten million' — as in 'not in a million years', no thanks needed.
T2-0665.t: Textbook-correct but a bit stiff; in daily life Koreans more often reply 아니에요.

T2-0666.m: well…; I'm not sure; let me see
T2-0666.x: Well, I'm not really sure about that either.
T2-0666.t: A soft way to hesitate or politely disagree without saying no directly.

T2-0667.forms: 잘 부탁해 (casual) · 잘 부탁해요 (polite) · 잘 부탁드립니다 (formal)
T2-0667.m: I look forward to working with you; please treat me well
T2-0667.x: Nice to meet you. I look forward to working with you.
T2-0667.e: Literally 'I ask you a favor well' — asking for goodwill in a new relationship.

T2-0668.m: cheer up; hang in there; you can do it
T2-0668.ex: 내일 시험이 있죠? 너무 걱정하지 말고 힘내세요!
T2-0668.x: You have an exam tomorrow, right? Don't worry too much — you've got this!
T2-0668.e: 힘 'strength' plus 내다 'bring out': literally 'bring out your strength'.

T2-0669.ex: 그는 사랑이 많은 따뜻한 가정에서 자랐어요.
T2-0669.x: He grew up in a warm, loving home.
T2-0669.t: Homonym: 가정 also means 'assumption' (假定); in family contexts it means home.

T2-0670.ex: 우리 집 식구는 모두 다섯 명이에요.
T2-0670.x: There are five people in my family.
T2-0670.e: Literally 'eating mouths' — the people who share meals under one roof.

T2-0671.x: I think parents' love is truly great.
T2-0671.t: When talking about your own or someone else's parents, say 부모님; bare 부모 sounds general or impersonal.

T2-0672.x: The couple next door get along very well.

T2-0673.ex: 택시 아저씨가 길을 친절하게 알려 주셨어요.
T2-0673.x: The taxi driver kindly told me the way.
T2-0673.e: Everyday address for a middle-aged man who isn't family.
T2-0673.t: Fine for shopkeepers or drivers, but don't call a young man 아저씨 — it makes him feel old.

T2-0674.x: The lady at the restaurant gave us more side dishes.
T2-0674.e: Polite address for a married or middle-aged woman; 아줌마 is the casual version.

T2-0675.ex: 아줌마, 여기 김밥 두 줄 주세요.
T2-0675.x: Ma'am, two rolls of gimbap here, please.
T2-0675.t: Can sound rude to a woman who doesn't see herself as middle-aged; many diners say 이모 or 사장님 instead.

T2-0676.ex: 친구 아버님은 요즘도 건강하게 잘 지내세요?
T2-0676.x: Is your friend's father still doing well and healthy these days?
T2-0676.t: Use for someone else's father or your father-in-law; for your own dad, 아버지 or 아빠 is normal.

T2-0677.x: My friend's mother made dinner for us.

T2-0678.m: uncle (father's younger, unmarried brother; casually any uncle)
T2-0678.ex: 삼촌이 생일 선물로 자전거를 사 주셨어요.
T2-0678.x: My uncle bought me a bicycle for my birthday.
T2-0678.e: Literally 'three degrees' of kinship; -촌 counts family distance: 사촌 = four degrees.
T2-0678.t: Strictly 삼촌 is a father's brother; a mother's brother is 외삼촌, though kids often just say 삼촌.

T2-0679.m: aunt (mother's sister); friendly term for a middle-aged woman
T2-0679.x: My aunt is three years younger than my mom.
T2-0679.t: Restaurant customers often call the server 이모 to sound warm and friendly.

T2-0680.ex: 설날에 고모 댁에 가서 세배를 했어요.
T2-0680.x: On Lunar New Year I went to my aunt's house and gave her a New Year's bow.

T2-0681.x: Every vacation I played with my younger cousin.

T2-0682.ex: 언니의 아들인 조카가 올해 초등학생이 됐어요.
T2-0682.x: My nephew, my sister's son, started elementary school this year.
T2-0682.e: One word for both nephew and niece; 조카딸 specifies a niece.

T2-0683.x: Grandma really adores her only grandson.

T2-0684.x: Grandpa read a storybook to his granddaughter.

T2-0685.ex: 추석에는 친척들이 모두 할머니 댁에 모여요.
T2-0685.x: On Chuseok all the relatives gather at Grandma's house.

T2-0686.x: I'm the youngest of three siblings.
T2-0686.e: Also used for the youngest member of a team or K-pop group.
T2-0686.t: Pronounced [망내] — ㄱ becomes ㅇ before ㄴ (nasalization).

T2-0687.ex: 우리 집 첫째는 올해 대학생이 됐어요.
T2-0687.x: The eldest in our family became a college student this year.
T2-0687.e: From 첫 'first' plus -째 'order'; the ordinal for 하나.
T2-0687.t: Ordinals add -째 to native numbers, but 'first' is irregular: 첫째, not 한째.

T2-0688.ex: 우리 둘째 딸은 집 근처 고등학교에 다녀요.
T2-0688.x: Our second daughter goes to a high school near home.

T2-0689.ex: 여행 셋째 날에는 가족과 바닷가에 갔어요.
T2-0689.x: On the third day of the trip, I went to the beach with my family.

T2-0690.e: 쌍 'pair' plus native -둥이, a suffix for a kind of child.

T2-0691.x: May 5th is Children's Day in Korea, so there's no school.
T2-0691.t: 어린이 is a bit formal, used on signs and holidays; in conversation 아이 or 애 is more common.

T2-0692.ex: 이 영화는 청소년이 볼 수 없습니다.
T2-0692.x: Teenagers are not allowed to see this movie.
T2-0692.e: Literally 'green, young years' — youth in its fresh stage.

T2-0693.x: There are seats for seniors on the subway.
T2-0693.t: 노인 is neutral or official; when speaking to or about an elder politely, use 어르신.

T2-0694.x: Sir, there's a seat here, so please sit down.
T2-0694.e: Related to 어른 'adult, elder'; the respectful term for older people.
T2-0694.t: A polite way to address an elderly stranger directly, like 'sir' or 'ma'am'.

T2-0695.ex: 이 옷은 남성과 여성 모두 입을 수 있습니다.
T2-0695.x: These clothes can be worn by both men and women.
T2-0695.t: 남성 is formal, seen in news, signs and surveys; in conversation say 남자.

T2-0696.x: These days the number of female athletes has grown a lot.

T2-0697.m: young lady, miss; husband's younger sister
T2-0697.ex: 저 아가씨가 길을 친절하게 가르쳐 줬어요.
T2-0697.x: That young lady kindly showed me the way.
T2-0697.e: Also what a wife calls her husband's younger sister.
T2-0697.t: Calling a server 아가씨 can sound condescending today; 저기요 'excuse me' is safer.

T2-0698.ex: 한 소년이 공원에서 강아지와 놀고 있어요.
T2-0698.x: A boy is playing with a puppy in the park.

T2-0699.ex: 그 소녀는 노래를 아주 잘 불러요.

T2-0700.ex: 기숙사 룸메이트와 같이 저녁을 만들어 먹었어요.
T2-0700.x: I made and ate dinner with my dorm roommate.
T2-0700.e: From English 'roommate'; often shortened to 룸메.

T2-0701.ex: 지영 씨, 오늘 점심 같이 먹을래요?
T2-0701.x: Jiyoung, do you want to have lunch together today?
T2-0701.e: Originally 'clan, family name'; now a polite title after a person's name.
T2-0701.t: Use after a given name or full name, never alone with a surname for seniors or with your own name.

T2-0702.x: Mr. Hong Gil-dong, please come into the exam room now.
T2-0702.e: Respect suffix also found in 선생님, 사장님 and 부모님.
T2-0702.t: More respectful than 씨; used by staff to customers and in online communities after usernames.

T2-0703.x: The child cleaned his own room by himself.
T2-0703.t: Couples also call each other 자기 ('honey'); otherwise it refers back to the subject of the sentence.

T2-0704.x: Above all, it's important to believe in yourself.
T2-0704.e: Literally 'self-body'; a different 자신 means 'confidence' (자신이 있다).

T2-0705.x: Our family lives helping one another.
T2-0705.e: Also works as a noun: 서로의 생각 'each other's thoughts'.

T2-0706.x: Everyone, that's all for today's class. Good work.
T2-0706.t: Used to address an audience and never includes the speaker; for 'all of us' say 우리 모두.

T2-0707.m: you (between spouses, in songs or writing); dear
T2-0707.x: Honey, I'm really happy thanks to you.
T2-0707.e: Originally 'the very person in question'; the syllables don't help much.
T2-0707.t: Don't use 당신 for 'you' with strangers — it can sound rude; use the person's name or title instead.

T2-0708.x: That person is the principal of our school.
T2-0708.e: 그 'that' + 분 'honorable person'; the polite form of 그 사람.

T2-0709.ex: 그녀는 소설 속에서 아주 용감한 사람이에요.
T2-0709.x: In the novel, she is a very brave person.
T2-0709.e: 그 'that' + 녀 'woman'; a modern written-style word.
T2-0709.t: 그녀 is rare in conversation; Koreans usually say 그 사람, 그분, or the person's name.

T2-0710.x: Someone is knocking on the door outside.
T2-0710.e: From 누구 'who' + -ㄴ가 'is it?' — a question turned into 'someone'.

T2-0711.t: 아무도 needs a negative verb ('nobody'), while 아무나 means 'anyone at all' with positive verbs.

T2-0712.x: I've been so busy that I haven't eaten anything since morning.
T2-0712.t: 아무거나 ('anything is fine') is very common when ordering food or choosing.

T2-0713.x: The weather in Seoul is really nice these days.
T2-0713.t: 요즘 and 요새 mean the same; 요새 sounds a little more casual.

T2-0714.x: I'm so busy these days because I have a lot of work.
T2-0714.e: Short for 요사이 'this interval'; a different 요새 means 'fortress'.

T2-0715.x: I recently bought a new phone.
T2-0715.t: Use 최근에 as an adverb ('recently') and 최근 + noun for 'recent ___'.

T2-0716.m: the old days, long ago; once upon a time
T2-0716.ex: 옛날에는 이 동네에 큰 나무가 많았어요.
T2-0716.x: In the old days, there were many big trees in this neighborhood.
T2-0716.t: Pronounced [옌날] — nasalization; folk tales begin with 옛날 옛적에 'once upon a time'.

T2-0717.x: My Korean has improved a lot compared to before.
T2-0717.e: Built on 예 'old times', the same root as 옛날.

T2-0718.ex: 과거는 바꿀 수 없지만 미래는 바꿀 수 있어요.
T2-0718.x: You can't change the past, but you can change the future.

T2-0719.x: The current temperature in Seoul is 5 degrees below zero.
T2-0719.e: Literally 'appearing and existing' — what is here now.
T2-0719.t: 현재 is more formal than 지금 and is common in news and reports.

T2-0720.x: In the future, I want to become an elementary school teacher.

T2-0721.x: I'm busy right now, so I'll call you again later.
T2-0721.t: Almost always used as 나중에 'later'; 나중에 봐요 is a friendly 'see you later'.

T2-0722.m: from now on, in the future; forward
T2-0722.x: From now on, I'll study Korean harder.
T2-0722.t: The literal sense also exists: 앞으로 가세요 means 'go straight ahead'.

T2-0723.m: a little later (today), in a while
T2-0723.ex: 이따가 회사 앞에서 점심 같이 먹어요.
T2-0723.x: Let's have lunch together in front of the office a little later.
T2-0723.t: Don't confuse it with 있다가 'stay and then'; 이따가 means 'later today'.

T2-0724.x: A friend from my hometown called me a little while ago.
T2-0724.t: 아까 is for earlier the same day; for days or years ago use 전에 or 예전에.

T2-0725.x: I just got home a moment ago, too.
T2-0725.t: 방금 points to the very recent past; 금방 usually means 'soon' or 'quickly'.

T2-0726.m: soon, in a moment; quickly; just now
T2-0726.x: I'll be there soon, please wait just a little.
T2-0726.e: Literally 'now-just'; flip the syllables and you get 방금 'just now'.

T2-0727.ex: 이제 한국 음식을 잘 먹을 수 있어요.
T2-0727.x: Now I can eat Korean food well.
T2-0727.e: 이 'this' + 제 'time', the same 제 as in 언제 'when'.
T2-0727.t: 이제 suggests a change from before; 지금 simply means the present moment.

T2-0728.x: The vacation I'd been waiting for so long has finally started.
T2-0728.t: 드디어 is for long-awaited results; for 'in the end' (often disappointing) use 결국.

T2-0729.forms: 언젠가 + future: 언젠가 가 보고 싶어요
T2-0729.x: I want to live in Korea someday.
T2-0729.e: From 언제 'when' + -ㄴ가, just like 누군가 'someone' from 누구.

T2-0730.e: Native day count: 하루 (1), 이틀 (2), 사흘 (3), 나흘 (4).
T2-0730.t: 하루 종일 means 'all day long' — a very common phrase.

T2-0731.ex: 감기 때문에 이틀 동안 학교에 못 갔어요.
T2-0731.x: I couldn't go to school for two days because of a cold.
T2-0731.e: Native day count: 하루 (1), 이틀 (2), 사흘 (3), 나흘 (4).

T2-0732.x: I work out three times a week.
T2-0732.t: 'X times a week' is 일주일에 X 번, with the particle 에.

T2-0733.x: I call my parents every Saturday.
T2-0733.e: 매- = every: 매일, 매주, 매달, 매년.

T2-0734.x: I have to pay rent at the end of every month.
T2-0734.t: 매달 and 매월 mean the same; 매월 sounds more formal.

T2-0735.x: Every summer I go to the beach with my family.

T2-0736.x: I came to Korea for the first time last year.

T2-0737.x: This year I really want to learn to drive.
T2-0737.e: Native 해 'year'; unlike 작년 and 내년, it is not Sino-Korean.

T2-0738.x: I'm going to graduate from college next year.

T2-0739.x: I went to a friend's birthday party last week.
T2-0739.t: 지난주 is written as one word, but 다음 주 and 이번 주 take a space.

T2-0740.x: I have a test next Monday.

T2-0742.x: I start working at a new company next month.
T2-0742.e: 다음 'next' + 달 'month'; written with a space, unlike 지난달.

T2-0743.x: I met a friend and saw a movie the day before yesterday.
T2-0743.t: The short form 그제 is also common in speech.

T2-0744.x: I couldn't sleep a wink all last night.
T2-0744.t: For 'to pull an all-nighter', say 밤을 새우다 (casually 밤새다): 어제 밤을 새웠어요.

T2-0745.x: After lunch, I took a short nap.
T2-0745.t: Use it with 자다: 낮잠을 자다 'to take a nap'. Pronounced [낟짬].

T2-0746.ex: 이 문제는 삼십 초 안에 풀어야 해요.
T2-0746.x: You have to solve this problem within thirty seconds.
T2-0746.e: Homonym warning: other 초 words mean 'candle' and 'beginning (of a period)'.
T2-0746.t: Seconds use Sino-Korean numbers: 십 초, 삼십 초.

T2-0747.forms: 말이 · 말을 (usually after a time word: 이번 달 말)
T2-0747.ex: 이번 달 말에 친구들과 여행을 가요.
T2-0747.x: I'm going on a trip with friends at the end of this month.
T2-0747.e: Homonym warning: other 말 words mean 'speech' and 'horse'.
T2-0747.t: It follows a time word: 이번 달 말, 학기 말; compounds include 주말, 월말, 연말.

T2-0748.x: At the end of the year, I spend time with my family.

T2-0749.x: During exam period, the library is crowded.

T2-0750.x: I take a walk in the park every morning.
T2-0750.t: Same meaning as 매일; -마다 attaches to other nouns too: 주말마다 'every weekend'.

T2-0751.x: On Lunar New Year's Day, families gather and eat rice cake soup.
T2-0751.e: 설 'new year' + 날 'day'; people eat 떡국 and bow to elders (세배).
T2-0751.t: Pronounced [설랄] — ㄴ becomes ㄹ next to ㄹ.

T2-0752.x: On Chuseok, I go to my hometown and make songpyeon.
T2-0752.e: Literally 'autumn evening' — the full moon of the eighth lunar month.

T2-0753.m: traditional holiday (such as Seollal or Chuseok)
T2-0753.ex: 명절에는 고향에 가는 고속도로가 많이 막혀요.
T2-0753.x: During the holidays, highways to people's hometowns get really jammed.
T2-0753.e: Literally 'famous festival' — mainly 설날 and 추석.

T2-0754.x: I exchanged small gifts with friends on Christmas.
T2-0754.e: From English 'Christmas'; the formal name is 성탄절. In Korea it's more of a couples' holiday.

T2-0755.x: I've decided to work out every day in the new year.
T2-0755.t: The standard greeting is 새해 복 많이 받으세요 — literally 'receive many blessings in the new year'.

T2-0756.x: My grandmother celebrates her birthday by the lunar calendar.
T2-0756.t: Pronounced [음녁] — nasalization; the solar calendar is 양력.

T2-0757.x: In Korea, the weather starts getting hot in June.
T2-0757.e: 육 'six' drops its ㄱ here: 유월, not 육월.
T2-0757.t: Only June and October change: 유월 and 시월; all other months are regular.

T2-0758.x: In October, the autumn leaves on the mountains are very pretty.
T2-0758.e: 십 'ten' drops its ㅂ here: 시월, not 십월.

T2-0759.ex: 어제 백화점에서 십만 원짜리 운동화를 샀어요.
T2-0759.x: Yesterday I bought sneakers that cost 100,000 won at the department store.
T2-0759.e: Literally 'ten ten-thousands' — Korean counts big numbers in units of 10,000.

T2-0760.ex: 이 도시에는 백만 명 이상이 살고 있어요.
T2-0760.x: More than a million people live in this city.

T2-0761.ex: 서울에서 아파트를 사려면 몇 억이 필요해요.
T2-0761.x: To buy an apartment in Seoul, you need several hundred million won.
T2-0761.e: The next big unit after 만: 10,000 × 10,000.

T2-0762.forms: 첫 번째 · 두 번째 · 세 번째
T2-0762.x: This is my second trip to Korea.
T2-0762.t: Use native numbers: 첫 번째 (not 한 번째), 두 번째, 세 번째.

T2-0763.forms: 여러 + noun: 여러 사람 · 여러 가지
T2-0763.x: I met friends from many different countries.
T2-0763.t: 여러 always comes right before a noun; it can't stand alone or take particles.

T2-0764.forms: 한 가지 · 두 가지 · 여러 가지
T2-0764.ex: 이 식당에는 여러 가지 메뉴가 있어요.
T2-0764.x: This restaurant has many kinds of dishes on the menu.
T2-0764.e: Homonym warning: other 가지 words mean 'branch' and 'eggplant'.
T2-0764.t: Count with native numbers: 한 가지, 두 가지, 세 가지.

T2-0765.forms: 모든 + noun: 모든 사람 · 모든 것
T2-0765.ex: 우리 반 모든 학생이 시험에 합격했어요.
T2-0765.x: Every student in our class passed the exam.
T2-0765.t: 모든 must come before a noun; on their own use 모두 or 다: 모두 왔어요.

T2-0766.m: all, everything, the whole; (as adverb) all
T2-0766.x: I finished all the homework I got today.

T2-0767.ex: 우리 반 전체가 함께 소풍을 갔어요.
T2-0767.x: Our whole class went on a picnic together.
T2-0767.t: 전체 is a noun for 'the whole'; for adverbial 'all' use 전부 or 모두.

T2-0768.x: Most students come to school by bus.

T2-0770.x: I split the pizza half and half with my friend.

T2-0771.m: little by little, a bit at a time, gradually
T2-0771.x: My Korean is getting better little by little.
T2-0771.t: 한 개씩 'one each', 두 명씩 'two at a time'.

T2-0772.ex: 우리 아이는 일부터 백까지 숫자를 읽을 수 있어요.
T2-0772.x: Our child can read the numbers from one to a hundred.
T2-0772.e: Literally 'counting letters'; the ㅅ in 숫 is an added linking sound.

T2-0773.ex: 이 식당은 음식 양이 정말 많아요.
T2-0773.x: This restaurant gives really big portions.
T2-0773.e: Homonym warning: other 양 words mean 'sheep' and 'both' (양쪽).
T2-0773.t: For portion size say 양이 많다/적다, not 크다/작다.

T2-0774.ex: 집에서 회사까지 삼십 분 정도 걸려요.
T2-0774.x: It takes about thirty minutes from home to the office.
T2-0774.t: After a number, 정도 means 'about': 한 시간 정도 'about an hour'.

T2-0775.ex: 이 영화는 열다섯 살 이상만 볼 수 있어요.
T2-0775.x: Only people aged fifteen and over can see this movie.
T2-0775.t: 이상 includes the number itself: 20세 이상 means 20 and older. A different 이상 means 'strange'.

T2-0776.m: or less, under, below; the following
T2-0776.ex: 키가 120센티미터 이하인 아이는 탈 수 없어요.
T2-0776.x: Children 120 centimeters tall or shorter can't ride.

T2-0777.x: The average score on this test is 75 points.

T2-0778.x: The kimchi my mom makes is the best.
T2-0778.t: 최고! on its own is a common compliment meaning 'the best!' or 'awesome!'.

T2-0779.x: I've lost about 3 kilograms since last month.
T2-0779.e: From English 'kilogram'; in speech often shortened to 킬로.
T2-0779.t: Korea uses the metric system, so body weight is given in kilograms, not pounds.

T2-0780.x: To make this cake, you need 200 grams of sugar.

T2-0781.forms: Sino numbers + 센티미터: 오십 센티미터, 백 센티미터; written cm
T2-0781.ex: 제 동생은 작년보다 키가 오 센티미터 컸어요.
T2-0781.x: My younger sibling grew five centimeters taller than last year.
T2-0781.e: From English 'centimeter'; often shortened to 센티 in speech.

T2-0782.forms: Native numbers + 송이: 한 송이, 두 송이, 장미 열 송이
T2-0782.m: counter for flowers; bunch (of grapes), cluster
T2-0782.ex: 생일에 친구에게 장미 열 송이를 선물했어요.
T2-0782.x: I gave my friend ten roses for her birthday.
T2-0782.e: Also counts grapes and bananas in bunches: 포도 한 송이.
T2-0782.t: Word order is noun + number + counter: 꽃 세 송이 = three flowers.

T2-0783.forms: Native numbers + 군데: 한 군데, 두 군데, 여러 군데
T2-0783.ex: 오늘 서점을 세 군데나 갔지만 그 책이 없었어요.
T2-0783.x: I went to three bookstores today, but none had that book.

T2-0784.e: Also works as a counter: 한 곳, 두 곳.

T2-0785.forms: Sino numbers + 퍼센트: 십 퍼센트, 오십 퍼센트; written %
T2-0785.ex: 이번 주말에 모든 옷을 삼십 퍼센트 할인해요.
T2-0785.x: All clothes are thirty percent off this weekend.
T2-0785.e: From English 'percent'; Korean adds 'eu' after the final t sound.

T2-0786.forms: 가져요 · 가졌어요 · 가질 거예요 · 가지세요 (short form of 가지다; vowel endings use 가지-)
T2-0786.m: to have, to own, to hold
T2-0786.ex: 저는 어릴 때부터 음악에 관심을 갖고 있었어요.
T2-0786.x: I have been interested in music since I was little.
T2-0786.e: Contracted from 가지다; the short form only joins consonant endings like -고, -는.
T2-0786.t: In speech 갖다 주다 means 'to bring something to someone': 물 좀 갖다 주세요.

T2-0787.m: to pay back, to repay; to return (a favor)
T2-0787.ex: 친구에게 빌린 돈을 다음 주에 갚을 거예요.
T2-0787.x: I'll pay back the money I borrowed from my friend next week.
T2-0787.e: Used for kindness too: 은혜를 갚다 = to repay a favor.

T2-0788.m: to look for, to find, to get (a job, a house)
T2-0788.x: I've been looking for a job since graduating.
T2-0788.e: Literally 'seek'; you seek and obtain something.
T2-0788.t: A different 구하다 (救) means 'to rescue': 사람을 구하다 = to save a person.

T2-0789.forms: 길러요 · 길렀어요 · 기를 거예요 · 기르세요 (르 irregular)
T2-0789.m: to raise, to bring up; to keep (a pet), to grow (plants); to grow (hair)
T2-0789.ex: 우리 가족은 강아지 한 마리를 길러요.
T2-0789.e: Also for hair or beards: 머리를 기르다 = to grow your hair out.

T2-0790.m: to raise, to bring up; to keep (a pet), to grow (plants)
T2-0790.ex: 저는 집에서 고양이 두 마리를 키워요.
T2-0790.x: I have two cats at home.
T2-0790.e: From 크다 'to be big' + causative -이우-: literally 'make big'.

T2-0791.m: to break, to be broken, to shatter
T2-0791.x: The glass fell on the floor and shattered.

T2-0792.x: I had a scary dream last night.
T2-0792.e: The noun 꿈 'dream' comes from 꾸- + -ㅁ.
T2-0792.t: Always say 꿈을 꾸다; Koreans 'dream a dream' rather than 'have' one.

T2-0793.m: to finish, to end, to complete
T2-0793.ex: 오늘 안에 이 숙제를 끝내야 해요.
T2-0793.x: I have to finish this homework today.
T2-0793.e: 끝 'end' + 내다 'put out': bring something to its end.
T2-0793.t: Pronounced [끈내다] — nasalization; 끝내다 takes an object, 끝나다 does not.

T2-0794.m: to come out, to appear; to happen, to break out; to grow
T2-0794.x: Suddenly there was a strange sound outside.
T2-0794.e: A super-productive verb: 화가 나다, 사고가 나다.
T2-0794.t: Learn it in chunks: 열이 나다 (have a fever), 냄새가 나다 (smell), 생각이 나다 (come to mind).

T2-0795.ex: 약속 시간에 늦은 친구가 한 시간 후에 나타났어요.
T2-0795.x: My late friend showed up an hour after the meeting time.
T2-0795.e: Built from 나다 'come out': something comes into view.

T2-0796.forms: 날아요 · 날았어요 · 날 거예요 · 나세요 (ㄹ drops)
T2-0796.ex: 새 한 마리가 하늘을 날고 있어요.
T2-0796.x: A bird is flying in the sky.
T2-0796.e: Related to 날개 'wing' and 날아가다 'fly away'.
T2-0796.t: The modifier is 나는 (나는 새 = a flying bird), which looks like 'I am'.

T2-0797.m: to exceed, to be over; to cross, to go over
T2-0797.e: 넘어지다 'fall over' and 넘치다 'overflow' share this root.

T2-0798.m: to fall down, to trip, to fall over
T2-0798.x: The road was slippery, so I fell in front of the school.
T2-0798.e: 넘다 'go over' + -어지다: you go over and fall.

T2-0799.ex: 한국에서 처음으로 가을 날씨의 아름다움을 느꼈어요.
T2-0799.x: In Korea I felt the beauty of autumn weather for the first time.
T2-0799.e: The noun 느낌 'feeling' comes from 느끼- + -ㅁ.

T2-0800.m: to resemble, to look like, to take after
T2-0800.x: I look more like my mother than my father.
T2-0800.t: Use the past form 닮았어요 for 'looks like' now; pronounced [담따].

T2-0801.ex: 오랜만에 고향에 가 보니 많이 달라졌어요.
T2-0801.x: When I visited my hometown after a long time, it had changed a lot.

T2-0802.m: to put in, to fill (a container); to contain
T2-0802.ex: 남은 음식을 그릇에 담아서 냉장고에 넣었어요.
T2-0802.x: I put the leftover food in a bowl and put it in the fridge.
T2-0802.e: Sounds just like 닮다 'resemble'; context tells them apart.

T2-0803.ex: 아이들이 공원에서 공을 던지며 놀고 있어요.
T2-0803.x: The kids are playing catch in the park.

T2-0804.ex: 어버이날에 부모님께 빨간 카네이션 꽃을 드렸어요.
T2-0804.x: On Parents' Day I gave my parents red carnations.
T2-0804.e: Humble counterpart of 주다, used when the receiver is higher in status.
T2-0804.t: Pair it with 께 instead of 에게: 선생님께 드려요; also in -아/어 드리다 'do for someone respected'.

T2-0805.m: to follow, to go along with; to keep up with
T2-0805.ex: 길을 잘 몰라서 앞에 가는 친구를 따라갔어요.
T2-0805.x: I didn't know the way well, so I followed my friend ahead of me.

T2-0806.forms: 따라요 · 따랐어요 · 따를 거예요 · 따르세요 (ㅡ drops)
T2-0806.m: to follow, to obey; to pour
T2-0806.x: We did the experiment following the teacher's explanation.
T2-0806.e: Two meanings share one spelling: 물을 따르다 means 'to pour water'.
T2-0806.t: -에 따라 means 'according to': 날씨에 따라 = depending on the weather.

T2-0807.forms: 떠들어요 · 떠들었어요 · 떠들 거예요 · 떠드세요 (ㄹ drops)
T2-0807.m: to make noise, to be loud, to chatter
T2-0807.ex: 도서관에서 큰 소리로 떠들면 안 돼요.
T2-0807.x: You must not talk loudly in the library.

T2-0808.m: to drop; to lower (a price, a score)
T2-0808.x: I dropped my phone on the subway and the screen cracked.
T2-0808.e: Transitive partner of 떨어지다 'to fall': you make something fall.

T2-0809.m: to run; to jump; to beat (heart)
T2-0809.x: I ran to the bus stop because I was afraid of missing the bus.
T2-0809.e: Also the heart: 가슴이 뛰다 = my heart is pounding.

T2-0810.forms: 떠요 · 떴어요 · 뜰 거예요 · 뜨세요 (ㅡ drops)
T2-0810.m: to rise (sun, moon); to float; to open (eyes)
T2-0810.x: The sun rises around six in the morning.
T2-0810.e: Several homonyms: 눈을 뜨다 'open eyes', 자리를 뜨다 'leave a seat'.
T2-0810.t: Opposite pairs: 해가 뜨다 / 해가 지다, and 눈을 뜨다 / 눈을 감다.

T2-0811.m: to finish, to complete, to end
T2-0811.x: After finishing class, I had lunch with my friends.

T2-0812.m: to block, to stop; to prevent
T2-0812.ex: 큰 차가 길을 막고 있어서 지나갈 수 없어요.
T2-0812.x: A big truck is blocking the road, so we can't get through.
T2-0812.e: Its passive 막히다 gives 길이 막히다 'traffic is jammed'.

T2-0813.x: Please don't touch the artwork with your hands in the museum.

T2-0814.m: to leave (in someone's care), to entrust; to assign
T2-0814.ex: 여행 가는 동안 강아지를 친구에게 맡겼어요.
T2-0814.x: I left my puppy with a friend while I was traveling.
T2-0814.e: Causative of 맡다 'to take charge of': make someone take charge.
T2-0814.t: Pronounced [맏끼다]; hotels use it for luggage: 짐을 맡길 수 있어요?

T2-0815.m: to take, to accompany (honorific); to live with and care for (elders)
T2-0815.x: On the weekend I took my grandmother to the hospital.
T2-0815.t: Use 모시고 가다 for elders, 데리고 가다 for kids or friends.

T2-0816.m: to gather, to get together, to meet; to be collected
T2-0816.ex: 설날에 온 가족이 할머니 댁에 모였어요.
T2-0816.x: On Lunar New Year the whole family got together at Grandma's house.
T2-0816.e: Passive of 모으다 'to gather, collect'; the noun 모임 means 'meeting'.
T2-0816.t: 모이다 needs no object (people gather); 모으다 takes one (돈을 모으다 = save money).

T2-0817.m: to be short, to be lacking, to be not enough
T2-0817.x: I was a little short of money, so I borrowed some from a friend.

T2-0818.ex: 저는 무슨 일이 있어도 친구의 말을 믿어요.
T2-0818.x: No matter what happens, I believe what my friend says.
T2-0818.e: The noun 믿음 'faith, trust' comes from 믿- + -음.

T2-0819.forms: 밀어요 · 밀었어요 · 밀 거예요 · 미세요 (ㄹ drops)
T2-0819.x: Even if I push the door hard, it won't open.
T2-0819.t: Door signs read 미세요 (push) and 당기세요 (pull).

T2-0820.m: to hope, to wish, to want
T2-0820.x: I hope all of you stay healthy in the new year.
T2-0820.e: The noun 바람 'wish' comes from 바라- + -ㅁ.
T2-0820.t: Standard form is 바라요, though many people say 바래요 in speech.

T2-0821.forms: 발라요 · 발랐어요 · 바를 거예요 · 바르세요 (르 irregular)
T2-0821.m: to apply, to put on, to spread (cream, lotion, butter)
T2-0821.ex: 밖에 나가기 전에 선크림을 꼭 바르세요.
T2-0821.x: Be sure to put on sunscreen before you go outside.
T2-0821.e: Homonym warning: the adjective 바르다 means 'upright, correct'.
T2-0821.t: Use 바르다 for anything spread on skin or bread: 약을 바르다, 버터를 바르다.

T2-0822.m: to step on, to tread on
T2-0822.x: I stepped on someone's foot on the subway.
T2-0822.t: Pronounced [밥따], but 밟아요 is [발바요] — the ㄹ comes back before vowels.

T2-0823.forms: 벌어요 · 벌었어요 · 벌 거예요 · 버세요 (ㄹ drops)
T2-0823.x: I earned money from a part-time job during vacation.

T2-0824.ex: 십 년 동안 이 동네가 많이 변했어요.
T2-0824.x: This neighborhood has changed a lot over ten years.
T2-0824.t: 변하다 is gradual change in nature; 바뀌다 is replacing one thing with another.

T2-0825.m: to send, to mail (a letter, package); to fry (pancakes)
T2-0825.ex: 어제 우체국에 가서 고향에 소포를 부쳤어요.
T2-0825.x: Yesterday I went to the post office and mailed a package home.
T2-0825.e: Homonym: 전을 부치다 means 'to pan-fry Korean pancakes'.
T2-0825.t: Don't confuse with 붙이다 'to stick, attach' — same pronunciation [부치다].

T2-0826.m: to be empty, to be vacant
T2-0826.ex: 실례지만 혹시 이 자리 비어 있어요?
T2-0826.x: Excuse me, is this seat free?
T2-0826.e: Usually in the form 비어 있다; 빈 자리 = an empty seat.

T2-0827.m: to fall into; to fall out, to come out; to be left out, to skip; to be into
T2-0827.ex: 요즘 한국 드라마에 빠져서 매일 봐요.
T2-0827.x: I'm really into Korean dramas lately, so I watch them every day.
T2-0827.e: Core idea is 'slip out or sink in': 머리가 빠지다, 물에 빠지다.
T2-0827.t: Common chunks: 살이 빠지다 (lose weight), 수업에 빠지다 (skip class), 사랑에 빠지다 (fall in love).

T2-0829.m: to come into being, to be newly made; to happen, to arise; to get, to have; to look (a certain way)
T2-0829.x: A new cafe opened in front of the school.
T2-0829.t: Use the past for states: 남자 친구가 생겼어요 = 'I've got a boyfriend.'

T2-0830.x: The child counted from one to ten on his fingers.
T2-0830.e: Homonym warning: the adjective 세다 means 'strong'; 셈 'counting' comes from this verb.
T2-0830.t: The polite form 세요 looks like the honorific ending -세요; context tells you which it is.

T2-0831.ex: 아이가 숨바꼭질을 하면서 문 뒤에 숨었어요.
T2-0831.x: The child hid behind the door while playing hide-and-seek.
T2-0831.e: Found in 숨바꼭질 'hide-and-seek'; its causative 숨기다 means 'to hide something'.

T2-0832.forms: 실어요 · 실었어요 · 실을 거예요 · 실으세요 (ㄷ irregular)
T2-0832.m: to load, to put (in a vehicle); to publish (an article)
T2-0832.ex: 이사하는 날 짐을 트럭에 모두 실었어요.
T2-0832.x: On moving day we loaded all our things onto the truck.
T2-0832.e: Also used for newspapers: 신문에 글을 싣다 = to run an article.

T2-0833.x: Please chew your food slowly and thoroughly.
T2-0833.t: Regular, not ㅂ irregular: 씹어요, never 씨워요.

T2-0834.m: to hug, to hold (in one's arms)
T2-0834.ex: 엄마가 우는 아기를 꼭 안아 주었어요.
T2-0834.x: The mom held the crying baby tight.
T2-0834.e: Homonym warning: 안다 is also 알다 'know' with -ㄴ다; 안기다 = be hugged.
T2-0834.t: Pronounced [안따]; don't mix it up with 앉다 'to sit', also pronounced [안따].

T2-0835.forms: 알아들어요 · 알아들었어요 · 알아들을 거예요 · 알아들으세요 (ㄷ irregular)
T2-0835.m: to understand (what one hears), to catch
T2-0835.ex: 선생님이 너무 빨리 말해서 잘 못 알아들었어요.
T2-0835.x: The teacher spoke too fast, so I couldn't really follow.
T2-0835.t: Handy phrase: 잘 못 알아들었어요. 다시 말해 주세요. — 'I didn't catch that; please say it again.'

T2-0836.m: to look into, to find out, to check; to recognize
T2-0836.ex: 여행 가기 전에 호텔 가격을 알아봤어요.
T2-0836.x: I checked hotel prices before the trip.

T2-0837.m: to get, to gain, to obtain; to receive (for free)
T2-0837.ex: 이번 여행에서 좋은 경험을 많이 얻었어요.
T2-0837.x: I gained a lot of good experiences on this trip.

T2-0838.m: to disappear, to be gone, to be lost
T2-0838.x: The wallet I left on the desk is gone.

T2-0839.m: to open, to be opened; to be held (an event)
T2-0839.x: The window opened by itself because of the wind.
T2-0839.e: Passive of 열다 'to open'; also 'bear fruit': 사과가 열리다.
T2-0839.t: Events are 'opened' in Korean: 축제가 열려요 = the festival is held.

T2-0840.x: I'm going to take the picture, so don't move.
T2-0840.e: The noun 움직임 'movement' comes from 움직이- + -ㅁ.
T2-0840.t: Moving house is 이사하다, not 움직이다.

T2-0841.x: Many people lost their homes in the accident.
T2-0841.t: Pronounced [일타], but 잃어요 is [이러요] — the ㅎ goes silent before vowels.

T2-0842.x: I forgot my friend's birthday and felt really sorry.
T2-0842.t: 잊다 is forgetting information; losing an object is 잃다 — don't mix them up.

T2-0843.x: I grew up in a small seaside village.

T2-0844.m: to catch, to grab, to hold; to take (a taxi)
T2-0844.ex: 길을 건널 때는 아이의 손을 꼭 잡으세요.
T2-0844.x: Hold your child's hand tightly when crossing the street.
T2-0844.t: Regular verb (잡아요); also 택시를 잡다 'hail a taxi' and 약속을 잡다 'set an appointment'.

T2-0845.x: I had my height and weight measured at the hospital today.

T2-0846.forms: 잠가요 · 잠갔어요 · 잠글 거예요 · 잠그세요 (ㅡ drops)
T2-0846.m: to lock; to turn off (a faucet)
T2-0846.x: Be sure to lock the door when you leave.
T2-0846.t: Correct form is 잠가요; 잠궈요 is a very common mistake, even among natives.

T2-0847.x: Please write your name and phone number here.
T2-0847.e: Homonym warning: the adjective 적다 means 'few, little'.
T2-0847.t: Pronounced [적따]; 적다 means jotting down info, while 쓰다 covers all writing.

T2-0848.m: to decide, to set, to fix
T2-0848.x: Let's set the date for our next get-together.

T2-0849.forms: 주워요 · 주웠어요 · 주울 거예요 · 주우세요 (ㅂ irregular)
T2-0849.ex: 길에서 지갑을 주워서 경찰서에 갖다 줬어요.
T2-0849.x: I picked up a wallet on the street and took it to the police station.
T2-0849.t: Don't confuse 주워요 'pick up' with 줘요 'give'.

T2-0850.forms: 지어요 · 지었어요 · 지을 거예요 · 지으세요 (ㅅ irregular)
T2-0850.m: to build; to make (rice, clothes); to give (a name); to write (a poem)
T2-0850.e: Core idea 'create': 집을 짓다, 밥을 짓다, 이름을 짓다.
T2-0850.t: Before vowels the ㅅ disappears: 지어요, not 짓어요.

T2-0851.m: to put up with, to endure, to hold back
T2-0851.ex: 너무 웃겨서 웃음을 참을 수 없었어요.
T2-0851.x: It was so funny that I couldn't hold back my laughter.

T2-0852.m: to pack, to take (with you), to remember to bring; to look after
T2-0852.x: They say it'll rain. Make sure to take an umbrella.
T2-0852.e: Also caring: 밥 잘 챙겨 먹어 = 'make sure you eat properly'.
T2-0852.t: Hard to translate: it means making sure something or someone is taken care of.

T2-0853.m: to burn, to be burned; to get tanned
T2-0853.ex: 고기를 너무 오래 구워서 다 탔어요.
T2-0853.x: I grilled the meat too long, so it all burned.
T2-0853.e: Homonym warning: 타다 also means 'ride', 'mix in' and 'receive (a prize)'.
T2-0853.t: Sun can 'burn' you too: 얼굴이 탔어요 = my face got tanned.

T2-0854.forms: 틀어요 · 틀었어요 · 틀 거예요 · 트세요 (ㄹ drops)
T2-0854.m: to turn on (TV, radio, AC, music); to twist, to turn
T2-0854.x: It was so hot that I turned on the air conditioner.
T2-0854.e: Core idea 'twist': old dials and faucets were twisted on.
T2-0854.t: 틀다 is common for media and AC; for lights use 켜다.

T2-0855.m: to avoid, to dodge, to take shelter from
T2-0855.ex: 갑자기 비가 와서 편의점 안에서 비를 피했어요.
T2-0855.x: It suddenly rained, so I took shelter in a convenience store.

T2-0856.forms: 흔들어요 · 흔들었어요 · 흔들 거예요 · 흔드세요 (ㄹ drops)
T2-0856.ex: 친구가 저를 보고 멀리서 손을 흔들었어요.
T2-0856.x: My friend saw me and waved from far away.
T2-0856.e: Passive 흔들리다 means 'to shake, sway': 배가 흔들려요.

T2-0857.m: to spill, to shed (tears, sweat); to drop (and lose)
T2-0857.ex: 운동을 많이 해서 땀을 많이 흘렸어요.
T2-0857.x: I worked out a lot, so I sweated a lot.
T2-0857.e: Causative of 흐르다 'to flow': make something flow.

T2-0858.forms: 흘러요 · 흘렀어요 · 흐를 거예요 · 흐른 (+noun) (르 irregular)
T2-0858.m: to flow, to run; to pass (time)
T2-0858.x: The Han River flows slowly through the middle of Seoul.
T2-0858.e: Its causative is 흘리다 'to spill, shed'.

T2-0859.m: to decide, to make a decision
T2-0859.ex: 저는 내년에 한국으로 유학을 가기로 결정했어요.
T2-0859.x: I decided to go study abroad in Korea next year.
T2-0859.e: Literally 'decide and fix' — once it's settled, it's decided.
T2-0859.t: Use -기로 결정하다 for 'decide to do': 가기로 결정했어요 = I decided to go. 결정 is pronounced [결쩡].

T2-0860.x: Have you ever had experience working abroad?
T2-0860.e: Literally 'going through a test' — what you learn by living it.
T2-0860.t: Say -(으)ㄴ 경험이 있다 for 'have experienced': 가 본 경험이 있어요 = I've been there.

T2-0861.ex: 이번 여행에서 한국 문화를 많이 경험했어요.
T2-0861.x: I experienced a lot of Korean culture on this trip.
T2-0861.e: Literally 'go through and test' something for yourself.

T2-0862.x: Even if it's hard, I'm going to keep exercising.
T2-0862.e: Two syllables that both mean 'carry on' — doubled for emphasis.
T2-0862.t: 계속 alone works as an adverb: 계속 비가 와요 = It keeps raining. Pronounced [계소카다].

T2-0863.m: to have a hard time, to suffer, to go through hardship
T2-0863.x: I had a hard time moving because I had so much stuff.
T2-0863.e: Literally 'bitter life' — a stretch of hardship.
T2-0863.t: 고생하셨어요 / 고생 많으셨습니다 is a warm 'thanks for your hard work' after a task is done.

T2-0864.x: You need effort to get good results.
T2-0864.e: Literally 'striving strength' — putting your power into it.

T2-0865.m: to try hard, to make an effort, to strive
T2-0865.ex: 한국어를 잘하고 싶어서 매일 노력하고 있어요.
T2-0865.x: I want to be good at Korean, so I'm working hard at it every day.
T2-0865.t: For 'try to do', use -(으)려고 노력하다: 일찍 자려고 노력해요 = I try to go to bed early.

T2-0866.x: I overslept yesterday, so I was late for class.
T2-0866.t: Always pair it with 자다: 늦잠을 자다, never 늦잠을 하다.

T2-0867.m: to register, to enroll, to sign up
T2-0867.ex: 다음 달부터 요가 학원에 등록할 거예요.
T2-0867.x: I'm going to sign up for a yoga studio starting next month.
T2-0867.e: Literally 'enter into the record' — put your name on the list.
T2-0867.t: Pronounced [등노카다]: ㄹ after ㅇ turns to ㄴ, and ㄱ+ㅎ becomes ㅋ.

T2-0868.m: to take a bath, to bathe
T2-0868.x: When I'm tired, I take a bath in warm water.
T2-0868.e: Literally 'wash the hair and bathe the body' — a full-body wash.
T2-0868.t: 목욕탕 is a Korean public bathhouse, a big part of traditional culture.

T2-0869.m: to oppose, to be against, to object
T2-0869.x: At first, my parents were against my marriage.
T2-0869.t: The noun 반대 also means 'opposite': 반대 방향 = the opposite direction.

T2-0870.m: to agree, to approve, to be in favor of
T2-0870.x: I agree with that opinion of my friend's.
T2-0870.e: Literally 'support and help complete' a plan.

T2-0871.x: Try comparing the prices at the two stores.
T2-0871.e: Two syllables that both mean 'compare', side by side.

T2-0872.x: May I use this computer for a moment?
T2-0872.t: 사용하다 is for tools and objects; 이용하다 is for services and facilities like the subway or library.

T2-0873.m: to come to mind, to remember, to be reminded of
T2-0873.x: When I hear this song, I think of my hometown.
T2-0873.e: 생각 (thought) + 나다 (to come out) = a thought pops up on its own.
T2-0873.t: The thing remembered is the subject: 이름이 생각 안 나요 = I can't remember the name. Pronounced [생강나다].

T2-0874.x: Please choose just one of the two.
T2-0874.e: Two syllables that both mean 'pick', doubled.

T2-0875.ex: 그 사람은 사업에 성공해서 부자가 되었어요.
T2-0875.x: That person succeeded in business and became rich.
T2-0875.t: Use N에 성공하다 for 'succeed at N': 다이어트에 성공했어요 = I succeeded at my diet.

T2-0876.ex: 한 번 실패해도 다시 하면 돼요.
T2-0876.x: Even if you fail once, you can just try again.

T2-0877.x: I wash my face right after I get up in the morning.
T2-0877.e: Literally 'wash hands', but in Korean it means washing your face.
T2-0877.t: For washing hands, say 손을 씻다.

T2-0878.ex: 영화가 곧 시작되니까 휴대폰을 꺼 주세요.
T2-0878.x: The movie is starting soon, so please turn off your phone.
T2-0878.e: Literally 'begin making'; -되다 makes it happen on its own.
T2-0878.t: 시작하다 takes an object (수업을 시작해요); 시작되다 has a subject (수업이 시작돼요).

T2-0879.m: to apply for, to sign up for, to request
T2-0879.x: You need this document to apply for the scholarship.

T2-0880.m: to use, to make use of (a service or facility); to take advantage of
T2-0880.x: I take the subway when I go to work.

T2-0881.ex: 요즘 이 가수가 젊은 사람들에게 인기가 많아요.
T2-0881.x: These days this singer is very popular with young people.
T2-0881.e: Literally 'people energy' — the buzz people give something.
T2-0881.t: Pronounced [인끼]. Say 인기가 많다/있다 for 'popular' — there's no adjective form.

T2-0882.m: to be good at, to do well; to treat well
T2-0882.x: My friend is really good at singing.
T2-0882.t: The skill takes 을/를: 한국어를 잘해요. Written as one word, unlike 잘 먹다 or 잘 자다.

T2-0883.m: to be bad at, to be unable to do; to be worse than
T2-0883.ex: 저는 수영을 못해서 바다가 좀 무서워요.
T2-0883.x: I can't swim, so the ocean scares me a little.
T2-0883.e: 못 (can't) + 하다 (to do); the opposite of 잘하다.
T2-0883.t: Pronounced [모태요] for 못해요: ㅅ sounds like ㄷ, then ㄷ+ㅎ becomes ㅌ.

T2-0884.ex: 시험 준비 때문에 요즘 너무 바빠요.
T2-0884.x: I'm really busy these days because of exam prep.
T2-0884.e: Literally 'bring up to standard and prepare'.

T2-0885.m: to attend, to be present at
T2-0885.x: Please be sure to attend tomorrow's meeting.
T2-0885.e: Literally 'join a seat' — take your place at the event.
T2-0885.t: Use N에 참석하다 for meetings, weddings and ceremonies: 결혼식에 참석했어요.

T2-0886.x: There's plenty of time, so there's no need to worry.
T2-0886.e: Literally 'must-need' — something you can't do without.
T2-0886.t: -(으)ㄹ 필요가 없다 = there's no need to: 올 필요가 없어요. Pronounced [피료].

T2-0887.m: to check, to confirm, to verify
T2-0887.ex: 출발하기 전에 비행기 시간을 다시 확인하세요.
T2-0887.x: Double-check your flight time before you leave.

T2-0888.ex: 새로 온 친구를 모두 박수로 환영했어요.
T2-0888.x: Everyone welcomed the new friend with applause.
T2-0888.t: 환영합니다 = 'Welcome!' on signs and in speeches; shops greet you with 어서 오세요 instead.

T2-0889.ex: 그때 공부를 열심히 안 해서 후회해요.
T2-0889.x: I regret not studying hard back then.
T2-0889.e: Literally 'regret afterward' — the feeling that comes too late.

T2-0890.x: With my friend's help, I finished moving quickly.
T2-0890.e: Noun made from 돕다 (to help): 도우- + -ㅁ.

T2-0891.forms: N에 도움이 돼요 · 도움이 됐어요 · 도움이 될 거예요
T2-0891.m: to be helpful, to help, to be useful
T2-0891.ex: 이 책이 한국어 공부에 도움이 많이 됐어요.
T2-0891.x: This book really helped with my Korean studies.
T2-0891.t: The helpful thing is the subject and the area takes 에: 운동이 건강에 도움이 돼요.

T2-0892.ex: 영화 끝에 정말 슬픈 장면이 나와요.
T2-0892.x: There's a really sad scene at the end of the movie.
T2-0892.e: Root of 끝나다 (to end) and 끝내다 (to finish).
T2-0892.t: 끝이 is pronounced [끄치] and 끝을 [끄틀] — ㅌ turns into ㅊ before 이.

T2-0893.x: He was very poor when he was young.
T2-0893.e: From older 간난 'hardship'; the sound softened to 가난 over time.

T2-0894.x: If I win the lottery, I'll become rich.
T2-0894.t: Korean has no common adjective for 'rich' — say 부자예요 or 돈이 많아요.

T2-0895.m: to be simple, to be easy, to be brief
T2-0895.x: I was busy, so I had a quick, simple lunch of gimbap.

T2-0896.m: to be strong, to be powerful; to be intense
T2-0896.x: The wind is blowing hard today, so it's cold.
T2-0896.t: For physical strength in casual speech, 힘이 세다 is more natural than 강하다.

T2-0897.m: to be weak, to be frail; to be mild
T2-0897.x: I was physically weak as a child.
T2-0897.e: Literally 'weak'; careful — 약 meaning 'medicine' is a different word.

T2-0898.ex: 아침을 안 먹어서 배가 너무 고파요.
T2-0898.x: I skipped breakfast, so I'm really hungry.
T2-0898.t: Always with 배: 배가 고파요. Casual speech often drops 가: 배고파요.

T2-0899.m: to be so, to be like that
T2-0899.x: Yes, that's right. I think so too.
T2-0899.e: Short for 그러하다, 'be that way'; part of the set 이렇다, 그렇다, 저렇다.
T2-0899.t: 그래요? = Really? and 그래요 = Okay / That's right — two of the most useful replies.

T2-0900.m: to be like this, to be this way
T2-0900.ex: 이런 날씨에는 집에 있는 게 좋아요.
T2-0900.x: In weather like this, it's better to stay home.
T2-0900.e: Short for 이러하다, 'be this way'; part of the set 이렇다, 그렇다, 저렇다.

T2-0901.m: to be how, to be what like
T2-0901.ex: 한국에 온 지 한 달 됐는데 생활은 어때요?
T2-0901.x: It's been a month since you came to Korea — how's life here?
T2-0901.e: Short for 어떠하다; the question member of the set 이렇다, 그렇다, 저렇다.
T2-0901.t: N은/는 어때요? asks opinions or makes suggestions: 내일은 어때요? = How about tomorrow?

T2-0902.m: to be deep; to be profound
T2-0902.x: This river is deep, so swimming in it is dangerous.
T2-0902.t: Pronounced [깁따]; 깊은 keeps the ㅍ sound: [기픈].

T2-0903.x: It's cold outside, so wear thick clothes.
T2-0903.t: For books, clothes and paper; for thick soup or color use 진하다, for thick fingers use 굵다.

T2-0904.ex: 날씨가 따뜻한 봄에는 얇은 옷을 입어요.
T2-0904.x: In spring, when it's warm, I wear thin clothes.
T2-0904.t: Pronounced [얄따]. For thin people say 날씬하다 or 마르다, not 얇다.

T2-0905.m: to be exactly the same, to be identical
T2-0905.x: My sister and I bought the exact same clothes.
T2-0905.e: 똑 (exactly) + 같다 (to be the same) — a stronger 같다.

T2-0906.m: to be similar, to be alike
T2-0906.x: The two of them have very similar personalities.

T2-0907.m: to be cool, to be stylish, to be wonderful
T2-0907.x: Wow, you look really great today!

T2-0908.x: It snowed, so the roads are very slippery.

T2-0909.m: to be complicated; to be crowded, congested
T2-0909.x: The subway is really crowded during rush hour.
T2-0909.t: Besides 'complicated', it's the everyday word for crowded places: 시장이 복잡해요.

T2-0910.m: to be soft, to be smooth, to be gentle
T2-0910.x: This bread is really soft and tasty.

T2-0911.m: to be new, to be fresh
T2-0911.ex: 저는 지난주에 새로운 회사에서 일을 시작했어요.
T2-0911.x: Last week I started working at a new company.
T2-0911.e: 새 (new) + -롭다 (having that quality); 새 alone goes right before a noun: 새 차.
T2-0911.t: 새 is only used before nouns (새 집); for 'is new' as a predicate, use 새로워요 or 새 거예요.

T2-0912.m: to be precious, to be dear, to be valuable
T2-0912.x: My family are the most precious people to me.
T2-0912.e: Literally 'that which weighs heavily' in your heart.

T2-0913.m: to be severe, to be serious; to be too much, harsh
T2-0913.ex: 감기가 심해서 오늘 학교에 못 갔어요.
T2-0913.x: My cold was bad, so I couldn't go to school today.

T2-0914.m: to be a waste, to be a shame; to be too good to lose
T2-0914.x: It felt like a waste to throw the food away, so I ate it all.
T2-0914.e: Related to 아끼다 (to save, to cherish) — losing what you'd rather keep.
