T2-0915.m: to be strange, to be weird, to be odd
T2-0915.x: This milk tastes a little strange.
T2-0915.t: Don't confuse it with 이상 'more than' or 이상 'ideal' — same sound, different words.

T2-0916.m: to be used to, to be familiar with
T2-0916.ex: 처음에는 매웠지만 이제 한국 음식에 익숙해졌어요.
T2-0916.x: It was spicy at first, but now I've gotten used to Korean food.
T2-0916.e: Probably related to 익다 (to ripen; to get used to) — what's 'ripe' is familiar.
T2-0916.t: N에 익숙하다 = be used to N; add -해지다 for 'get used to'. Pronounced [익쑤카다].

T2-0917.m: to be suitable, to be appropriate; to be moderate, just right
T2-0917.ex: 운동은 매일 적당히 하는 게 좋아요.
T2-0917.x: It's good to exercise moderately every day.
T2-0917.e: Literally 'suited and proper' — not too much, not too little.
T2-0917.t: 적당히 can also mean 'half-heartedly': 적당히 하지 마세요 = Don't just do it halfway.

T2-0918.m: to be accurate, to be exact, to be correct
T2-0918.ex: 내일 모임의 정확한 시간을 알려 주세요.
T2-0918.x: Please tell me the exact time of tomorrow's get-together.

T2-0919.m: to be strong, to be thick (of drinks, flavors); to be dark, deep (of colors)
T2-0919.x: I drink strong coffee every morning.
T2-0919.e: Think of a thick, concentrated liquid — the opposite of watery.
T2-0919.t: Strong coffee is 진한 커피, not 강한 커피; light coffee or pale colors are 연하다.

T2-0920.m: to be enough, to be sufficient
T2-0920.x: There's still plenty of time, so take it slow.

T2-0921.m: to be special, to be particular
T2-0921.x: Today is my birthday, so it's a special day.

T2-0922.m: to be sturdy, to be strong, to be durable; to be healthy
T2-0922.ex: 이 가방은 튼튼해서 오래 쓸 수 있어요.
T2-0922.x: This bag is sturdy, so you can use it for a long time.

T2-0923.m: to be convenient, to be handy
T2-0923.x: There's a subway station near my house, so it's convenient.
T2-0923.t: Pronounced [펼리하다] — ㄴ before ㄹ becomes ㄹ (liquidization).

T2-0924.m: to be urgent, to be in a hurry; to be impatient
T2-0924.ex: 급한 일이 생겨서 먼저 가야 해요.
T2-0924.x: Something urgent came up, so I have to leave first.
T2-0924.t: 성격이 급하다 = to be impatient by nature. Pronounced [그파다].

T2-0925.m: to be lacking, to be insufficient, to be short of
T2-0925.x: I have a lot of work lately, so I'm not getting enough sleep.

T2-0926.m: to not matter, to be unrelated; to not care
T2-0926.x: Any food at all is fine with me.
T2-0926.t: Pronounced [상과넙따]. Handy reply when asked your preference: 저는 상관없어요.

T2-0927.forms: 가장 + adjective/adverb; 제일 is the casual equivalent
T2-0927.ex: 저는 사계절 중에서 가을을 가장 좋아해요.
T2-0927.x: Of the four seasons, I like fall the most.
T2-0927.t: N 중에서 가장 = the most among N; 가장 is a bit more formal than 제일.

T2-0928.ex: 길을 걷는데 갑자기 비가 내리기 시작했어요.
T2-0928.x: I was walking down the street when it suddenly started raining.

T2-0929.ex: 오늘 해야 하는 숙제를 거의 다 했어요.
T2-0929.x: I've almost finished the homework I have to do today.
T2-0929.t: With a negative it means 'hardly': 거의 안 먹어요 = I hardly eat. Usually pronounced [거이].

T2-0930.m: in the end, eventually, after all
T2-0930.ex: 오래 고민했지만 결국 그 집을 샀어요.
T2-0930.x: I thought about it for a long time, but in the end I bought that house.
T2-0930.e: Literally 'the tying-up of the situation' — how things end.
T2-0930.t: 결국 is neutral or negative ('ended up'); 드디어 is for a long-awaited happy result.

T2-0931.m: stop (doing), no more; just, without meaning to
T2-0931.ex: 밤이 늦었으니까 이제 게임 그만하고 자세요.
T2-0931.x: It's late, so stop playing games now and go to bed.
T2-0931.e: Root of 그만두다 (to quit) and 그만하다 (to stop).

T2-0932.forms: 그렇게 + verb/adjective: 그렇게 해요 · 그렇게 비싸요?
T2-0932.m: like that, that way; so, that much
T2-0932.ex: 그렇게 하면 더 빨리 끝날 거예요.
T2-0932.x: If you do it that way, you'll finish faster.
T2-0932.t: 그렇게 할게요 = I'll do that — a polite way to agree. Pronounced [그러케].

T2-0933.forms: 이렇게 + verb/adjective: 이렇게 해 보세요 · 이렇게 많아요?
T2-0933.m: like this, this way; so, this much
T2-0933.ex: 이 버튼을 이렇게 누르면 문이 열려요.
T2-0933.x: If you press this button like this, the door opens.
T2-0933.e: From 이렇다 (to be like this) + -게 (adverb ending).

T2-0934.forms: 꽤 + adjective/adverb: 꽤 맛있어요 · 꽤 많이
T2-0934.ex: 그 식당은 비싸지만 음식이 꽤 맛있어요.
T2-0934.x: That restaurant is expensive, but the food is pretty good.
T2-0934.t: 꽤 is weaker than 아주 but stronger than 좀 — like English 'pretty' or 'quite'.

T2-0935.x: If you study consistently every day, your skills will improve.
T2-0935.e: Adverb form of 꾸준하다 (to be steady).

T2-0936.x: That friend always has a smiling face.
T2-0936.e: Don't confuse it with 늘다 (to increase) — a different word.

T2-0937.forms: 다행히 + clause; 다행이에요 = What a relief
T2-0937.ex: 다행히 비가 그쳐서 소풍을 갈 수 있었어요.
T2-0937.x: Fortunately, the rain stopped, so we could go on the picnic.
T2-0937.t: 다행이다! (What a relief!) is a very common reaction on its own.

T2-0938.forms: 더욱 + adjective/verb; 더욱더 = even more and more
T2-0938.x: After I started exercising, I got even healthier.
T2-0938.e: A stronger, more written-sounding cousin of 더 'more'.

T2-0939.x: My friend and I paid separately.
T2-0939.e: Doubled as 따로따로 for 'each one on its own'.

T2-0940.forms: 또한 at the start or middle of a sentence; casual equivalent: 또
T2-0940.ex: 이 식당은 음식이 맛있고 또한 가격도 싸요.
T2-0940.x: This restaurant's food is tasty, and the prices are also cheap.
T2-0940.e: Built on 또 'again, also'; a more formal, written-style version.
T2-0940.t: 또한 sounds formal; in everyday speech people usually just say 또 or use -도.

T2-0941.forms: 마음대로 하세요 = Do as you like; casual: 맘대로
T2-0941.m: as one pleases, freely, at will
T2-0941.ex: 여기 있는 책은 마음대로 읽어도 돼요.
T2-0941.x: You can read the books here as you like.
T2-0941.e: 마음 'heart, mind' + 대로 'according to' — 'as your heart says'.

T2-0942.forms: 매우 + adjective; casual equivalents: 아주, 진짜
T2-0942.x: The weather is very cold this morning.
T2-0942.t: 매우 sounds formal or written; in conversation 아주, 너무 or 진짜 are more natural.

T2-0943.x: It was really great to see my friend after so long.

T2-0944.forms: 물론이에요 = Of course; 물론 A지만 B = A, of course, but B
T2-0944.x: Of course I'm going to the party too.
T2-0944.e: Literally 'no need to discuss' — so obvious it goes without saying.

T2-0945.ex: 이 약은 반드시 식사 후에 드세요.
T2-0945.x: Be sure to take this medicine after meals.
T2-0945.e: Sounds like 반듯이 'straight, neatly' — different spelling and meaning.

T2-0946.forms: 새로 + verb: 새로 사다, 새로 오다
T2-0946.x: I wore the new shoes I bought yesterday.
T2-0946.e: From 새 'new' + -로; compare 새 차 'a new car'.

T2-0948.x: No matter how busy I am, I always eat breakfast.
T2-0948.t: 아무리 almost always teams up with -아도/어도 later in the sentence.

T2-0949.forms: 아직도 + verb/adjective; 아직 안 = not yet
T2-0949.ex: 민수 씨는 그 영화를 아직도 안 봤어요?
T2-0949.x: Minsu, you still haven't seen that movie?
T2-0949.e: 아직 'still, yet' + 도 for emphasis; often sounds surprised.

T2-0950.ex: 이 국은 약간 짠 것 같아요.
T2-0950.x: I think this soup is a little salty.
T2-0950.e: Sino-Korean, but the syllables don't add up; learn it as a whole.

T2-0951.forms: 얼른 + verb or command: 얼른 오세요
T2-0951.x: We're late, so let's hurry and take a taxi.
T2-0951.t: 얼른 is conversational and urgent, often used in commands to children or friends.

T2-0952.ex: 할머니는 언제나 저를 반갑게 맞아 주세요.
T2-0952.x: My grandmother always welcomes me warmly.

T2-0953.forms: 역시 + sentence; 역시! = I knew it!
T2-0953.ex: 역시 엄마가 만든 김치가 제일 맛있어요.
T2-0953.x: As expected, the kimchi Mom makes is the best.
T2-0953.t: 역시! on its own means 'I knew it!' when something meets expectations.

T2-0954.forms: 오랫동안 + verb; 오랜만에 = after a long time
T2-0954.ex: 우리는 그 가게 앞에서 오랫동안 기다렸어요.
T2-0954.x: We waited in front of that store for a long time.
T2-0954.t: Pronounced [오래똥안] — the ㅅ in the middle makes 동 tense.

T2-0955.x: That's because I have an exam tomorrow.
T2-0955.e: Literally 'if you ask why': 왜 'why' + -냐 + 하면 'if one says'.
T2-0955.t: 왜냐하면 normally ends with -기 때문이에요 or -거든요.

T2-0956.forms: 우선 + verb; 우선 A, 그리고 B
T2-0956.m: first (of all), before anything else; for now
T2-0956.x: First, let's wash our hands, then eat.
T2-0956.e: Built around 'first' — do this before anything else.

T2-0957.forms: 일부러 + verb; 일부러 그런 거 아니에요 = I didn't mean it
T2-0957.x: I came out early on purpose to meet my friend.
T2-0957.t: 일부러 그런 거 아니에요 is the go-to phrase for 'I didn't do it on purpose.'

T2-0958.forms: 자꾸 + verb = keep (doing); 자꾸자꾸 = over and over
T2-0958.x: Lately, for some reason, I keep getting headaches.
T2-0958.e: Doubled as 자꾸자꾸 for 'over and over'.

T2-0959.forms: 자세히 + verb; 자세하다 = to be detailed
T2-0959.x: The teacher explained the grammar in detail.
T2-0959.e: Literally 'careful and fine' — looking at the fine details.

T2-0960.forms: 잠시만요 = Just a moment; 잠시 후에 = shortly
T2-0960.ex: 손님 여러분, 잠시 후에 열차가 출발합니다.
T2-0960.x: Passengers, the train will depart shortly.
T2-0960.t: 잠시만요 is a polite 'One moment, please' or 'Excuse me' when squeezing past people.

T2-0961.m: gradually, more and more, little by little
T2-0961.x: Spring is here, so it's getting warmer and warmer.

T2-0962.x: Thank you so much for helping me yesterday.
T2-0962.e: Literally 'with true words': 정 'true' + native 말 'words' + -로.

T2-0963.forms: 제대로 + verb; often 제대로 못 + verb
T2-0963.m: properly, right, as it should be
T2-0963.x: I couldn't sleep properly last night.
T2-0963.e: 제 'its own' + 대로 'according to' — 'in its proper way'.

T2-0964.forms: 조용히 하세요 = Please be quiet; 조용하다 = to be quiet
T2-0964.x: You always have to talk quietly in the library.

T2-0965.forms: 주로 + verb; 주로 뭐 해요? = What do you usually do?
T2-0965.x: On weekends I mostly watch movies at home.

T2-0966.forms: 직접 + verb: 직접 만들다, 직접 가다
T2-0966.e: Literally 'direct contact' — no one in between.
T2-0966.t: Pronounced [직쩝] — the ㅈ tenses after the ㄱ batchim.

T2-0967.x: The sky is really clear and pretty today.
T2-0967.e: Also a native noun meaning 'truth', as in 참말 'true words'.
T2-0967.t: Said alone, 참! means 'Oh, right!' when you suddenly remember something.

T2-0968.ex: 저는 과일 중에서 특히 딸기를 좋아해요.
T2-0968.x: Among fruits, I especially like strawberries.
T2-0968.t: Pronounced [트키] — ㄱ and ㅎ merge into an aspirated ㅋ.

T2-0969.forms: 한번 -아/어 보세요 = Give it a try
T2-0969.ex: 제가 만든 김치찌개를 한번 드셔 보세요.
T2-0969.x: Try the kimchi stew I made.
T2-0969.e: 한 'one' + 번 'time' — but often just softens a suggestion.
T2-0969.t: Write 한번 for 'try, sometime' but 한 번, with a space, for literally 'one time'.

T2-0970.m: by any chance, perhaps; just in case
T2-0970.x: Is there a pharmacy around here, by any chance?
T2-0970.e: Literally 'perhaps it is' — a soft opener for questions.
T2-0970.t: Starting a question with 혹시 makes it sound softer and more polite.

T2-0971.x: To Seoul, the train is much faster than the bus.

T2-0972.forms: 깜짝 놀라다 = to be startled; 깜짝 파티 = surprise party
T2-0972.ex: 갑자기 큰 소리가 나서 깜짝 놀랐어요.
T2-0972.x: There was a sudden loud noise, and I was startled.
T2-0972.t: 깜짝이야! is what Koreans blurt out when startled — like 'Oh, you scared me!'

T2-0973.forms: 미리 + verb: 미리 예약하다, 미리 준비하다
T2-0973.m: in advance, beforehand, ahead of time
T2-0973.x: It's crowded on weekends, so book in advance.

T2-0974.forms: 살짝 + verb: 살짝 웃다, 살짝 닫다
T2-0974.ex: 아기가 자니까 문을 살짝 닫아 주세요.
T2-0974.x: The baby is sleeping, so please close the door gently.

T2-0975.ex: 이 비밀은 절대로 다른 사람에게 말하지 마세요.
T2-0975.x: Never tell this secret to anyone else.
T2-0975.e: Literally 'cut off from any opposite' — absolute, beyond comparison.
T2-0975.t: Pronounced [절때로]; mostly used with negatives like 안, 못 or -지 마세요.

T2-0976.x: Yesterday I rested at home all day.
T2-0976.e: 하루 'one day' + 종일, literally 'to the end of the day'.

T2-0977.forms: 가만히 있어요 = Stay still; 가만! = Wait a sec!
T2-0977.ex: 사진을 찍을 때 가만히 있어 주세요.
T2-0977.x: Please hold still while I take the photo.

T2-0978.forms: 쉽게 + verb; from 쉽다 (ㅂ irregular: 쉬워요)
T2-0978.ex: 이 책은 아이들도 쉽게 읽을 수 있어요.
T2-0978.x: Even kids can read this book easily.
T2-0978.e: From 쉽다 'to be easy' + -게, the usual way to make an adverb.

T2-0979.x: So I need to go to bed early tonight.
T2-0979.t: In conversation, 그러니까! alone means 'Exactly! That's what I'm saying.'

T2-0980.m: then, in that case, if so

T2-0981.x: Even so, I like this job.
T2-0981.e: 그렇다 'to be so' + -아도 'even if' — 'even if that's so'.

T2-0982.ex: 그렇지만 아직 숙제를 다 못 했어요.
T2-0982.x: But I still haven't finished my homework.
T2-0982.t: Pronounced [그러치만] — ㅎ and ㅈ merge into ㅊ.

T2-0983.m: and then, while doing that; if you keep that up
T2-0983.x: And then it suddenly started to rain.

T2-0984.m: besides, on top of that, moreover
T2-0984.ex: 게다가 그 식당은 가격도 아주 싸요.
T2-0984.x: On top of that, the restaurant is very cheap too.
T2-0984.e: Probably a contraction of 거기에다가 'adding to that'.

T2-0985.forms: A 아니면 B = A or B; between two questions
T2-0985.x: Would you like coffee, or tea?
T2-0985.t: 아니면 is the everyday 'or' between questions; 또는 is more formal or written.

T2-0986.ex: 따라서 내일은 학교에서 수업을 하지 않습니다.
T2-0986.x: Therefore, there will be no classes at school tomorrow.

T2-0987.forms: 그런 + noun; 그런 거 = that kind of thing (casual)
T2-0987.x: I really like that kind of movie.
T2-0987.e: Short for 그러한, from 그렇다 'to be like that'.
T2-0987.t: 그런 points to something just mentioned or known to the listener.

T2-0988.x: In weather like this, I want to stay home.
T2-0988.e: Short for 이러한, from 이렇다 'to be like this'.
T2-0988.t: Said alone, 이런! is a mild 'Oh no!' or 'Darn!'

T2-0989.ex: 저런 가방은 어디에서 살 수 있어요?
T2-0989.x: Where can I buy a bag like that?
T2-0989.e: Short for 저러한, from 저렇다 'to be like that (over there)'.

T2-0990.ex: 죄송한데 이 옷은 다른 색깔도 있어요?
T2-0990.x: Excuse me, does this come in another color?
T2-0990.e: Modifier form of 다르다 'to be different'.
T2-0990.t: For 'different', use 다르다, not 틀리다, which means 'wrong'.

T2-0991.forms: Same form after any noun, with or without batchim: 꽃처럼, 학생처럼
T2-0991.x: My younger sibling sings as well as a singer.
T2-0991.t: N처럼 and N같이 are interchangeable: 꽃처럼 = 꽃같이 'like a flower'.
rel: to be the same, be like

T2-0992.forms: Same form after any noun: 날마다, 주말마다, 사람마다
T2-0992.ex: 저는 주말마다 집 근처 공원에서 운동해요.
T2-0992.x: I exercise in the park near my house every weekend.
T2-0992.t: 사람마다 달라요 'It differs from person to person' is a very handy pattern.

T2-0993.forms: Same form after any noun; ALWAYS followed by a negative: 밖에 없다, 밖에 안/못 …
T2-0993.ex: 지금 제 지갑에 천 원밖에 없어요.
T2-0993.x: I only have 1,000 won in my wallet right now.
T2-0993.e: Literally 'outside of' (밖 'outside' + 에): nothing beyond this amount.
T2-0993.t: Unlike 만, 밖에 must be followed by a negative: 하나밖에 없어요, never 하나밖에 있어요.

T2-0994.forms: Honorific subject particle; replaces 이/가 after a respected person: 할머니께서; topic: 께서는
T2-0994.ex: 우리 할아버지께서는 매일 아침 신문을 읽으세요.
T2-0994.x: My grandfather reads the newspaper every morning.
T2-0994.t: Pair 께서 with the honorific -(으)시- verb ending: 아버지께서 오셨어요.

T2-0995.forms: Honorific of 에게/한테; used after a respected person: 선생님께
T2-0995.ex: 저는 어버이날에 어머니께 예쁜 꽃을 드렸어요.
T2-0995.x: On Parents' Day, I gave my mother pretty flowers.
T2-0995.t: Pair 께 with humble verbs: 주다 becomes 드리다, 말하다 becomes 말씀드리다.

T2-0996.forms: 이나 after a consonant (책이나), 나 after a vowel (커피나)
T2-0996.m: or; … or something; as many as
T2-0996.x: Shall we watch a movie or something this weekend?
T2-0996.t: With numbers it shows surprise: 세 시간이나 기다렸어요 'I waited a whole three hours.'

T2-0997.forms: 이랑 after a consonant (동생이랑), 랑 after a vowel (친구랑)
T2-0997.x: Yesterday I watched a movie with a friend.

T2-0998.forms: Same form after any person or animal; casual (often shortened to 한테)
T2-0998.x: Yesterday, on my birthday, I got a present from my younger sibling.
T2-0998.t: Use 한테서 for people and 에서 for places: 친구한테서, 학교에서.

T2-0999.forms: Same form after any person or animal; more formal or written than 한테서
T2-0999.ex: 저는 이 편지를 고향 친구에게서 받았어요.
T2-0999.x: I got this letter from a friend back home.

T2-1000.forms: 와! (exclamation); stretched 와아 or 우와 for extra excitement
T2-1000.x: Wow, the view here is really beautiful!
T2-1000.e: Homonym warning: 와 is also the particle 'and', as in 사과와 배.

T2-1001.x: Oh my, is it already this late?
T2-1001.e: Stretched to 어머나 for extra surprise.
T2-1001.t: 어머 tends to sound feminine; men more often say 어, 와 or 아이고.

T2-1002.m: oh my, oh dear, ouch, ugh
T2-1002.x: Oh, my back really hurts today.
T2-1002.e: Often softened to 아이구 or 에구 in speech.

T2-1003.x: Excuse me, could we get some water here?
T2-1003.e: 저기 'over there' + 요 for politeness — literally 'over there!'
T2-1003.t: In restaurants, calling staff with 저기요 or 여기요 is polite and completely normal.

T2-1004.x: When my friends ask me something, I usually answer 'yeah.'
T2-1004.t: Use 응 only with close friends or younger people; say 네 to elders and strangers.

T2-1005.e: Literally 'ground and place' — two 'place' syllables together.

T2-1006.x: On the weekend I went shopping downtown with a friend.
T2-1006.t: Homonym: native 시내 also means 'stream, creek'; context makes it clear.

T2-1007.x: A big festival was held in front of City Hall.
T2-1007.t: Homonym: 시청 also means 'TV viewing', as in 시청자 'viewer'.

T2-1008.ex: 저는 동네 주민센터에서 요가 수업을 들어요.
T2-1008.x: I take a yoga class at the local community center.
T2-1008.t: Formerly called 동사무소; you go there for official documents and cheap hobby classes.

T2-1009.x: I lost my wallet, so I went to a nearby police station.
T2-1009.t: Pronounced [경찰써] — 서 becomes tense after the ㄹ.

T2-1010.ex: 우리 동네 빵집은 빵이 아주 맛있어요.
T2-1010.x: The bakery in my neighborhood has really tasty bread.
T2-1010.e: 빵 'bread', from Portuguese 'pão' via Japanese, + 집 'shop'.
T2-1010.t: Pronounced [빵찝] — 집 becomes tense in this compound.

T2-1011.x: I bought a single rose at the flower shop.
T2-1011.e: 꽃 'flower' + 집 'house, shop' — 집 forms many shop names.
T2-1011.t: Pronounced [꼳찝] — ㅊ sounds like ㄷ, then 집 becomes tense.

T2-1012.x: I bought pants at a clothing store downtown.

T2-1013.x: I bought a notebook at the stationery store in front of the school.

T2-1014.x: Yesterday I dropped off my winter coat at the dry cleaner's.
T2-1014.e: Literally 'washing place'; -소 = place for an activity: 세탁소, 주유소.

T2-1015.m: Korean sauna, jjimjilbang (public bathhouse with heated rooms)
T2-1015.x: I went to a jjimjilbang with my family on the weekend.

T2-1016.x: My car was out of gas, so I stopped by a gas station.
T2-1016.t: Koreans say 기름을 넣다, literally 'put in oil', for filling up with gas.

T2-1017.x: Yesterday I saw a movie with a friend at the theater.
T2-1017.e: Literally 'drama place'; used for both stage and movie theaters.
T2-1017.t: Pronounced [극짱] — the ㅈ tenses after ㄱ.

T2-1018.x: I play basketball with friends in the school gym.

T2-1019.ex: 시청 앞 광장에 사람들이 많이 모였어요.
T2-1019.x: Lots of people gathered in the square in front of City Hall.
T2-1019.e: Literally 'wide place' — an open public square.

T2-1020.x: The kids are having fun playing at the playground.

T2-1021.x: Our company's parking lot is on the second basement level.
T2-1021.t: Floors below ground are 지하 1층, 지하 2층 — like B1 and B2 in English.

T2-1022.x: If you go up to the rooftop, you can see the night sky well.
T2-1022.t: 옥상 is the flat rooftop you can stand on; 지붕 is the roof covering itself.

T2-1023.m: snack bar, cheap Korean snack restaurant
T2-1023.x: I ate tteokbokki at the snack bar in front of school.

T2-1024.x: I want to enjoy beautiful nature in the countryside.
T2-1024.e: Literally 'so by itself' — things as they naturally are.
T2-1024.t: 자연스럽다 means 'natural' as in not awkward: 자연스러운 한국어 'natural Korean'.

T2-1025.x: It rained a lot, so the ground got wet.

T2-1026.ex: 산 위에 아주 큰 바위가 있어요.
T2-1026.x: There is a very big rock on top of the mountain.
T2-1026.t: 돌 is any stone or pebble; 바위 is a big rock or boulder.

T2-1027.x: The kids are making a castle out of sand at the beach.

T2-1028.x: Walking in the forest makes me feel better.
T2-1028.t: Alone it sounds like [숩], but the ㅍ returns before a vowel: 숲이 [수피].

T2-1029.x: In the summer I went to a mountain valley with my family.
T2-1029.e: Literally 'stream valley' — a mountain valley with a creek.

T2-1030.ex: 오늘은 바람이 많이 불어서 파도가 높아요.
T2-1030.x: It's very windy today, so the waves are high.
T2-1030.e: Both syllables mean 'wave' — big rolling waves.
T2-1030.t: Waves 'strike' in Korean: 파도가 치다 'waves break'.

T2-1031.x: Now that we're in the mountains, the air is really clean.
T2-1031.e: Literally 'empty air' — the air filling space.

T2-1032.x: I reduce my trash to protect the environment.
T2-1032.t: A very common collocation is 환경 보호 'environmental protection'.

T2-1033.x: In autumn, the leaves turn red.
T2-1033.e: 나무 'tree' + 잎 'leaf', joined by the in-between ㅅ.

T2-1034.x: I got roses from my boyfriend on my birthday.
T2-1034.e: From an old two-syllable Chinese word for the rose; the syllables aren't reused elsewhere.
T2-1034.t: Count flowers with 송이: 장미 한 송이 'one rose'.

T2-1035.ex: 우리 집 강아지는 산책을 정말 좋아해요.
T2-1035.x: Our puppy really loves going for walks.
T2-1035.e: Probably 개 'dog' + baby suffix -아지, as in 송아지 'calf', 망아지 'foal'.
T2-1035.t: Koreans often call any pet dog 강아지, not just puppies, because it sounds cuter.

T2-1036.x: The rabbit is happily eating a carrot.
T2-1036.e: Koreans see a rabbit pounding rice cakes on the moon.

T2-1037.x: I saw a really big bear at the zoo.
T2-1037.e: In Korea's founding myth, a bear became a woman and gave birth to Dangun.

T2-1038.x: Tigers often appear in old Korean folk tales.
T2-1038.e: Korea's iconic animal; tiger mascots represented the 1988 and 2018 Olympics in Korea.

T2-1039.x: People call the lion the king of animals.

T2-1040.ex: 동물원에 있는 코끼리는 코가 아주 길어요.
T2-1040.x: The elephant at the zoo has a very long trunk.
T2-1040.e: Probably from 코 'nose' + 길다 'long': the long-nosed animal.

T2-1041.x: The monkey climbs the tree and eats a banana.

T2-1042.x: Last summer I rode a horse for the first time on Jeju Island.
T2-1042.e: Homonym: 말 also means 'words, speech'; context tells you which.
T2-1042.t: Older speakers say speech 말 with a long vowel and horse 말 short; most young speakers no longer distinguish them.

T2-1043.ex: 저는 어렸을 때부터 뱀이 정말 무서워요.
T2-1043.x: I've been really scared of snakes since I was little.

T2-1044.ex: 꽃 위에 노란 나비가 앉아 있어요.
T2-1044.x: A yellow butterfly is sitting on the flower.
T2-1044.e: Also a classic name for a cat — '나비야!' is how people call a kitty.

T2-1045.ex: 어젯밤에 모기 때문에 잠을 못 잤어요.
T2-1045.x: I couldn't sleep last night because of mosquitoes.
T2-1045.t: Mosquitoes 'bite' with 물다: 모기한테 물렸어요 'I got bitten by a mosquito.'

T2-1046.x: These days, many people have pets.
T2-1046.e: Literally 'love-and-play animal'; 반려동물 'companion animal' is now often preferred.

T2-1047.ex: 주말에는 이 거리에 사람이 아주 많아요.
T2-1047.x: On weekends, this street is very crowded.
T2-1047.e: Homonym: 거리 also means 'distance' and 'material, something to do'.
T2-1047.t: 길 is any road or path; 거리 is a street with shops and people.

T2-1048.x: My wallet and phone are inside my bag.
T2-1048.e: Also means gut or heart: 속이 안 좋아요 'my stomach is upset'.
T2-1048.t: 안 is the general 'inside'; 속 suggests deep inside something filled, like a bag, forest or water.

T2-1049.x: The weather outside is really cold today.
T2-1049.t: 바깥이 is pronounced [바까치] — ㅌ becomes ㅊ before 이 (palatalization).

T2-1050.x: There are many trees on both sides of the road.

T2-1051.ex: 우리 집은 학교와 회사 중간에 있어요.
T2-1051.x: My house is halfway between the school and my office.
T2-1051.t: 중간고사 is a midterm exam, and 기말고사 is a final exam.

T2-1052.x: There's a convenience store and a park around my house.
T2-1052.e: Literally 'around the edges' — the surrounding area.

T2-1053.x: This bag looks like a fake to me.
T2-1053.e: 가 'false' + native suffix -짜, just like 진짜 'real'.

T2-1054.x: Yesterday my younger sibling lied to Mom.
T2-1054.t: Pronounced [거진말] — the final ㅅ sounds like ㄷ, then nasalizes to ㄴ before ㅁ.

T2-1055.forms: 거짓말해요 · 거짓말했어요 · 거짓말할 거예요 · 거짓말하지 마세요
T2-1055.m: to lie, to tell a lie
T2-1055.ex: 아무리 힘들어도 친구에게 거짓말하면 안 돼요.
T2-1055.x: No matter how hard it is, you shouldn't lie to your friends.

T2-1056.x: In case of rain, the event will be canceled.
T2-1056.t: Pattern -(으)ㄴ/는 경우(에) means 'in case, when': 아픈 경우에 연락하세요.

T2-1057.x: I have good relationships with my coworkers.

T2-1058.ex: 서울은 다른 도시보다 생활비가 많이 들어요.
T2-1058.x: Living expenses in Seoul are higher than in other cities.
T2-1058.e: Literally 'living cost'. -비 = cost or fee: 교통비, 식비.
T2-1058.t: Costs 'go into' something with 들다: 생활비가 많이 들어요.

T2-1059.x: As evening came, the trees' shadows grew longer.
T2-1059.e: Probably related to 그리다 'to draw' and 그림 'picture'.

T2-1060.x: This machine is very easy to use.

T2-1061.ex: 저는 다음 달에 한국에서 일할 기회가 생겼어요.
T2-1061.x: I got a chance to work in Korea next month.
T2-1061.t: You 'catch' chances with 잡다 (기회를 잡다) and miss them with 놓치다.

T2-1062.x: These pants are a little short.

T2-1063.ex: 이 산의 높이는 천 미터쯤 돼요.
T2-1063.x: This mountain is about 1,000 meters high.
T2-1063.e: 높다 'high' + -이. Also an adverb: 높이 날다 'fly high'.
T2-1063.t: Use 키 for a person's height; 높이 is for buildings, mountains and objects.

T2-1064.t: Weight 'comes out' with 나가다: 무게가 많이 나가요 'it's heavy'.

T2-1065.ex: 너무 피곤해서 나머지 숙제는 내일 할게요.
T2-1065.x: I'm so tired, so I'll do the rest of my homework tomorrow.
T2-1065.e: Related to 남다 'to remain' — whatever is left over.

T2-1066.x: The content of this book is a bit difficult.

T2-1067.x: The puppy is sniffing the ground.
T2-1067.t: 냄새 is neutral or unpleasant; for a pleasant scent, use 향기. Smell something actively with 맡다.

T2-1068.forms: 냄새가 나요 · 냄새가 났어요; N에서 냄새가 나다
T2-1068.m: to smell, to give off a smell
T2-1068.ex: 엄마가 요리하셔서 부엌에서 맛있는 냄새가 나요.
T2-1068.x: Mom is cooking, so something smells delicious in the kitchen.
T2-1068.t: Mark the source with 에서: 방에서 이상한 냄새가 나요 'The room smells weird.'

T2-1069.x: This song has a warm feeling to it.

T2-1070.x: I gave the presentation instead of my sick friend.
T2-1070.e: Literally 'replacing body' — standing in someone's place.
T2-1070.t: N 대신 means 'instead of N'; V-는 대신 often means 'in exchange for doing'.

T2-1071.ex: 선생님 덕분에 한국어 실력이 많이 늘었어요.
T2-1071.x: Thanks to my teacher, my Korean has improved a lot.
T2-1071.e: Literally 'a share of virtue' — benefiting from someone's goodness.
T2-1071.t: Use 덕분에 for good results; for bad ones use 때문에 or 탓에.

T2-1072.x: I couldn't go to school because of a cold.
T2-1072.t: Use 때문에 for reasons, but not with requests or suggestions; use -(으)니까 there instead.

T2-1073.x: My grandmother lives in a small country village.
T2-1073.t: 마을 is a village or small community; 동네 is your neighborhood, even in a big city.

T2-1074.ex: 수업 시간에는 선생님 말씀을 잘 들으세요.
T2-1074.x: Listen carefully to what the teacher says during class.
T2-1074.e: Honorific and humble form of 말 'words'.
T2-1074.t: 말씀하시다 honors the speaker; 말씀드리다 humbly describes yourself speaking to someone senior.

T2-1075.ex: 올해 제 목표는 토픽 3급을 따는 거예요.
T2-1075.x: My goal this year is to get TOPIK Level 3.
T2-1075.e: Literally 'eye mark' — the target your eye aims at.
T2-1075.t: Set a goal with 세우다 (목표를 세우다) and reach it with 이루다.

T2-1076.x: I'm very interested in Korean culture.
T2-1076.e: Literally 'transformed by writing' — civilization and culture.

T2-1077.x: Please tell me how to get good at Korean.
T2-1077.t: Pattern V-는 방법 means 'how to V': 김치 만드는 방법 'how to make kimchi'.

T2-1078.ex: 이 부분이 잘 이해가 안 돼요.
T2-1078.x: I don't really understand this part.
T2-1078.t: 대부분 'most' adds 대 'big': 대부분의 사람들 'most people'.

T2-1079.ex: 이건 우리 둘만의 비밀이니까 아무한테도 말하지 마세요.
T2-1079.x: This is a secret between us two, so don't tell anyone.
T2-1079.e: Both syllables mean 'hidden, close' — a secret.
T2-1079.t: Keep a secret with 지키다: 비밀을 지켜 주세요 'Please keep it secret.'

T2-1080.ex: 사실은 저도 그 영화를 아직 안 봤어요.
T2-1080.x: Actually, I haven't seen that movie yet either.
T2-1080.t: 사실은 at the start of a sentence means 'actually, to be honest'.

T2-1081.ex: 오늘은 몸 상태가 별로 안 좋아요.
T2-1081.x: I'm not in very good shape today.

T2-1082.x: Try drawing a straight line on the paper.
T2-1082.e: Homonym: 선 also means 'goodness' and a matchmaking date (선을 보다).
T2-1082.t: 선을 넘다 'to cross the line' means to go too far, just like in English.

T2-1083.x: I love my mom more than anyone in the world.
T2-1083.e: Literally 'upon the world' — the world we live in.

T2-1084.x: Yesterday I heard the news that my friend is getting married.
T2-1084.e: Literally 'waning and growing' — word of how things are going.
T2-1084.t: 소식 is personal news or word from someone; 뉴스 is news from the media.

T2-1085.ex: 제 소원은 세계 여행을 하는 거예요.
T2-1085.x: My wish is to travel around the world.
T2-1085.t: Make a wish with 빌다: 생일 케이크 앞에서 소원을 빌어요.

T2-1086.x: Yesterday I sent a package home from the post office.

T2-1087.x: I was sweating, so I wiped my face with a handkerchief.

T2-1088.ex: 저는 매일 아침 운동하는 습관이 있어요.
T2-1088.x: I have a habit of exercising every morning.
T2-1088.t: Pronounced [습꽌]. 버릇 often means a bad habit, while 습관 is neutral.

T2-1089.ex: 오늘 새 학기 시간표가 학교 홈페이지에 나왔어요.
T2-1089.x: The new semester's class schedule was posted on the school website today.

T2-1090.ex: 은행에 갈 때 신분증을 꼭 가져가세요.
T2-1090.x: Be sure to bring your ID when you go to the bank.
T2-1090.e: Literally 'status proof'. -증 = certificate or card: 학생증, 운전면허증.

T2-1091.ex: 어제 친구랑 재미있는 얘기를 많이 했어요.
T2-1091.x: Yesterday I talked about a lot of fun stuff with a friend.
T2-1091.t: 얘기 is casual and spoken; 이야기 is preferred in writing.

T2-1092.ex: 저는 세 가지 언어를 할 수 있어요.

T2-1093.x: Excuse me, but how old is your grandfather?
T2-1093.e: Literally 'years and age'; the respectful word for an elder's age.
T2-1093.t: Use 연세 instead of 나이 for elders: 연세가 어떻게 되세요? is the polite way to ask.

T2-1094.ex: 선생님이 이해하기 쉬운 예를 하나 들어 주셨어요.
T2-1094.x: The teacher gave us an example that was easy to understand.
T2-1094.e: Best learned in the set phrase 예를 들면, 'for example'.
T2-1094.t: Don't confuse it with 예 meaning 'yes'; to give an example is 예를 들다.

T2-1095.ex: 저는 다음 주에 부산에 갈 예정이에요.
T2-1095.x: I'm planning to go to Busan next week.
T2-1095.t: Use the pattern -(으)ㄹ 예정이에요 to say something is scheduled or planned.

T2-1096.ex: 친구와 작은 오해가 생겨서 마음이 안 좋아요.
T2-1096.x: I had a small misunderstanding with my friend, so I feel bad.
T2-1096.t: A misunderstanding 'happens' with 오해가 생기다 and is cleared up with 오해를 풀다.

T2-1097.ex: 편지 봉투에 우표를 붙이고 우체국에 갔어요.
T2-1097.x: I put a stamp on the envelope and went to the post office.

T2-1098.ex: 여행 중에 친구에게 예쁜 엽서를 보냈어요.
T2-1098.x: I sent my friend a pretty postcard while traveling.
T2-1098.e: Literally 'leaf writing', a message on a single thin sheet.
T2-1098.t: Pronounced [엽써]: the ㅅ becomes tense after the ㅂ batchim.

T2-1099.ex: 오늘은 시험 문제가 쉬워서 정말 운이 좋았어요.
T2-1099.x: The test questions were easy today, so I was really lucky.
T2-1099.t: Say 운이 좋다 for 'lucky' and 운이 없다 or 운이 나쁘다 for 'unlucky'.

T2-1100.ex: 이 호텔은 위치가 좋아서 지하철역에서 가까워요.
T2-1100.x: This hotel has a good location, so it's close to the subway station.
T2-1100.e: Literally 'the place where something is put'.

T2-1101.x: I'm not sure what this word means.
T2-1101.t: 뜻 is the everyday native synonym; 의미 also covers 'significance', as in 의미가 있다.

T2-1102.ex: 이 문제에 대해 여러분의 의견을 말해 주세요.
T2-1102.x: Please share your opinions on this issue.

T2-1103.ex: 저는 매일 밤 자기 전에 일기를 써요.
T2-1103.x: I write in my diary every night before bed.
T2-1103.t: Keep a diary with 일기를 쓰다; a different 일기 means 'weather', as in 일기 예보.

T2-1104.ex: 이 박물관의 입장료는 어른 오천 원이에요.
T2-1104.x: Admission to this museum is 5,000 won for adults.
T2-1104.t: Pronounced [입짱뇨]: ㄹ turns into ㄴ after ㅇ.

T2-1105.ex: 아이가 생일 선물로 장난감을 받고 좋아했어요.
T2-1105.x: The child got a toy as a birthday present and was happy.
T2-1105.e: 장난 'play, mischief' + 감 'material', so literally 'stuff to play with'.

T2-1106.ex: 이 휴대폰의 장점은 가볍고 싸다는 거예요.
T2-1106.x: The good thing about this phone is that it's light and cheap.
T2-1106.e: Literally 'long point', where you measure up well.
T2-1106.t: Pronounced [장쩜]; it pairs naturally with its opposite 단점.

T2-1107.ex: 제 단점은 성격이 너무 급하다는 거예요.
T2-1107.x: My weakness is that I'm too impatient.
T2-1107.e: Literally 'short point', where you fall short.

T2-1108.ex: 이 계획에서 가장 좋은 점이 뭐라고 생각해요?
T2-1108.x: What do you think is the best thing about this plan?
T2-1108.t: After numbers it means 'points' on a test: 90점 is 'ninety points'.

T2-1109.x: I found a lot of travel information online.

T2-1110.ex: 어제 들은 노래 제목이 뭔지 알아요?
T2-1110.x: Do you know the title of the song we heard yesterday?

T2-1111.ex: 그 식당 앞에는 항상 줄이 길어요.
T2-1111.x: There's always a long line in front of that restaurant.
T2-1111.e: One word for anything long and thin: a rope, a string, a line of text, a queue.
T2-1111.t: A long line is 줄이 길다; 첫 줄 = 'the first line'.

T2-1112.forms: 줄을 서요 · 줄을 섰어요 · 줄을 설 거예요 · 줄을 서세요
T2-1112.m: to stand in line, to line up
T2-1112.ex: 유명한 빵집 앞에서 한 시간 동안 줄을 섰어요.
T2-1112.x: I stood in line for an hour in front of a famous bakery.
T2-1112.t: In casual speech the particle often drops: 줄 서요, 줄 서세요.

T2-1113.x: I'll return the book I borrowed last time today.
T2-1113.t: Usually used with 에 as a time word: 지난번에 'last time'.

T2-1114.m: turn; order, sequence; table of contents
T2-1114.x: Next is Minsu's turn. Please get ready.
T2-1114.t: Don't confuse it with the homonym 차례 meaning the holiday ancestral rite on Seollal and Chuseok.

T2-1115.ex: 오늘은 평소보다 한 시간 일찍 일어났어요.
T2-1115.x: Today I got up an hour earlier than usual.
T2-1115.e: Literally 'ordinary and plain', your normal everyday state.
T2-1115.t: Mostly used as 평소에 'usually', 평소처럼 'as usual', or 평소보다 'than usual'.

T2-1116.ex: 선물을 받은 동생의 표정이 아주 밝았어요.
T2-1116.x: My little brother's face lit up when he got the present.
T2-1116.t: 표정 is the look on your face; 표현 is expressing something in words or art.

T2-1117.ex: 한국어로 제 마음을 표현하기가 아직 어려워요.
T2-1117.x: It's still hard for me to express my feelings in Korean.

T2-1118.ex: 이번 주말에 학교에서 큰 행사가 있어요.
T2-1118.x: There's a big event at school this weekend.
T2-1118.t: Stores also use 행사 for a sale or promotion: 할인 행사 'discount event'.

T2-1119.ex: 동생이 노래 대회에 나가서 일 등을 했어요.
T2-1119.x: My younger sibling entered a singing contest and won first place.
T2-1119.t: Enter a contest with 대회에 나가다; 말하기 대회 is a speech contest.

T2-1120.ex: 이 영화는 외국에서 큰 상을 여러 번 탔어요.
T2-1120.x: This movie has won major awards abroad several times.
T2-1120.t: Homonym alert: another 상 means 'table', as in 밥상; context makes it clear.

T2-1121.forms: 상을 받아요 · 상을 받았어요 · 상을 받을 거예요 · 상을 받은 (+noun)
T2-1121.m: to win a prize, to receive an award
T2-1121.ex: 제 친구가 글쓰기 대회에서 상을 받았어요.
T2-1121.x: My friend won a prize in a writing contest.
T2-1121.e: Literally 'to receive a prize'; 상을 타다 means the same.

T2-1122.forms: Use with Sino numbers: 1회, 2회, 3회 (일 회, 이 회, 삼 회)
T2-1122.x: This class meets twice a week.
T2-1122.e: The formal, written counterpart of 번; seen on schedules, labels and TV episodes.
T2-1122.t: In everyday speech say 두 번 'twice'; 2회 sounds formal and appears mostly in writing.

T2-9001.x: I didn't hear the alarm, so I overslept.
T2-9001.t: Set an alarm: 알람을 맞추다; turn it off: 알람을 끄다. Snoozing again and again is a very relatable morning struggle.

T2-9002.x: Even when it's cold, I drink iced americanos.
T2-9002.e: From Italian 'americano' — espresso diluted with water.
T2-9002.t: Iced americano is often shortened to 아아 (casual). The joke 얼죽아 (얼어 죽어도 아이스 아메리카노) means 'iced americano even if I freeze to death'.

T2-9003.x: On the hottest days of summer, we go out for samgyetang.
T2-9003.e: Literally 'ginseng chicken soup': a whole young chicken stuffed with rice, ginseng and jujube.
T2-9003.t: Eaten on 복날 (초복, 중복, 말복), three 'dog days' spread over the hottest stretch of summer, to beat the heat with heat (이열치열).

T2-9004.x: A birthday table isn't complete without japchae.
T2-9004.e: Literally 'mixed vegetables'. It was first a vegetable dish; glass noodles (당면) were added later.
T2-9004.t: A must at birthdays, holidays and parties.

T2-9005.x: At the tteokbokki place, we ordered sundae too.
T2-9005.e: Word of uncertain origin (one theory links it to a Manchu word for blood sausage). It's pig intestine stuffed with glass noodles and pork blood, then steamed.
T2-9005.t: Not the ice-cream sundae! 떡튀순 (떡볶이 + 튀김 + 순대) is the classic snack-bar combo.

T2-9006.x: On cold days, fish cake broth is the best.
T2-9006.e: 어 'fish' + 묵 'jelly, curd' — pressed fish paste.
T2-9006.t: Many people still say 오뎅 (from Japanese 'oden'); 어묵 is the standard word. Street stalls serve skewers with free broth.

T2-9007.ex: 오징어 튀김을 떡볶이 국물에 찍어 먹어요.
T2-9007.x: I dip squid fritters in the tteokbokki sauce.
T2-9007.t: Snack-bar 튀김 includes squid, sweet potato, dumplings and 김말이 (glass noodles rolled in seaweed).

T2-9008.ex: 비 오는 날에는 파전에 막걸리가 생각나요.
T2-9008.x: On rainy days, I crave pajeon with makgeolli.
T2-9008.e: Native word: 막 'roughly, just' + 거르다 'to strain' — roughly strained rice wine.
T2-9008.t: Pronounced [막껄리]. Milky and lightly sparkling; it's often drunk from small bowls. Rainy days and 파전 (green onion pancake) go with it.

T2-9009.x: Shall we all raise our glasses and make a toast?
T2-9009.e: Literally 'dry the cup' — drain your glass.
T2-9009.t: Say 건배! when clinking glasses. With elders, hold your glass with two hands and turn your head slightly away when you drink.

T2-9010.e: Probably from Japanese 'champon', a Nagasaki noodle dish; the Korean version became red and spicy.
T2-9010.t: 짜장면 or 짬뽕 is a classic dilemma, so some places sell 짬짜면, half of each. Casually, 짬뽕 also means 'a jumble, a mix'.

T2-9011.x: Every weekend I go to the neighborhood bathhouse with my father.
T2-9011.t: Pronounced [모굑탕]. Shower and wash thoroughly before getting into the hot tubs.

T2-9012.ex: 날씨 좋은 날에는 한강에서 치킨을 시켜 먹어요.
T2-9012.x: On nice days we order chicken and eat it by the Han River.
T2-9012.e: The hanja 漢 is usually explained as a way of writing the native word 한 'big'. It is not 韓 'Korea'.
T2-9012.t: Picnics in the riverside parks (한강공원), with chicken delivered right to the riverbank, are a Seoul classic.

T2-9013.ex: 제가 제일 좋아하는 그룹은 멤버가 일곱 명이에요.
T2-9013.x: My favorite group has seven members.
T2-9013.t: 보이 그룹 and 걸 그룹 are boy and girl groups. 그룹 also means a business conglomerate.

T2-9014.ex: 이 그룹에서 노래를 제일 잘하는 멤버가 누구예요?
T2-9014.x: Who is the best singer in this group?
T2-9014.t: Group roles include 리더 (leader), 메인 보컬 (main vocalist) and 막내 (the youngest member).

T2-9015.ex: 영화 보기 전에 팝콘이랑 콜라를 샀어요.
T2-9015.x: Before the movie, I bought popcorn and a cola.
T2-9015.t: Korean cinemas sell sweet caramel popcorn (캐러멜 팝콘) and 반반 'half-and-half', half caramel and half salted.

T2-9016.ex: 마이크 소리가 너무 작아서 잘 안 들려요.
T2-9016.x: The mic is too quiet, so I can't hear well.
T2-9016.t: At a 노래방, 마이크를 잡다 'to grab the mic' means to take your turn singing.

T2-9017.x: When the song ended, everyone clapped.
T2-9017.t: Pronounced [박쑤]. Clap is 박수를 치다; hosts say 박수 부탁드립니다 'a round of applause, please'.

T2-9018.m: triangle gimbap (triangular rice ball wrapped in seaweed)
T2-9018.x: I bought a triangle gimbap at the convenience store and ate it.
T2-9018.t: Pronounced [삼각낌밥]: the ㄱ of 김 becomes tense after the ㄱ of 각. To open one, pull the numbered tabs 1-2-3 in order so the film slides out and the seaweed stays crisp.

T2-9019.x: Pour hot water into the cup noodles and wait just three minutes.
T2-9019.t: Pronounced [컴나면]: the ㄹ becomes ㄴ after ㅂ, and the ㅂ then becomes ㅁ before that ㄴ. Convenience stores have hot-water dispensers and a counter, so people often eat it right there.

T2-9020.x: Please put empty cans out for recycling.
T2-9020.t: In apartment recycling areas, cans go in the bin marked 캔류 'cans'. Common combos: 캔 커피 'canned coffee', 캔 맥주 'canned beer'.

T2-9021.ex: 위층에서 밤마다 쿵쿵 뛰는 소리가 나요.
T2-9021.x: Every night there's a thumping sound of someone running upstairs.
T2-9021.e: Native 위 'above' + 층 'floor, story'. Opposite: 아래층 'downstairs'.
T2-9021.t: Spelled 위층, never 윗층: no ㅅ is added before an aspirated sound like ㅊ. Noise from the flat above (층간 소음 'between-floor noise') is a classic cause of neighbor disputes in Korean apartments.

T2-9022.m: to give birth to, to have (a baby); to lay (eggs)
T2-9022.x: My older sister had a beautiful baby girl last month.
T2-9022.e: Native verb. It is the mirror of 태어나다: the mother 낳다 'gives birth', the baby 태어나다 'is born'.
T2-9022.t: Pronounced [나타]: ㅎ and ㄷ merge into ㅌ; before a vowel the ㅎ is silent, so 낳아요 sounds like [나아요]. That makes it sound just like 나아요 from 낫다 'to get better'.

T2-9023.x: As soon as we got to the campsite, we pitched the tent.
T2-9023.t: Pitch a tent: 텐트를 치다. This 치다 is the one for putting up or hanging something (as in 커튼을 치다), not 'to hit'. Taking it down is 텐트를 걷다.

T2-9024.x: I bought a new swimsuit to go to the beach.
T2-9024.t: Many Koreans wear a 래시가드 'rash guard' at the beach for sun protection, and indoor pools usually require a swim cap (수영모) as well.

T2-9025.x: On the weekend I went to the ballpark with a friend and cheered.
T2-9025.t: Korean ballparks are known for loud organized cheering led by cheerleaders, a chant for every player, and fans eating fried chicken with beer in the stands.

T2-9026.ex: 배경이 예뻐서 셀카를 한 장 찍었어요.
T2-9026.x: The background was pretty, so I took a selfie.
T2-9026.e: Konglish: short for 셀프 카메라 'self camera', not from English 'selfie'.
T2-9026.t: Take a selfie: 셀카를 찍다. A selfie stick is 셀카봉.

T2-9027.ex: 프라이팬을 충분히 달군 후에 고기를 구우세요.
T2-9027.x: Heat the frying pan well, then cook the meat.
T2-9027.t: Recipes often begin with 프라이팬에 기름을 두르다 'coat the pan with oil'.

T2-9028.x: Pork belly tastes best wrapped in lettuce.
T2-9028.e: Usually traced to Sino-Korean 생채 'raw vegetable'; today it is felt as a native word.
T2-9028.t: At Korean BBQ you wrap meat, garlic and 쌈장 (dipping paste) in a lettuce leaf; this kind of wrap is called 쌈, so a lettuce wrap is 상추쌈.

T2-9029.ex: 저는 땅콩 알레르기가 있어서 늘 조심해요.
T2-9029.x: I have a peanut allergy, so I'm always careful.
T2-9029.e: 땅 'ground, earth' + 콩 'bean': the bean that grows underground.
T2-9029.t: Peanut butter is 땅콩버터. Roasted peanuts are a common snack served with beer (안주).

T2-9030.ex: 옛날이야기에는 꾀 많은 여우가 자주 나와요.
T2-9030.x: Clever foxes often appear in old folktales.
T2-9030.e: Native word. Korean folklore has the 구미호, a nine-tailed fox spirit that turns into a beautiful woman.
T2-9030.t: Calling someone 여우 or saying 여우 같다 means they are sly, or cleverly charming; it can be teasing or a real criticism depending on tone.

T2-9031.ex: 봄이 되면 마당에 꽃을 심을 거예요.
T2-9031.x: When spring comes, I'm going to plant flowers in the yard.
T2-9031.e: Native verb. Proverb: 콩 심은 데 콩 나고 팥 심은 데 팥 난다 'where you plant beans, beans grow' — you reap what you sow.
T2-9031.t: Pronounced [심따]: the ㄷ becomes tense after the stem-final ㅁ. April 5 is 식목일 'Arbor Day', the traditional day for planting trees.

T2-9032.x: The baby's eyes are round and really cute.
T2-9032.e: Related to 둥글다 'round'; the bright vowel ㅗ gives a smaller, cuter feel. The noun is 동그라미 'circle'.
T2-9032.t: Pronounced [동그라타]: ㅎ and ㄷ merge into ㅌ. As an ㅎ irregular, the ㅎ drops before endings: 동그란 얼굴 'a round face'.

T2-9033.ex: 저는 동그란 접시보다 네모 접시가 좋아요.
T2-9033.x: I like square plates better than round ones.
T2-9033.e: Native: 네 'four' + 모 'corner, edge'. Likewise 세모 'triangle' (세 'three').
T2-9033.t: The adjective is 네모나다: 네모난 상자 'a square box'. Everyday 네모 covers squares and rectangles alike; 정사각형 and 직사각형 are the math terms.

T2-9034.x: My younger sibling plays drums in the school band.
T2-9034.t: Play drums: 드럼을 치다, the same verb as for piano and guitar. Traditional Korean drums are 북 and 장구.

T2-9035.ex: 그 얘기를 듣고 다들 하하 웃었어요.
T2-9035.x: Everyone laughed 'ha-ha' when they heard that story.
T2-9035.e: 의성어 (sound word) for open, hearty laughter. Its dark-vowel partner 허허 is a deeper, calmer laugh, typical of older men.
T2-9035.t: In text messages, ㅎㅎ is a soft, friendly laugh, while ㅋㅋ is closer to 'lol'.

T2-9036.x: The neighbor's puppy barks 'woof woof' every night.
T2-9036.e: 의성어 (sound word) imitating a dog's bark.
T2-9036.t: 멍멍이 is baby talk for 'doggy'. The verb for barking is 짖다.

T2-9037.forms: 야옹 + 하고 울다 · pet name: 야옹이
T2-9037.ex: 고양이가 배가 고픈지 야옹 하고 울어요.
T2-9037.x: The cat is meowing, maybe because it's hungry.
T2-9037.e: 의성어 (sound word) imitating a cat's cry.
T2-9037.t: 야옹이 'kitty' is a common pet name. Online, cat lovers say 냥이 for a cat (casual).

T2-9038.m: knock knock (on a door); drip drip
T2-9038.x: Someone is knocking on the door.
T2-9038.e: 의성어 (sound word) for light tapping or small drops falling. For drops, the dark-vowel partner 뚝뚝 means bigger, heavier drops.
T2-9038.t: Don't confuse it with 똑똑하다 'to be smart', which is an unrelated word.

T2-9039.x: The baby is happily munching on her baby food.
T2-9039.e: Both 의성어 and 의태어: the sound and look of someone eating with relish.
T2-9039.t: Parents tell toddlers 냠냠 먹자! 'Let's eat up!'. Adults use it in cute food posts online.

T2-9040.x: The stars are twinkling in the night sky.
T2-9040.e: 의태어 (manner word) for small lights flickering on and off. Its dark-vowel partner 번쩍번쩍 is for big, strong flashes, like lightning.
T2-9040.t: Pronounced [반짝빤짝]: the second ㅂ becomes tense after ㄱ. Verbs: 반짝이다 and 반짝거리다 'to twinkle, to sparkle'.

T2-9041.m: to be unwell, to be sick (honorific)
T2-9041.x: My grandmother has been quite unwell lately.
T2-9041.e: 편찮다 is short for 편하지 않다 'not comfortable', plus the honorific -(으)시-.
T2-9041.t: Pronounced [편차느시다]: ㅎ is silent before a vowel. The plain word is 아프다; use 편찮으시다 for parents, grandparents and other elders, never for yourself.

T2-9042.forms: 뵙겠습니다 · 뵙고 · vowel endings use 뵈다: 봬요 · 뵀어요 · 뵐게요
T2-9042.m: to see, to meet (humble, someone senior)
T2-9042.x: Professor, I'll come and see you next week.
T2-9042.e: Humble verb: you lower yourself when meeting someone higher in status. Before vowel endings it switches to 뵈다 (뵈어요 → 봬요).
T2-9042.t: Pronounced [뵙따]: 다 turns tense after ㅂ. The plain words are 보다 and 만나다; use 뵙다 for meeting teachers, bosses or elders, as in 처음 뵙겠습니다 'Nice to meet you'.

T2-9043.m: home, house (honorific); you (to a stranger, distant)
T2-9043.e: From hanja 宅 'house', the respectful word for someone else's home.
T2-9043.t: The plain word is 집; say 댁 for the homes of elders, teachers or customers, but 저희 집 for your own. Used as 'you' (댁은 누구세요?) it sounds distant or even rude.

T2-9044.x: Excuse me, may I have your name?
T2-9044.e: Literally 'surname and title': the respectful word for a person's full name.
T2-9044.t: The plain word is 이름; use 성함 when asking elders, customers or anyone you don't know well. For your own name always say 이름.

T2-9045.e: Native Korean honorific word for 'meal', with no hanja.
T2-9045.t: The plain word is 밥; use 진지 for grandparents and other elders, with 드시다 or 잡수시다 instead of 먹다.

T2-9046.x: Next Saturday is my father's birthday.
T2-9046.e: Literally 'birth day': 生 'birth' + 辰 'day, time'.
T2-9046.t: The plain word is 생일; use 생신 for parents, grandparents and other elders, and congratulate them with 생신 축하드려요.

T2-9047.m: to take, to bring along (someone of equal or lower status)
T2-9047.x: On the weekend I took my child to the park.
T2-9047.e: Native verb that is rarely used on its own; it lives on in 데리고, 데리러 and the compounds 데려가다 and 데려오다.
T2-9047.t: Use 데리다 for children, friends and pets. For parents, teachers and other elders, switch to the honorific 모시다: 할머니를 모시고 갔어요.

T2-9048.ex: 계좌 번호 알려 주시면 바로 보내 드릴게요.
T2-9048.x: If you tell me your account number, I'll send it right away.
T2-9048.t: Always give the bank name with it: 은행 이름하고 계좌 번호. The digits are read one by one with Sino-Korean numbers.

T2-9049.ex: 신용 카드 대신 체크카드를 쓰니까 돈을 덜 쓰게 돼요.
T2-9049.x: Since I use a debit card instead of a credit card, I end up spending less.
T2-9049.e: Konglish from English 'check' + 'card'; in English it's a 'debit card'.
T2-9049.t: The money comes straight out of your bank account, so you can't spend more than you have, unlike a 신용 카드. Banks usually issue one when you open an account.

T2-9050.e: A stretched form of 와 'wow', with 우 added for extra excitement.
T2-9050.t: Bright and a little childlike, but adults use it too when genuinely impressed.

T2-9051.forms: 깜짝이야! · 아, 깜짝이야! · polite: 깜짝 놀랐어요
T2-9051.m: you scared me!, oh, you startled me!
T2-9051.x: Oh, you scared me! When did you come in?
T2-9051.e: 깜짝 'with a start' + -이야 'it is': literally '(that was) a start!'
T2-9051.t: Blurted out on reflex, even to older people; to sound more polite afterwards, add 깜짝 놀랐어요 'I was startled'.

T2-9052.forms: 예를 들면 … · 예를 들어(서) · 예를 들자면
T2-9052.ex: 저는 운동을 좋아해요. 예를 들면 수영이나 테니스요.
T2-9052.x: I like sports. For example, swimming or tennis.
T2-9052.e: 예 'example' + 를 + 들다 'to hold up, give' + -면 'if': 'if I give an example'.
T2-9052.t: 예를 들어 is equally common, especially in writing and presentations.

T2-9053.forms: casual: 있잖아 · polite: 있잖아요 · 저기, 있잖아요…
T2-9053.m: you know, …; listen, … (bringing up a topic)
T2-9053.x: You know what? I'm getting married next month.
T2-9053.e: 있다 'to exist' + -잖아요 'you know': literally 'there's (this thing), you know'.
T2-9053.t: Pronounced [읻짜나요]. Grabs attention before news or a delicate topic, or reminds: 그 카페 있잖아요, 거기서 만나요.
rel: to be, to exist; to have

T2-9054.x: Well, the thing is… I actually forgot.
T2-9054.e: Contraction of 그것이 'that (thing)' + the subject marker 이.
T2-9054.t: Used when you hesitate before explaining something awkward. Literal use is common too: 그게 뭐예요? 'What's that?'

T2-9055.forms: casual short form of 그런데 · starts a sentence
T2-9055.m: but; by the way (spoken form of 그런데)
T2-9055.x: By the way, what time is tomorrow's get-together?
T2-9055.e: Spoken contraction of 그런데 'but; by the way'.
T2-9055.t: Very common in speech and texts, even in polite 요 sentences. In writing or formal speech, use 그런데 or 하지만.

T2-9056.forms: 되게 + adjective/verb: 되게 커요, 되게 잘해요
T2-9056.x: The tteokbokki at this place is really good.
T2-9056.t: Casual spoken word, often pronounced [디게]. In writing, use 매우 or 아주.

T2-9057.forms: 완전 + adjective/verb: 완전 좋아요 · standard adverb: 완전히
T2-9057.x: The movie I saw yesterday was so much fun.
T2-9057.e: Literally 'complete and whole'; as a noun it means 'completeness'.
T2-9057.t: Putting 완전 straight before an adjective is casual, youthful speech. In writing, use 완전히 or 아주.

T2-9058.m: I know, right?; exactly; I wonder (agreeing)
T2-9058.x: I know, right? It's really hot today.
T2-9058.e: From 그러다 'to be so' + the ending -게, roughly 'that's just it'.
T2-9058.t: Used to agree with what someone just said. It can also mean 'I wonder': 그러게요, 왜 안 올까요? 'I wonder why they're not coming.'

T2-9059.x: This swimming pool is 50 meters long.
T2-9059.t: Use Sino-Korean numbers with it: 오십 미터, not 쉰 미터.

T2-9060.ex: 물은 하루에 2리터 정도 마시는 게 좋대요.
T2-9060.x: They say it's good to drink about 2 liters of water a day.
T2-9060.t: Decimals are read with 점 'point': 1.5리터 = 일 점 오 리터.
